We present FuzzAgent, a multi-agent system that builds and evolves a complete fuzzing campaign from a source tree alone. Specialized agents acquire project knowledge and repair campaign artifacts automatically. Hierarchical coverage diagnosis localizes blockers from modules down to branches, and dependency-aware generation converts them into harnesses with the required API lifecycle. Crash validation recovers runtime object states to distinguish harness misuse from library bugs.
  We evaluate FuzzAgent on 20 real-world C/C++ libraries against five state-of-the-art baselines (OSS-Fuzz, OSS-Fuzz-Gen, PromptFuzz, PromeFuzz, and ProteusFuzz). FuzzAgent completes the full fuzzing lifecycle for all 20 libraries without human intervention at $3.17 per library. On the 20 libraries, it reaches 179619 branches, exceeding OSS-Fuzz, PromptFuzz, ProteusFuzz, PromeFuzz, and OSS-Fuzz-Gen by 45.1%, 73.2%, 87.7%, 92.1%, and 191.2%, respectively. FuzzAgent also identifies 102 new library bugs, 90 of which have already been acknowledged or fixed by upstream maintainers.

Software Engineering.title: Lost in the Latent Space: How Code Embeddings Represent Functional Intent and Implementation Fidelity
Software Engineering.summary: Code embedding models have become a key building block for many software engineering applications, yet their internal representations remain poorly understood. Existing evaluations tend to focus on downstream task performance, offering limited insight into whether a single embedding can support both functional abstraction and implementation-sensitive analysis. To address this gap, we present a large-scale empirical study of 14 state-of-the-art code embedding models. We evaluate their representational behavior through three complementary analyses: supervised probing for functional abstraction and implementation fidelity, zero-shot retrieval experiments to assess geometric similarity, and controlled perturbation experiments that measure embedding responses to semantics-preserving code transformations. The results reveal a consistent abstraction-fidelity tension: models that better preserve stylistic and structural signals tend to do so at the expense of semantic generalization, while models with similar retrieval performance can nevertheless respond very differently to the same implementation changes. Overall, our findings suggest that a single universal code representation remains out of reach, motivating more representation-aware evaluation, selection, and deployment of code embedding models in software engineering.

Software Engineering.title: BlueCodeAgent: A Blue Teaming Agent Powered by Automated Red Teaming for CodeGen AI
Software Engineering.summary: Existing research on CodeGen AI security mainly focuses on red teaming, which aims to uncover vulnerabilities and risks in AI-generated code. However, progress on the blue teaming side remains limited, as effective defenses require a deep security analysis of given tasks and edge cases. To fill in this gap, we propose BlueCodeAgent, an end-to-end blue teaming agent powered by automated red teaming. Our red teaming component generates diverse risky instances, providing effective edge cases and guidance for the subsequent blue teaming process. Our blue teaming agent then conducts multi-level defense, leveraging these red teaming examples to detect previously seen and unseen risk scenarios through constitution summarization and dynamic code analysis. Our evaluation across four representative code-related tasks (bias instruction detection, malicious instruction detection, vulnerable code detection, and prompt injection detection) shows that BlueCodeAgent achieves significant gains over diverse baselines. In particular, for vulnerability detection tasks, BlueCodeAgent integrates dynamic analysis to effectively reduce false positives, a challenging problem as base models tend to be over-conservative. Overall, with GPT-4o as the base model, BlueCodeAgent achieves an average F1 score improvement of 14.7% across four tasks compared to directly prompting the model, attributed to its ability to summarize actionable constitutions and perform dynamic analysis. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/1mocat/BlueCodeAgent.

Software Engineering.title: When Static Reachability Says No: Checking Joern-Based Negative Verdicts for Python Against Execution
Software Engineering.summary: A negative reachability verdict removes a finding from human review. We check such verdicts against execution. Our pipeline, SourceLens, maps Semgrep findings to a Python program's call graph, whose edges a query takes from the calls that Joern links in its code property graph. We ran two command-line programs from the PyCG macro-benchmark, in which the benchmark's manual call graph and Joern disagree, under coverage and recorded the calls between their functions. On these edges, 123 functions of asciinema are unreachable from the program's entry points. The project's own integration script executes 86 of them, and all our runs 113. In Sublist3r, 19 of 24 are executed. The latest Joern release gives the same verdicts. The missing calls go through values, such as classes and functions passed around, or have no call expression, as in with blocks and property reads. In asciinema, four missing edges make 50 of the 113 executed functions reachable. The manual call graphs also lack observed calls, in asciinema many of them property reads and with blocks, which the benchmark may not count as calls. A rule that turns negative verdicts into unknown recovers 62 of the 113 and 15 of the 19, mostly through dunder and private method names. It recovers 0 of the 5 security findings with a negative verdict, all in executed functions. Its selectivity cannot be measured, as only 10 and 5 negative verdicts were not executed, and under library entry-point models it degrades every negative verdict.

Software Engineering.title: ASTOR: Multi-Task Code Reinforcement Learning via Utility-Driven Coordination
Software Engineering.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has proven effective at post-training LLMs for coding, yet deploying separate task-specific specialists incurs costs that scale with the number of tasks, motivating a unified multi-task RL (MTRL) approach. However, existing MTRL methods treat all coding tasks uniformly, relying on fixed data curricula under a shared optimization strategy, ultimately limiting the effectiveness of multi-task training. To address these limitations, we propose ASTOR, a multi-tASk code reinforcement learning framework via uTility-driven coORdination. Centered on task utility, a signal capturing each task learning potential and cross-task synergy, ASTOR comprises two coupled modules: 1) Hierarchical Utility-Routed Data Scheduling module hierarchically allocates training budget and prioritizes informative prompts, steering training toward the most valuable data and 2) Adaptive Utility-Calibrated Policy Optimization module dynamically scales per-task KL regularization, matching update constraints to each tasks current training state. Experiments on two widely-used LLMs across four representative coding tasks demonstrate that ASTOR consistently improves a single model across all tasks, outperforming the best task-specific specialist by 9.0%-9.5% and surpassing the strongest MTRL baseline by 7.5%-12.8%.

Software Engineering.title: Program Bindings Inside Code Models
Software Engineering.summary: Code language models complete, review, and repair programs without exposing the program structure encoded in their hidden states. In this paper, we test whether the hidden states of a code model can be described and edited using the information a compiler front end computes. For each token of a Python program, standard analyzers provide its position in the abstract syntax tree, its scope, its definition-use links, and its syntactic category. We fit a decomposition that expresses every hidden state of a frozen model as a sum of one term per token, each combining the token with this structural label, and we replace the model's own states with the decomposition at every layer while it predicts the output of a small program. If the model still answers correctly, the decomposition preserves the information the model uses. We apply this test to 14 open models, seven of them trained for code, and compare against a baseline decomposition of the same size built from token positions. The static-analysis decomposition preserves the model's answers better than the positional one in 10 of the 14 models, including six of the seven code models, and deleting the definition-use links from it removes most of that advantage on the two models tested. Editing the decomposition, for instance rebinding the argument of a call, makes StarCoder2-15B produce the answer of the edited program in 90 of 100 cases, compared with 19 for the positional baseline. The Qwen2.5 family is the exception on several measures. For most of the models tested, standard static analysis therefore provides both a description of what the hidden states encode about a program and a way to change it without retraining.

Software Engineering.title: RedCodeAgent: Automatic Red-teaming Agent against Diverse Code Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Code agents have gained widespread adoption due to their strong code generation capabilities and integration with code interpreters, enabling dynamic execution, debugging, and interactive programming capabilities. While these advancements have streamlined complex workflows, they have also introduced critical safety and security risks. Current static safety benchmarks and red-teaming tools are inadequate for identifying emerging real-world risky scenarios, as they fail to cover certain boundary conditions, such as the combined effects of different jailbreak tools. In this work, we propose RedCodeAgent, the first automated red-teaming agent designed to systematically uncover vulnerabilities in diverse code agents. With an adaptive memory module, RedCodeAgent can leverage existing jailbreak knowledge, dynamically select the most effective red-teaming tools and tool combinations in a tailored toolbox for a given input query, thus identifying vulnerabilities that might otherwise be overlooked. For reliable evaluation, we develop simulated sandbox environments to additionally evaluate the execution results of code agents, mitigating potential biases of LLM-based judges that only rely on static code. Through extensive evaluations across multiple state-of-the-art code agents, diverse risky scenarios, and various programming languages, RedCodeAgent consistently outperforms existing red-teaming methods, achieving higher attack success rates and lower rejection rates with high efficiency. We further validate RedCodeAgent on real-world code assistants, e.g., Cursor and Codeium, exposing previously unidentified security risks. By automating and optimizing red-teaming processes, RedCodeAgent enables scalable, adaptive, and effective safety assessments of code agents. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/1mocat/RedCodeAgent.

Software Engineering.title: Soei: Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent for Multi-Agent AI Software Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: AI coding agents now do long, multi-step and multi-session software work with little supervision. When a developer comes back to that work, the useful question is not what the model said but what was actually done, by whom, and whether it is finished. We study this in three parts. First, we verify Agenttrail, an open-source local observability tool for coding agents, against its source at commit e4ba2da: nine documented constants and mechanisms hold at file-and-line level, two event pipelines are never unified, and its Map service has an unauthenticated local mutation surface. Second, we run a prototype of our system on 45 real coding-agent sessions (102,233 records, 20,577 tool executions, 2,336 human-to-agent episodes). With a blind-audited classifier (precision 83.3% and 96.7%) we estimate that 23.4% (95% CI 17.1 to 35.7) of code-editing episodes end with no independent check after the last edit, and that 57.8% of to-dos the agent marked complete after editing had no proof in between. A 10-minute timing heuristic for session hand-offs recovers 6 of the 24 session pairs that content lineage links. 42% of sessions run longer than 24 hours, 48.1% of transcript bytes lie past a 2 MiB replay bound, and 1,326 records in 16 sessions contain credential-like strings. Third, we propose Soei (Structured Observability of Evidence and Intent): an acknowledgement-aware event schema, a hash-chained local ledger, a W3C PROV-aligned graph, calibrated inference for attribution and lineage, and a verification layer that keeps a claim of completion apart from proof. On the same corpus the ledger is 20% of raw size, holds no content or credentials, verifies at about 126k events/s, detects tampering and replays deterministically. We position the work against concurrent 2026 proposals and define autonomy levels with evidence gates and harness metrics baselined on our data.

Software Engineering.title: Towards Functional Correctness of Code Models with Selective Generation
Software Engineering.summary: The hallucination of code generation models hinders their applicability to systems requiring higher safety standards. One critical bottleneck in addressing code hallucination is the difficulty of identifying the functional correctness of generated code, due to its unnatural form. We address this core bottleneck by automatically generating unit tests using dynamic code analysis tools, leveraging the \emph{executable nature} of code. Accordingly, we propose a \emph{selective code generator} that abstains from uncertain generations -- based on the functional correctness evaluated by generated unit tests -- to theoretically control the correctness among non-abstained answers, \ie the false discovery rate. Finally, we propose to use generated unit tests in evaluation as well as in learning for precise code evaluation, calling this paradigm \emph{FuzzEval}. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method along with the controllability of code hallucination and reasonable selection efficiency.

Software Engineering.title: Well-Specified and Well-Tested? Assessing SWE-bench-Style Datasets with a Self-Evolving Agent
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on software engineering (SE) tasks, driving the need for high-quality datasets for reliable training and evaluation. SWE-bench-style datasets (SWE datasets) are widely used to evaluate LLM-based coding agents on real-world software issues, where task clarity and test coverage directly affect whether instances are solvable and verifiable. However, quality issues persist in existing SWE datasets, and manual annotation is costly and labor-intensive, motivating LLM-based annotation. Existing approaches typically rely on static, overly general rubrics, limiting their ability to handle diverse and nuanced scenarios and often yielding high false positive rates. In contrast, human annotators draw on accumulated experience to make context-aware judgments. Inspired by this, we propose ExLabel, an LLM-based, self-evolving, experience-guided assistant for task clarity and test coverage assessment in SWE datasets. ExLabel maintains an evolving experience bank that distills cross-instance knowledge into stable yet adaptive judgment criteria and reuses relevant experience to guide the assessment of new instances. For systematic evaluation, we construct SWE-TQ, a new benchmark spanning eight programming languages, by cleaning human annotations from SWE-bench and Multi-SWE-bench. Experiments with three backbone LLMs show that ExLabel achieves the best F1 across all settings, with relative improvements of 44.2%/49.9% and 24.0%/18.4% over the best baseline for task clarity and test coverage assessment on the Python/Multilingual subsets, respectively. Moreover, a coding model fine-tuned on SWE-rebench data filtered by ExLabel resolves 66.2% of issues on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the model trained on data filtered by the best baseline by 14.5%.

Software Engineering.title: QSoftCore: A Conceptual Foundation for Quantum Software Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: Quantum software engineering (QSE) requires understanding application requirements, quantum programs and algorithms, quantum computation paradigms, executions, and deployment. However, relevant quantum computing (QC) concepts are often defined across physical, mathematical, and paradigm-specific levels of abstraction, making it difficult for the QSE community and hence proposed methods to refer to them consistently. To this end, we present QSoftCore, a conceptual model that reorganizes established QC concepts from a software engineering perspective and connects quantum applications, computational problems, algorithms, configurations, programs, and paradigm-specific computation specifications with state evolution, execution results, and backends. Our assessment against QSE literature across key software engineering activities indicates that QSoftCore provides shared QC referents for quantum computations, executions, deployment configurations, backends, and measurement evidence across the QSE lifecycle.

Software Engineering.title: MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection
Software Engineering.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to automate vulnerability detection, but reliable detection is challenging because agents must distinguish subtle, security-relevant fixes from benign code variation. While underlying LLM capability has improved significantly, the accuracy of the agent still depends heavily on the harness: the code that defines the scaffolding around the LLM. Harnesses are typically fixed, and largely hand-written, limiting adaptation to evaluator feedback. Additionally, when harnesses are static, improvements on one dataset or model may not transfer to others. To address these challenges, we introduce MetaVul, a self-improving framework for harness discovery in vulnerability detection. Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul uses a workflow-based optimization loop to iteratively refine the harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions, while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. At each iteration, it searches over the history of prior harnesses, with access to their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and it returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses. We apply MetaVul to discover agent harnesses for various architectures. A validation set (202 pairs) is used for optimization, while an unseen dataset (430 pairs) is kept as the held-out set. We test whether harnesses learned from one model transfer to others not seen during optimization. Results on both frontier and small LLMs show that the optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability detection up to 23.3 percentage points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness. Harnesses learned with one model also transfer to others. We show that harnesses optimized with one model transfer to another, improving held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points without further optimization.

Software Engineering.title: Data-Efficient Unknown Attack Detection in IoT Networks Using Pretrained Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: The rapid evolution of cyberattacks continues to drive the emergence of unknown (zero-day) threats, posing significant challenges for network intrusion detection systems in Internet of Things (IoT) networks. Existing machine learning and deep learning approaches typically rely on large labeled datasets, payload inspection, or closed-set classification, limiting their effectiveness under data scarcity, encrypted traffic, and distribution shifts. To address these limitations, we propose SiamXBERT, a data-efficient, open-set Siamese meta-learning framework built on a pretrained language model for unknown-attack detection. The framework constructs a dual-modality feature representation by integrating flow-level and packet-level information, enabling richer behavioral modeling while remaining compatible with encrypted traffic. The model learns similarity patterns for known benign and attack classes using 100 labeled samples per class. It flags traffic that does not sufficiently match any known class as potentially unknown, using a threshold set without unknown-attack data. We evaluate SiamXBERT on two IoT intrusion detection datasets against five state-of-the-art detection methods. When training and testing are performed on the same dataset at this labeling budget, SiamXBERT attains the highest unknown F1-score, exceeding the strongest competing method on each dataset by 84.8% and 37.4%; the improvement is statistically significant against all five methods on one dataset and against four of the five on the other. When a model trained on one dataset is tested on another, SiamXBERT transfers effectively in one direction but degrades in the reverse, reflecting the rejection behavior learned from the source traffic rather than the choice of threshold. These results highlight the practicality of SiamXBERT for data-efficient unknown attack detection in real-world IoT environments.

Software Engineering.title: GUITestScape: Towards Open-set Evaluation on Exploratory GUI Testing
Software Engineering.summary: Exploratory GUI testing is a particularly demanding setting for MLLM agents: without predefined test scripts, an agent must autonomously navigate an application and discover defects through its own interaction. However, current evaluation falls short on two fronts. First, existing benchmarks focus almost exclusively on interaction defects, leaving display defects outside the evaluation frame. Second, evaluation protocols are bound to predefined defect annotations, collapsing the testing process into a single end-state judgment that conflates qualitatively distinct failure modes. To address these challenges, we present GUITestScape, an interactive benchmark covering 61 real-world Android applications and 508 preset defects spanning interaction and display types, and introduce GUIJudge, an open-set evaluator that decomposes an agent's testing trajectory into independently diagnosable capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that GUIJudge achieves reliable process-aware evaluation beyond predefined annotations, substantially outperforming all baselines. Benchmarking on GUITestScape further reveals that detection remains the critical bottleneck for existing models across both defect types, and that integrating GUIJudge's verifiers into existing agents significantly boosts their detection performance without retraining.

Software Engineering.title: Benchmarking Coding Agents under Evolving Requirements
Software Engineering.summary: Software development with coding agents often begins with a rough request that users refine after trying the implementation. Final correctness alone does not capture the repeated guidance this process requires. We introduce FeatureLoop, a benchmark of 61 human-reviewed tasks from 34 repositories across five primary programming languages and seven software forms. Each task follows one development goal in a persistent workspace through evolution feedback, which adds or clarifies requirements, and completion feedback, which reports failures of stated requirements. Cumulative executable checks track new behavior, repair, and preservation of earlier functionality. We evaluate 12 frontier models and find that the strongest completes 72.1% of tasks with both feedback types. Across models, however, only 15.4% of observed failed stages recover within two corrective revisions. Further analysis reveals incomplete repairs, regressions, and model-specific differences in feedback use and token efficiency, identifying obstacles to reliable, low-intervention development.

Software Engineering.title: Broken on Arrival: Non-Functional Quantized LLM Artifacts in Public Model Registries and How to Catch Them
Software Engineering.summary: Developers download quantized large language models (LLMs) from public registries to run them locally. None of the registries we examined documented functional testing of their files. We tested all 305 eligible code-capable GGUF tags (the llama.cpp format) across 15 model lines in the official Ollama library, plus 22 popular Hugging Face community files. A 15-task code screen identified suspects, which we retested on all 164 HumanEval+ tasks. Seven official tags (2.3%) solved at most six of them. All were low-bit quantizations of models with at most four billion parameters. We rebuilt five suspect files from the original weights. All five registry files matched our uncalibrated rebuilds tensor for tensor, so none was corrupted. Exact reproducibility did not imply function. With the weights, toolchain and tensor mix held fixed, adding an importance matrix raised Qwen2.5-Coder-3B scores at three quantization levels from zero to 76-113 of 164 tasks. The same uncalibrated recipe left the smaller Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B functional, showing that the recipe alone does not predict failure. None of 66 sampled tags that passed the screen was non-functional. We release the audit data and the quantcheck tool and recommend screening low-bit tags before publication, then calibrating or withholding failures.
Software Engineering.comment: v3 revises the diagnosis of one community file pair (Sec. V, RQ2): a template test on the same hardware shows the two deepseek-coder-6.7B community files fail for lack of a chat template, not by backend; release v3.4 adds the test. All other results unchanged. Code and data: https://github.com/aditi-p31/quantcheck (release v3.4)

Software Engineering.title: Omission-Safe Conditional Contracts for Evidence-Closed CI Qualification
Software Engineering.summary: Continuous-integration evidence is conditional: a workflow determines which jobs should run, while an archive records which jobs remain observable. Reconstructing requirements from those observations lets an omission erase its own obligation. We present a qualification method that compiles a pinned workflow into conditional job requirements independently of target presence, retains a fixed capture inventory, and checks source-complete derivation certificates with a separate implementation. For a fixed source, context, scope and binding universe, with sound obligations and applicability judgments that preserve established truth under information extension, withdrawing observation facts cannot create authorization. The implementation handles static matrices, dependency guards and bounded pinned reusable workflows, preserving unknown applicability and separating tolerated outcomes from evidence coverage. Both implementations match the 45 hand-specified authorization controls, reject 180 source-certificate attacks, and exhibit no authorization gain over 704 distinct proper development erasures. An explicitly witnessed 12-job platform run qualifies in both implementations; all 4,095 proper payload-subset erasures block authorization. A frozen collection spans 240 runs in eight workflow families across six projects. All 160 evaluation source certificates independently validate, but unavailable historical execution-source identities leave actual qualification open. Initial gate diagnoses agree on 155/160 runs; a preserved unknown-propagation repair yields 160/160 agreement in a retrospective rerun. The study establishes bounded source extraction and omission resistance, rather than natural-fault prevalence or producer authenticity.

Software Engineering.title: PyReprism: A Shared Lexical Foundation for Polyglot Code Analysis
Software Engineering.summary: Empirical studies of polyglot repositories apply the same analyses to every language of a corpus, such as separating code from comments, computing metrics, normalizing identifiers, and screening for duplicated code. Assembling them from specialized tools introduces differences in language coverage, measurement conventions, and workflows. We present PYREPRISM, an open-source Python library and command-line tool that separates language-specific lexical processing from reusable analyses: each language declares its lexical surface, which yields a lossless stream of typed tokens, and every analysis is implemented once on that stream. Across 187 built-in languages, language-specific declarations have a median length of 16 lines, and no language overrides a shared analysis. Against a reference parser, comment and string classification reach F1 scores of 0.994 and 0.958 on 1,412 files in 12 languages that were never used to develop the tokenizer. In a study of a polyglot repository, one tool replaces three; with matched inputs and analysis operations, it takes 2.9s instead of 8.7s on one core. We also characterize where lexical analysis falls short, in complexity estimation and clone screening. Tool: https://github.com/unlv-evol/PyReprism Video: https://youtu.be/IXc-NP5t4GU
Software Engineering.comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, Submitted to SANER 2027 Tool Demo Track

Software Engineering.title: Confident Learning-based Network for Detecting Bug-Inducing Commits on SZZ with Noisy Labels
Software Engineering.summary: The Just-In-Time (JIT) defect prediction model serves as a critical tool for ensuring the quality of software development and enhancing software performance. It assists development teams in promptly identifying and addressing potential issues by predicting whether code submissions may introduce defects. However, due to the existence of data noise and insufficient semantic connections in real-world scenarios, existing approaches face challenges in accurately identifying the code commits that introduce defects and capturing the potential semantic relationships. To address these challenges, we propose the BIC- Hunter(Bug-Inducing Commits Hunter) model, which mitigates data noise and improves semantic understanding, thereby enhancing the accuracy of bug-inducing commit identification. BIC - Hunter model consists of two components: a data denoising component and a semantic relationship capturing component. Specifically, the data denoising component addresses the challenges posed by inaccurate annotations and inconsistencies in real-world data, enhancing the reliability of training data and improving overall model robustness. The semantic relation- ship capturing component constructs homogeneous graphs and applies graph convolutional networks to facilitate a more comprehensive analysis of code context, enabling the identification of defects caused by code commits and enhancing the confidence in pinpointing their root causes. Experimental studies on a large-scale dataset integrated from three open-source datasets show that BIC- Hunter exhibits outstanding performance. BIC- Hunter outperforms the state-of-the-art by 6.16%, 7.13%, and 5.53% on Recall@1, Recall@2, and Recall@3, respectively, while the MFR index increases by 8.43% to 32.82%. These results demonstrate the superior capability of our method in identifying bug-inducing commits.
Software Engineering.comment: After careful re-evaluation by all authors, we identify critical flaws in the experimental design and validation setup of this preliminary version. The empirical results and related claims cannot be reliably supported. Therefore we withdraw this preprint to avoid misleading readers. A substantially revised and revalidated version will be prepared in the future

Software Engineering.title: Rebuild Dossier: Mechanically-Enforced Specs for Agentic App Rebuilds, and What Model-Tier Failures Reveal
Software Engineering.summary:
An AI agent's rebuild is only as good as the process that produced it. Prior work found that once a model is strong enough, a multi-agent rebuild pipeline loses to the simplest approach: giving the model the original code and one instruction (AgentModernize). We present rebuild-dossier, an open-source tool that locks an application's real interface - its exact inputs and outputs - before any code is written, then enforces one-test-at-a-time building through automated checks, not written instructions alone.
  Three results shape this evaluation, with differing amounts of evidence. First, in a small comparison, the compliant agent failed a held-back test while the rule-breaking agent passed everything - proof that a passing suite doesn't certify correctness when tests can be gamed. Second, we tested whether this beats simply giving the weaker model the source and one instruction: tied on a small app, but lost outright on a larger one where the automated check wasn't even running - pointing to the check mechanism, not interface-locking, which held up separately. Third, every claim here is checked at three levels - the agent's own report, an automated log, and the actual files produced - catching real errors, including a bug in our own logging code, that a single level would have missed.
  These risks reproduce on a different model and toolchain: a stronger model followed our process three times running, something the weaker model never managed. The tool is public, MIT licensed, and reproduces end to end against our own applications.
Software Engineering.comment: 48 pages, 1 figure. Code and evaluation artifacts: https://github.com/Parker-Fawcett/rebuild-dossier (archived at DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22036801)

Software Engineering.title: Do Open-Source Video Ad Clients Follow VAST 4.3? An Empirical Study of Player Conformance
Software Engineering.summary:
Context. Video ads reach streaming and connected-TV apps through VAST documents, and companies count ads from the HTTP requests the player's client library sends. A tracking error can leave playback intact and surface later as disagreeing counts.
  Objective. To measure how far open-source VAST clients meet the player duties of VAST 4.3, whether verdicts depend on the runtime, what generated inputs add, and when deviations were introduced.
  Method. A catalog of 108 requirements was extracted from the specification. Six open-source clients in eight configurations ran against 69 crafted test vectors and the IAB's sample tags, under Node.js and in five browsers on three engines, with every request recorded. Grids, fuzzing and a sweep over 36 releases extend the catalog; Google's closed IMA SDK is a comparison.
  Results. The open-source clients have 78 findings and 3 to 21 must-level deviations per configuration. None of the tested open-source clients that follow redirect (Wrapper) chains fills the required macros in a Wrapper's request; the archived IMA 3.794.0 configuration tested does. One library's timeout throws an exception no caller can catch, ending a Node.js process. In a pod (ads played back to back), one player credits a finishing ad's completion to the next ad, fixed in release 5.3.0. A library can conform under jsdom and deviate in every tested Chrome- and Safari-family browser.
  Conclusions. The tested clients diverge on the duties other companies use to count and diagnose ads. A shared conformance suite run in real browsers could expose most graded deviations; the harness and vectors are released.
Software Engineering.comment: 51 pages, 20 tables, 3 figures. Harness, test vectors and results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23581408

Programming Languages.title: A Rowhammer attack on Fil-C's software capabilities
Programming Languages.summary: Fil-C retrofits spatial and temporal memory safety onto C/C++ using software capabilities (bounds that are checked at every pointer dereference). Fil-C's guarantee rests on an unstated hardware assumption: that DRAM preserves the capabilities. We show that Rowhammer breaks it. In Fil-C 0.679 a part of each heap pointer's capability lives in a 16-byte header stored inline in ordinary DRAM immediately before the object pointed to, with no mechanism to prevent capabilities from corruption. A single 0 → 1 bit flip in the capability's upper-bound expands the pointer's permitted range by 2k bytes and is invisible to the runtime, raising no panic or signal. We demonstrate this by using Fil-C to convert existing Rowhammer attacks into concrete attacks against a heterogeneous collection of victim software. To aid reproducibility (not everybody has DRAM vulnerable to Rowhammer) we split our demonstration into two paths. First, along a deterministic path, we isolate Fil-C as a novel attack vector using a deterministic, Rowhammer-like fault-injection model. Across four case studies, this model corrupts the upper-bound word of a pointer, permitting previously out-of-bounds reads and writes. We use this to achieve a bounded read/write window, secret disclosure, privilege escalation by flipping an adjacent is_admin field, and the leakage of a tenant API key in a multi-tenant credential service backed by SQLite (compiled under Fil-C). Second, along a physical end-to-end path, we demonstrate all four attacks on real hardware equipped with DDR3 memory, and with Target Row Refresh (TRR) equipped DDR4, proving the exploits are physically realisable. The latter attack shows that the TRR defence does not close the Fil-C delivery channel. We close with a discussion of Fil-C-specific mitigations.

Programming Languages.title: crush: Extensible Proof Automation for Lean
Programming Languages.summary: Lean's rich expressiveness supports higher-order functions, inductive datatypes, and user-defined abstractions, making it challenging to translate proof obligations into first-order Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) queries and reconstruct kernel checked proofs. We present crush, an extensible SMT-backed proof automation framework for Lean. To bridge the gap between Lean's higher-order constructs and the solver's first-order logic, crush uses defunctionalization to encode function values and their applications. We formalize this translation for a supported higher-order fragment and prove its soundness. Moreover, crush provides metaprogramming interfaces for extending both Lean-to-SMT translation and the reconstruction of Lean proofs from solver certificates without modifying the translation pipeline. We implement crush as both a tactic and a backend for other third-party automation systems. We show that across four such use cases that target verification and general proof automation, crush discharges more obligations than the competing backends and reconstructs more kernel-checked proofs than the baselines.

Programming Languages.title: Countable Nondeterminism in Weighted Programming with an Application to Mechanized Foundations for Probabilistic Program Verification
Programming Languages.summary: Weighted programming is a framework by Batz et al. for describing mathematical models or optimization problems as imperative programs parametrized over semirings and then analyzing them with program verification techniques like weakest precondition calculi. Applications include reasoning about expected outcomes of probabilistic programs and competitive analysis of online algorithms. We extend weighted programming with (1) countable nondeterminism and (2) user-defined additive rewards, where programs are parametrized over modules instead of semirings. The resulting framework enables reasoning about expected resource consumption of probabilistic programs and about optimal scores of combinatorial games. A technical challenge is that wp-calculi for weighted programs with (1) and (2) over arbitrary modules can be unsound, because it is well-known that continuity properties commonly used in program semantics break in the presence of countable nondeterminism. We study conditions under which a wp-style transformer for reasoning about weighted programs is sound with respect to an operational ground truth defined in terms of weighted decision processes (WDPs) - transition systems that generalize Markov decision processes by drawing transition weights and state rewards from a module. Based on those conditions, we show that a range of concrete instances of the weighted programming framework enjoy sound weakest precondition reasoning. We demonstrate the usefulness of our wp-semantics through case studies for different modules. We mechanized our extended weighted programming framework and our main soundness results in the interactive theorem prover Lean. Instantiating these results for probabilistic programming yields, to the best of our knowledge, the first mechanized proof of a fixed point characterization of minimal expected rewards in Markov decision processes with countable nondeterminism.

Programming Languages.title: Automated Verification of Hamiltonian Simulation by Quantum Signal Processing
Programming Languages.summary: We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first fully automated verification framework for QSP-based Hamiltonian simulation. Our framework exploits the structure of the simulation algorithm: Hamiltonians are given as weighted sums of Pauli strings, embedded into larger unitaries through block encodings, and transformed into time-evolution operators by quantum signal processing (QSP). Using a symbolic Pauli-sum semantics for ancilla-indexed circuit blocks, our verifier proves that the distinguished all-zero ancilla block is proportional to the target Hamiltonian and infers the subnormalization factor automatically. It then verifies the QSP layer by extracting the implemented polynomial transformation and certifying its approximation error. This structure-aware abstraction is essential for scalability. Composing our verified block encoding and QSP wrapper yields an estimated macro-expanded size of about 1.52 million gates. The verifier certifies the block encoding once and checks the QSP layer through its abstract interface, without expanding the oracle calls. Our implementation verifies block encodings of structured Pauli-sum Hamiltonians with up to 256 system qubits and verifies QSP Hamiltonian-simulation instances by extracting their implemented polynomials and checking the resulting approximation bounds. These results show that fully automated verification can handle common Hamiltonian-simulation circuits at substantial scale when it exploits their algorithmic structure.

Programming Languages.title: DualGuard: Comprehensive and Efficient Memory Safety across Sequential and Speculative Execution
Programming Languages.summary:
Although decades of research have yielded sophisticated mechanisms for enforcing memory safety, speculative execution can subvert these protections through transient memory operations. Conversely, defenses designed specifically for speculative safety, such as Speculative Load Hardening (SLH), cannot enforce memory safety during non-speculative execution. A naive combination of defenses from both domains raises two fundamental challenges: (1) which combination of otherwise fragmented defenses can ensure dual memory safety under speculative and non-speculative executions? (2) whether such combinations introduce redundant protections that incur unnecessary performance overhead?
  We present DualGuard, a unified framework for dual memory protection under non-speculative and speculative executions. DualGuard systematically analyzes memory behaviors, classifying them into four categories, and further identifies the minimal composition requirements for dual memory safety, which allow us to strategically combine existing mitigations and design new ones to avoid redundant or excessive protections. We implement DualGuard through a combination of static analysis and runtime enforcement within the LLVM infrastructure. Our evaluation demonstrates that DualGuard reduces overhead by 3%-72% compared to naive compositions of fragmented defenses. In some cases, it even incurs lower overhead than approaches that guarantee memory safety solely under either non-speculative or speculative execution.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Functorial Analysis of Group-Alphabet Cellular Automata
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: Let $G$ be a group and let $n\in\mathbb N$. We consider one-dimensional cellular automata of length $n$ over the alphabet $G$, with periodic boundary conditions and with local rules $φ$ given by words. We construct a functor $F$ from $\mathbf{Grp}$, the category of groups (or any similar algebraic structure), to the category of pointed digraphs, and show its faithfulness. We introduce the image category $\mathcal C_{n,φ}$ of state transition graphs of all such group-alphabet cellular automata, and show $F$ is an equivalence onto this category. Consequently we investigate the translation of categorical structures in $\mathbf{Grp}$ in terms of automata, and give examples of how standard methods of homological algebra may now be applied to automata. Additionally, a graph-theoretical construction of the product in $\mathcal C_{n,φ}$ is given, together with a formula for cycle lengths and multiplicities in this product. When $G$ is abelian, further structural properties of state transition graphs follow, and we contrast these results with non-abelian counterexamples.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Reachability in Five-Dimensional Vector Addition Systems Is PSPACE-Complete
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: Vector addition systems (VAS) are a fundamental model of concurrent computation in which transitions update nonnegative integer counters by adding integer vectors, provided all counters remain nonnegative. Closely related to Petri nets, VAS are the single-state counterpart of vector addition systems with states (VASS), which use finitely many states to restrict the available transitions. A classical simulation of $d$-VASS by $(d+3)$-VAS connects their reachability problems, but the complexity-theoretic picture of fixed-dimensional VAS remains largely unclear. While reachability in $2$-VASS is PSPACE-complete under binary encoding, the best known upper bound for $5$-VAS was only elementary. We prove that every reachable $5$-VAS instance has a reachability witness of length polynomial in its unary size. Consequently, $5$-VAS reachability is NL-complete under unary encoding and PSPACE-complete under binary encoding. We also establish a polynomial factorization of the reachability relation of every $d$-VAS with $d \ge 3$. For $5$-VAS, this strengthens Hopcroft and Pansiot's effective semilinearity of reachability sets to the full reachability relation. For every fixed $d\ge3$, it also yields an $\mathsf F_d$ upper bound for reachability in $(d+3)$-VAS.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Block-exchange descent for insertion: commuting projections and minimum masks
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: For fixed nonempty words $u,v$, the minimum insertion degree of a shuffle is the least number of inserted-source runs among its representations. We prove that, after a block exchange from a minimum mask of degree $r$, the minimum over masks with commuting source projections is exactly $r-1$; a larger decrease occurs precisely when a noncommuting mask has fewer runs. If either source is unary, every such exchange is exact. We prove an explicit repair for an infinite periodic degree-three family. Computer-assisted results establish first-mask descent through combined length seventeen over every alphabet, degree-three first-mask descent through length thirty, and a uniform repair of all degree-three failures through length thirty, including all further letter identifications. Counterexamples to arbitrary, first, and last minimum-mask choices explain the need for alternative masks. Finally, we prove that minimum iteration depths have no gaps for arbitrary languages. General block-exchange descent and Singleton No-Gap remain open.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: 22 pages, 10 tables. Software and verification data: https://github.com/the-omega-institute/insertion-degree-descent/releases/tag/v1.0

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Exact Avoid-or-Compress Extrema for Dense Reachable Images: Defects Four and Five
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: Let $S$ be a reachable image of a strongly connected synchronizing automaton and $\varnothing\ne A\subsetneq S$. We determine the maximum shortest avoid-or-compress length over binary and arbitrary finite alphabets for $m=n-|S|=4$ and $m=5$. The exact values are $\min(n-|A|,11)$ and $\min(n-|A|,14)$, respectively. Uniform binary constructions attain both bounds. For the upper bounds, short-pair graphs and actual-image constraints reduce all parameters to finite necessary domains. Exhaustive checks exclude the domains, apart from a single relaxation eliminated by a multipartite overlap lemma. The largest calculation covers 3,206,988 domains.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Computer-assisted upper bounds

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Tree Equivalence of Higher-Order Recursion Schemes Is Undecidable
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary:
Higher-order recursion schemes (HORS) are finite, simply typed recursive programs that generate potentially infinite trees. Their monadic second-order model-checking problem is decidable. We prove that tree equivalence of deterministic HORS is undecidable and, more precisely, $Π^0_1$-complete under total computable many-one reductions. The lower bound holds for safe, productive schemes of order at most four over the fixed ranked alphabet $Σ_2=\{e:0,d:2\}$, consisting of one nullary and one binary symbol.
  Adapting the counter-guard witness of Boiret, Piorkowski, and Schmude, we generate all candidate executions of a two-counter machine by producing both continuations at every counter test. An integer weight is nonzero exactly on legal prefixes. Functions at fixed simple types represent the polynomial of growing degree. A shift recurrence updates them without storing a separate step counter, allowing the witness to be implemented by safe applicative HORS rules. At candidate halts, the intermediate schemes generate unary observation subtrees whose lengths encode the two natural-number components of the signed weight. Invalid candidates give matching observations; a legal halt produces a finite discrepancy. Fixed constructor contexts encode these intermediate trees over $Σ_2$.
  For the upper bound, a finite monotone semantics decides head convergence and supports an algorithm computing exact tree prefixes at any prescribed finite depth, including positions labelled $\bot$.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Learning Erasing Equal-Length Relational Pattern Languages in the Limit from Positive Data over Binary Alphabets
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: Relational pattern languages generalize Angluin's pattern languages by requiring the strings substituted for repeated occurrences of a variable to stand in a given relation, rather than to be identical. We study erasing pattern languages under the equal-length relation, where all occurrences of a variable must be replaced by strings of the same length. Over alphabets with at least three letters, this class is known to be learnable in the limit from positive data. We show that over a binary alphabet it is not, which resolves an open question from earlier work. Our proof reveals that non-learnability already holds for the restricted subclass of languages generated by patterns that have exactly three maximal substrings of variables. We then show that patterns with at most two maximal substrings of variables are learnable in the limit from positive data for every alphabet of size at least two. If the target pattern is known to have at most one maximal substring of variables, this can even be achieved by an iterative learner, which updates its hypothesis using only the current example and its previous hypothesis.

Symbolic Computation.title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
Symbolic Computation.summary: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

Symbolic Computation.title: Construction and formal verification of a special topology on {\mathbb{Z}}^{n}: characterization of connected subsets
Symbolic Computation.summary: We examine whether the integers admit a topology whose connected subsets are precisely the sets of consecutive integers. The main result gives a construction for every integer lattice {\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, n>0; the answer for Z is then obtained as a corollary. We prove that the neighborhoods determined by the parity of the sum of the coordinates form a basis and that topological connectedness agrees exactly with accessibility by finite paths of unit lattice steps. We also present a deductive audit and the correspondence between this argument and a verification in Lean 4 and Mathlib, including the empty set and the independent formal characterization of integer intervals. The construction and mathematical result originate in Problem 5712, proposed by Dan Marcus and solved in 1970 by the Cleveland State University group; the present article contributes a detailed exposition and a report on formal verification.

Symbolic Computation.title: Quasilinear multiplication in the Cayley-Dickson tower
Symbolic Computation.summary: Direct evaluation of the defining product of the Cayley-Dickson algebra $A_n$ of rank $N:=2^n$ over a unital commutative ring $R$ in which $2$ is invertible requires a quadratic number of arithmetic operations. This paper gives a uniform bilinear algorithm for multiplication in this algebra costing $O(N \log N)$ arithmetic operations in $R$ and $O(N)$ auxiliary storage when the doubling parameters of $A_n$ are units whose square roots lie in a fixed commutative coefficient algebra $S$ finitely generated as an $R$-module and admitting an $R$-linear map $π\colon S \to R$ with $π(1) = 1$. In particular, over $\mathbb{R}$ and every finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ of odd characteristic, a quadratic field extension contains a square root of every possible doubling parameter, so the algorithm applies to every Cayley-Dickson tower over these fields, and the tensor rank of multiplication in $A_n$ over them is at most $(9n-21)2^n+28$ when $n\ge2$. When the top doubling parameter is a non-square, as in the standard real tower, the bound is $(9n-15)2^{n-1}+10$. To the author's knowledge, the algorithm presented in this paper is the first uniform subquadratic algorithm for multiplication in $A_n$. When $R=\mathbb{R}$ with every doubling parameter equal to $-1$, the real quasilinear schedule uses fewer total arithmetic operations than both direct multiplication and a uniform algorithm of Cariow-Cariowa for $n\ge4$. An implementation for the standard real tower is available in the MIT-licensed C11 library fastCD, with a NumPy-backed Python interface. In single-core benchmarks against direct multiplication and the uniform Cariow-Cariowa method, the quasilinear implementation had the lowest mean time of the three at every tested dimension $N\ge32$, for both single and batched products, and was over $17$ times faster than direct multiplication at $N=1024$.
Symbolic Computation.comment: 28 pages, 2 tables. v2: title changed from 'Quasilinear multiplication in the real Cayley--Dickson tower'; results generalized from $\mathbb R$ to unital commutative rings with $2$ invertible, with finite-field and tensor-rank corollaries; benchmarks updated. Code: https://git.tanuki-cd.com/algebraity/fastCD

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Grounding Image Composition with Label-Conditioned Visual Evidence
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Image composition labels such as center, diagonal, or rule of thirds describe visual structure rather than object categories. KU-PCP provides image-level labels and class-specific geometric elements, but does not show which visible regions people associate with each of its nine classes. We introduce KU-PCP Elements (KU-PCPE), a label-conditioned region-evidence benchmark for photographic composition. Given an image and a label already judged applicable, the task is to segment the visible regions that explain why the label applies. KU-PCPE contains 4,093 single-annotator training masks and a 1,327-task expert test split with three masks per image-label task. The annotations also include exploratory segment-versus-line ratings that describe whether region or semantic-guideline evidence better explains the label. A held-out expert reaches .867 Dice against the other experts, while the strongest deployable model reaches .664, a proposal oracle .672, and the best vision-language model (VLM) proposal selector .395. KU-PCPE exposes the gap between recognizing a composition label and grounding the human-aligned visual evidence that makes it plausible in a particular image.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Single-Annotation, Multi-Hypothesis Segmentation with Semantic-Spatial Residual Banks
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multi-rater segmentation datasets show that a single image can admit several valid masks, yet most training sets expose only one annotation per image. We study single-annotation multi-hypothesis segmentation: each training image exposes one fixed mask, while the model must return a finite bank that covers held-out human annotations at test time. Our experiments reveal a representation tradeoff. Banks learned directly from images recover variations in local boundaries and extent but lose structural hypotheses, whereas frozen semantic features preserve structural grouping but underrepresent spatial variation. We introduce the Semantic-Spatial Residual Bank (SSRB), which freezes a semantic bank trained with balanced assignments and learns a residual from the image for each hypothesis. Across five medical endpoints, SSRB improves coverage of held-out masks at $K=8$ over a Probabilistic U-Net under the same one-mask constraint. On LIDC and LIDC-hard, it also produces substantially more distinct useful masks. On BSDS, it preserves the semantic bank's performance in grouping regions. Its advantage grows as more masks are returned, showing that residuals learned for corresponding heads improve coverage of local annotation variation while preserving how regions are grouped.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Segment Anything Pancreas: A Unified MRI Segmentation Model for Pancreatic Cancer Radiotherapy
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Background: Limited tumor annotations and incomplete labels across MRI datasets hinder unified segmentation of pancreatic tumors and organs at risk (OARs) for MRI-guided radiotherapy. Purpose: We propose Pancreas-MedNeXt, a unified model that segments the whole pancreas, its subregions, tumors, and surrounding OARs from one MRI volume. Methods: The model uses a shared MedNeXt encoder-decoder with supervised whole-pancreas and subregion pretraining, followed by multitask fine-tuning. Three output heads predict the pancreatic subregions, tumor, and OARs (stomach, duodenum, kidneys). An annotation-aware loss allows training on partially labeled data without treating unannotated structures as background. Pancreas and tumor were evaluated by three-fold cross-validation on 142 PANTHER patients (92 diagnostic, 50 MR-Linac), subregions and OARs on Cyst-X and AMOS test sets, and pancreas and OARs on 33 external T1-weighted TotalSegmentator scans. Comparisons with nnU-Net, MedNeXt, VISTA3D, and Swin UNETR used the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with paired bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: Pancreas-MedNeXt achieved the highest mean pancreas and tumor DSC on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI. Tumor DSC was 58.41% and 42.55%, exceeding task-specific MedNeXt by 4.94 (95% CI: 0.28-9.45) and 5.89 (95% CI: 2.37-9.72) percentage points, respectively. Whole-pancreas DSC was 85.73% and 70.66%. Pretraining improved head, body, and tail DSC by 2.01, 3.00, and 3.78 percentage points over training from scratch. It also achieved the highest DSC for the pancreas, duodenum, and right kidney on AMOS, and for all five organs on external MRI, exceeding the next-best method by 4.92-8.85 percentage points.Conclusion: A single Pancreas-MedNeXt model segments tumors, pancreatic subregions, and OARs on diagnostic and MR-Linac MRI, which could streamline contouring for pancreatic cancer radiotherapy.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: WebOverlay: High-Throughput Vision-Only Distillation for Extreme Aspect-Ratio Web Overlay Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Web overlays, such as cookie consent banners, newsletter prompts, and age gates, obstruct automated web crawlers and degrade downstream document representations. While proprietary multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can accurately identify overlays, their latency and inference cost preclude web-scale ingestion. Conversely, lightweight vision models struggle with full-page renderings characterized by extreme vertical aspect ratios, where standard isotropic resizing collapses critical text features and causes false positives. In this work, we present WebOverlay, a high-throughput vision-only detector trained via distillation from a frontier vision-language teacher. We establish a dynamic tiling strategy that partitions extreme aspect-ratio web renders into aspect-preserving patches with spatial overlap, coupled with an aspect-ratio-aware boundary adjudication mechanism to eliminate boundary artifacts. To eliminate cross-modal latency overheads, our student model relies purely on visual cues, bypassing DOM tree parsing. WebOverlay significantly outperforms DOM-based heuristics and achieves competitive precision and recall against heavy proprietary MLLM baselines while delivering multiple orders of magnitude higher throughput and substantially reduced deployment costs.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Dreams Are Cheaper Than Flights: Curated World-Model Data Improves Aerial Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Robot perception is increasingly data driven, yet field data is slow, costly, and sometimes disruptive to collect. Video world models offer a cheaper source: seeded with real frames, they extend a recorded scene into new footage with the deployment's sensor, altitude, and environment. We ask whether such synthetic data matches the utility of real field data and whether detectors trained with it perform in the field. Seeding a 7B-parameter world model with wildlife drone video, we more than double the training set with curated frames. On held-out videos from the same drones, mAP@50--95 rises 4.3\% when these frames are added to real data and 10.3\% when they replace it, and up to 33.5\% on an urban benchmark. Although an expert rejects an estimated 87.5\% of generated clips, the data costs about \$1,100 of GPU time, against more than \$3,200 of field labor alone for a less useful real training set. Synthetic data thus shifts data costs from fieldwork to compute.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PRISM: Feed-Forward Single-Image 3D Reconstruction via Geometric Warp-Residual Modeling
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reconstructing 3D scenes from a single image is a fundamental challenge in computer vision, with broad applications in virtual reality, robotics, and content creation. Recent methods achieve outstanding performance by leveraging camera-controlled video diffusion models, but rely on iterative diffusion sampling, which greatly limits their practical deployment. We observe that geometric forward warping alone can cover the majority of a target view directly from the input image, with only a compact residual left for the encoder to correct. Motivated by this observation, we propose PRISM, a feed-forward framework that decomposes multi-view latent prediction into a parameter-free geometric prior and a learned residual correction, with no diffusion sampling required at inference. To enable generalization from purely synthetic training data, we devise a two-stage training strategy combining latents supervised distillation for geometric generalization and perceptual fine-tuning for appearance quality optimization. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM achieves competitive reconstruction quality compared with diffusion-based methods, while reducing inference time dramatically to only 36 seconds per scene. Our code is available at https://github.com/microjie372/PRISM.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RDGSplat: Render-Dedicated Geometry for Novel View Synthesis
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent 3D foundation models extend to novel view synthesis by carrying a Gaussian head on the representation they already use for reconstruction. However, their rendering quality lags far behind their reconstruction accuracy, because the renderer reads a geometry and a representation that are both optimized for metric reconstruction. Prior methods alleviate this by updating the backbone weights, but they thereby sacrifice the metric predictions the model was built for. To this end, we propose RDGSplat, which decodes a geometry dedicated to rendering from a frozen 3D foundation model while keeping its metric predictions exact. In particular, we devise Render-Dedicated Geometry Decoding, which duplicates the pretrained decoders and optimizes the duplicates under photometric supervision alone. Then, a Target-Pose Conditioned Adapter is introduced to adapt the representation those decoders read towards rendering, conditioned on the predicted target pose. Extensive experiments show that RDGSplat improves novel view synthesis for three feed-forward models of two architectures on four benchmarks, with every pretrained weight frozen. On RE10K, it raises WM2.0 from 20.918 to 25.149dB by training 205.5M added parameters against a frozen 1.4B backbone, and leaves its predicted depth and pose unchanged.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Prior-Guided Single-Exposure HDR Novel View Synthesis via Base-Gain Representation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Single-exposure high dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) recovers HDR scenes from low dynamic range (LDR) views captured at a single exposure and estimates camera response function (CRF) for LDR re-exposure. Without HDR ground-truth, using single-exposure LDR views as the sole source of direct supervision underconstrains HDR reconstruction and cannot ensure its faithful recovery, motivating the need for learned LDR-to-HDR reconstruction priors. Moreover, single-exposure LDR views supervise CRF only over a limited range, necessitating a learnable prior for reliable re-exposure beyond it. We propose PriorGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both challenges by (1) guiding HDR recovery with pseudo-HDR supervision from 2D single-exposure HDR reconstruction methods while anchoring it to input LDR views through a closed reconstruction loop; and (2) regularizing CRF modeling with a learnable prior that guarantees monotonicity and promotes plausible responses. Yet cross-view inconsistencies in independently generated pseudo-HDR targets impair scene reconstruction when HDR is encoded directly as Gaussian's color attribute. We therefore introduce a 3D base-gain HDR representation that factors HDR radiance into an LDR base and an overlaid 3D gain field, promoting robustness to such inconsistencies and enabling 3D HDR appearance editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate PriorGS's substantial superiority over baselines.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RADI3N: GeometRic ImAge EDiting via ParametrIc 3D CoNtrol
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent diffusion-based methods have substantially advanced image editing, yet parametric 3D control at the part level remains challenging. Existing approaches either operate on whole objects with manual rigging, or revert to 2D handles at the part level. They also struggle to model appearance and texture under large transformations, leading to unrealistic outputs in geometry-intensive edits. To address these limitations, we introduce RADI3N, a framework for semantically-grounded part-aware object manipulation with parametric 3D control. Our CS-ARAP deformation module suppresses rotation-field discontinuities at part boundaries via neighborhood covariance smoothing, producing structurally consistent deformations under complex part-level edits. We further introduce an inversion-free selective texture transfer mechanism that suppresses high-frequency positional biases and scales up low-frequency semantic cues within cross-image attention. This eliminates strict spatial bias and supports semantic matching, allowing source appearance to follow the edited part onto its new geometry. Experiments demonstrate that RADI3N achieves state-of-the-art performance in geometric fidelity, viewpoint consistency, and controllability.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TalkFlow: Structured Latent Flow Matching for Speech Driven Holistic Motion Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Holistic co-speech motion generation aims to synthesize coordinated facial expressions, hand gestures, and body movements from speech, which is challenging due to heterogeneous part-specific dynamics, long-range temporal coherence, and cross-part coordination. Directly modeling high-dimensional motion can be unstable, while overly compact or unstructured latent spaces may lose fine-grained motion details. We present \textbf{TalkFlow}, a structured latent flow framework for speech-driven holistic motion generation. TalkFlow learns a continuous three-stream latent representation for upper-body motion, lower-body motion, and facial expressions, preserving part-specific dynamics without forcing heterogeneous motion components into a single latent space. To maintain holistic coordination, lightweight cross-stream interactions are incorporated in both latent representation learning and flow-based generation. Conditioned on multi-level speech features, TalkFlow performs speech-conditioned latent flow matching, learning a continuous transport process from source latents to realistic motion latents. Experiments on the BEAT2 dataset demonstrate strong performance across facial expression accuracy, body gesture quality, and speech-motion synchronization. Qualitative comparisons and user studies further show that TalkFlow generates more natural, expressive, and speech-aligned holistic motion than state-of-the-art methods. The project page is available at https://xinmuwang.github.io/TalkFlow/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FieldGuideRAG: Image-Grounded GraphRAG for Fine-Grained Recognition with Vision-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present FieldGuideRAG, a training-free GraphRAG method in which a vision-language model, or VLM, recognizes fine-grained species by comparing the query with real photographs stored on the nodes of a knowledge graph. Multimodal GraphRAG systems describe each entity in text, and text conveys little of the visual detail that separates look-alike species. Our graph stores one photograph on every species node and links each species to its relatives, its geographic range and its ecological facts. A frozen VLM verifies the query against the photograph of each candidate node. FieldGuideRAG fuses the verification scores with the range edge and answers questions about the organism from the fact edges of the verified species. On CUB-200, a Wikidata graph and four iNaturalist domains, the node photograph improves verification over the species name on every graph, while text descriptions add little. Verification of the candidate pool exceeds a SigLIP retriever by up to 16 points, the range edge adds 7 to 19 points on iNaturalist, and answering from fact edges is correct on up to 89.5% of 28,820 ecological questions. The verification scores also detect queries whose species is missing from the graph. Graphs, prompts and code will be released.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: CAMEL: Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning for Ultra-Lightweight Retinal Foundation Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Recent progress in deep learning has substantially advanced automated grading of ophthalmologic pathologies, supported by large annotated datasets and improved representation learning. However, a significant gap remains between state-of-the-art performance and clinical scalability. In particular, foundation models have reshaped image-based medical screening and diagnosis. These large-scale architectures trained on extensive datasets learn rich, generalizable feature representations that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks. In ophthalmology, RETFound, one of the most relevant foundation models for retinal images, performs strongly across classification, segmentation, and risk prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, foundation models are often computationally prohibitive, hindering their deployment in real-world clinical environments where hardware constraints and latency are critical. To bridge this gap, we introduce CAMEL (Cross-Architecture Masked Embedding Learning), a novel cross-architecture distillation framework that uses an asymmetric masking strategy during embedding learning to effectively transfer knowledge from massive teacher foundation models to compact, lightweight student models. Our experimental evaluation across four datasets shows that CAMEL preserves accuracy while drastically reducing computational complexity, enabling lightweight yet highly accurate models suitable for resource-limited clinical settings.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AVID: A Weakly Aligned RGB-Infrared Dataset and Perturbation Benchmark for Tiny Aerial Targets
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Long-range detection of small drones is complicated by their visual similarity to birds and by the limited detail available from ground-based cameras. Combining visible and infrared observations offers complementary information, but their usefulness depends on target size, cross-modal alignment, and image quality. We present AVID, a benchmark for studying these factors using real RGB-infrared bird-drone surveillance footage originating from the Drone Detection Dataset and curated for the IEEE ICIP 2025 Video and Image Processing Cup. AVID comprises 32,040 corresponding frame pairs from 115 videos, with 35,952 existing bird and drone annotations at $320\times256$ resolution. Targets occupy an unusually narrow size range: 68.1\% have a geometric-mean bounding-box side of 8--16 pixels, and 99.0\% meet the COCO small-object criterion. To characterize the geometric difficulty of combining the modalities, we introduce an object-relative alignment ratio and an alignment burden curve. In a sample of 300 frame pairs, 32.3\% have estimated global translations greater than 5 pixels; among the 264 pairs with matching annotations, 16.3\% exceed one median target side. We further introduce AVID-C, which simulates seven families of image degradation at five severity levels independently in RGB, infrared, or both. A fixed-feature analysis examines how scale, degradation, and added cross-modal shifts affect fitted bird-drone class overlap. At 12--16 pixels, the Bhattacharyya error bounds are 0.148 for RGB, 0.198 for infrared, and 0.046 for their combined features. These values describe separation in the specified feature and density models, not detector accuracy. Together, AVID and AVID-C support scale-aware, alignment-aware, and sensor-specific studies of tiny aerial targets.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: UFMF: Radar-Guided Kinematic Priors for Real-Time 4D Occupancy Forecasting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Real-time 4D occupancy forecasting requires reliably extrapolating both ego motion and surrounding actor motion under strict latency budgets. Recent occupancy world models improve long-horizon fidelity through generative decoders and 3D volumetric modeling, yet their computational cost makes real-time deployment challenging. Light-weight BEV forecasters meet latency requirements but often blur or suppress fast-moving actors at longer horizons. We present UFMF (Ultra-Fast Multi-modal Forecaster), a real-time forecaster that keeps an attention-free diagonal state-space temporal core while injecting targeted kinematic and geometric structure where lightweight models typically fail. A radar-guided velocity-aware dynamic prior (VADP) decomposes future displacement into a linear extrapolation plus a learned horizon-dependent residual. The resulting per-cell flow fields transport a compact dynamic latent subspace during rollout. Two auxiliary training constraints complement this branch: world-frame dynamic supervision enforces inter-horizon trajectory coherence, and class-conditioned vertical-profile supervision regularizes BEV-to-3D lifting. UFMF operates at 122 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and reaches 0.45 fast-displacement mIoU on nuScenes, outperforming recent occupancy world models at a fraction of their computational cost.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Let LiDAR Decide Where to Look: Geometry-Measured Token Selection for Efficient Sparse Latent World Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-centric autonomous driving models encode thousands of image tokens per frame, yet most depict sky, buildings, or empty road---content irrelevant to planning. Worse, these tokens dilute the planner's attention: we show that randomly discarding 75% of tokens already outperforms the dense model, because the planner can concentrate on the remaining driving-critical content. Building on this finding, we present Geometry-Aware Token Selection (GATS), which uses LiDAR and radar point projections to select a small fraction of image tokens before the vision backbone runs. Because the selector operates on measured 3D geometry rather than visual features, the backbone encodes only the selected patches, cutting end-to-end FLOPs by up to $18\times$.
