Subsequently, we apply HumiTransfer to 1,200 in-the-wild videos, producing approximately 500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 26-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and the 23-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robot, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. Across both robots, HumiTransfer achieves superior motion fidelity, preserves inter-body relationships, and maintains contact accuracy compared with existing baselines. Moreover, we demonstrate that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for synthesizing interactive humanoid motions following a human partner. Finally, our real robot deployments confirm the physical executability of the transferred motions in real-world settings. Our project is available at https://aioznetwork.github.io/HumiMimic/

Robotics.title: SwarmCoDe: A Scalable Co-Design Framework for Heterogeneous Robot Swarms via Dynamic Speciation
Robotics.summary: Robot swarm co-design requires optimizing not only individual robot designs and behaviors, but also the heterogeneous swarm structure: how many robot types should exist, how they specialize and cooperate, and in what proportions they are deployed. However, these structural choices are often specified in advance rather than optimized. We present SwarmCoDe, a Cooperative Co-Evolutionary Algorithm (CCEA) that incorporates swarm decomposition into the optimization process without requiring the number of species to be specified in advance. SwarmCoDe combines dynamic speciation with evolved genetic tags, partner selectivity, and relative dominance to jointly optimize robot hardware, task-planning behavior, cooperative relationships, and deployed swarm composition. Across replicated simulated foraging experiments, SwarmCoDe discovers task-dependent swarm decompositions and adapts them when task requirements change, in contrast to fixed-K CCEAs which are sensitive to their pre-defined decomposition. We further show that fabrication budgets can change the preferred swarm composition and robot designs, and that SwarmCoDe can adapt its co-design under these resource constraints. Finally, SwarmCoDe co-designs 200-agent swarms using only 50 evolutionary individuals, demonstrating deployment at four times the evolutionary population size. Together, these results demonstrate that the heterogeneous structure of a robot swarm can be incorporated as a design variable and optimized alongside the robots themselves.
Robotics.comment: Revised and expanded version. 13 pages, 8 figures

Robotics.title: Coupled Guidance for Flow Matching
Robotics.summary: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.

Robotics.title: Learning Safe Flow Matching Robot Policies from Binary Feasibility Oracles
Robotics.summary: Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.

Robotics.title: Don't Risk It!: Trajectory-Conditioned Distributional Risk for LiDAR-Only Crowd Navigation
Robotics.summary: Efficient crowd navigation requires anticipating dynamic collision-free space without relying on fragile object tracking. We propose the Don't Risk It Planner (DRIP), an end-to-end LiDAR-only planning framework that couples occupancy forecasting with trajectory-conditioned clearance and uncertainty estimation. Operating directly on LiDAR-derived occupancy grid histories, DRIP predicts a distribution over minimum robot-obstacle clearance for candidate control sequences to evaluate collision risk. The model is trained using a risk cost that grounds predictive uncertainty directly in empirical collision outcomes rather than geometric regression alone. In closed-loop experiments with up to 45 pedestrians, DRIP achieves higher success rates with fewer collisions and reduced freezing behavior compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Robotics.title: Normalizing Flow-Enhanced Message Passing for Multirobot Collaborative Localization
Robotics.summary: Accurate, robust, and adaptive localization is essential for various robotic operations. This paper proposes a parametric message passing (MP) algorithm for distributed collaborative localization, unifying Gaussian belief propagation (GBP) for robot state estimation and mean-field (MF) approximation for noise inference. Unlike conventional MP algorithms, the proposed formulation directly optimizes the natural parameters of beliefs, establishing a principled connection between MP and gradient estimators for handling non-conjugate terms arising from nonlinear measurement models. Beyond linearization and sampling, we further design a normalizing flow (NF)-based gradient estimator, enabling learnable sampling. End-to-end training tunes NF parameters according to the behavior of MP, improving estimation accuracy while reducing the required number of iterations. To support robot states involving rotations, the method is extended to Lie group spaces. Finally, the method is applied to a multirobot localization task fusing odometry, global navigation satellite system (GNSS) measurements, and inter-robot ultra wideband (UWB) ranging. Extensive simulations and experiments on autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) demonstrate superior state estimation accuracy, enhanced robustness and adaptability under ranging outliers and varying noise statistics, as well as good generalization across different operating conditions.
Robotics.comment: 20 pages; accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Robotics; updated to the accepted manuscript

Systems and Control.title: A Closed-loop Framework to Discriminate Models Using Optimal Control
Systems and Control.summary: Predicting the response of an observed system to a known input is a fruitful first step to accurately control the system's dynamics. Despite the recent advances in fully data-driven algorithms, the most interpretable way to reach this goal is through mechanistic mathematical modeling. Here, we leverage optimal control and propose a closed-loop iterative method to choose among a set of candidate models the one that most accurately predicts an observed system. We assume that one has control over an input of the observed system and access to measurements of its response. Our approach is to identify the input control that maximally discriminates the response of the candidate models, allowing us to determine which model is best by comparing such responses with the observed data. We demonstrate our proposed framework in numerical simulations before applying it during an electrophysiology experiment, successfully discriminating between different models for photocurrents produced via opsin dynamics.

Systems and Control.title: A Robust Approach to Belief Mismatch in Non-cooperative Dynamic Games
Systems and Control.summary: Game-theoretic models are increasingly used to describe multi-agent interactions in control and robotics applications. However, theoretical and computational complexity makes these models intractable in many dynamic, incomplete information scenarios. Recent work makes strong assumptions to reduce computational complexity: agents share sensor measurements with one another and maintain a common estimate of state uncertainty. Unfortunately, these assumptions enforce a degree of cooperation in generically noncooperative interactions. This paper takes the perspective of an ego agent seeking both computational tractability and robustness to unanticipated behavior of other agents due to mismatched state estimates from private---rather than shared---sensor measurements. To that end, we formulate the game theoretic planning problem in an augmented belief space with perturbed Bayesian dynamics that allows the ego to predict all agents' potentially divergent state estimates. These perturbations are chosen by a hypothetical adversary, ``nature,'' to reflect how non-ego agents' state estimates---based on measurements the ego agent will not see at runtime---may deviate from the ego's own belief. Ultimately, our approach can be understood in the spirit of classical H-infinity robust control, extended to noncooperative, stochastic dynamic games. We present a solver with polynomial-time iterations and conduct two experiments which show how robust belief space reasoning leads ego agents to proactively limit their future vulnerability to model misspecification of other agents' beliefs and actions, reducing performance degradation by over 48%.

Systems and Control.title: A Temporal Cellular Sheaf Framework for Multi-Agent Systems with Switching Communication Topologies
Systems and Control.summary: Cellular sheaves serve as a natural modeling framework for encoding heterogeneity in the state and interaction spaces of multi-agent systems. This work examines switching communication graphs with the use of temporal cellular sheaves, which we construct to represent heterogeneous agent state spaces, the maps that relate them, and their respective communication constraints. We then develop sufficient conditions under which a multi-agent system defined on a temporal cellular sheaf can solve the target tracking problem by generalizing the existing concept of joint connectivity. Using a Lyapunov-based stability analysis, we demonstrate that the target tracking error of the network converges to a neighborhood of the origin.

Systems and Control.title: RC Prediction: A Python Package for Parameter-Aware Reservoir Computing
Systems and Control.summary: A nonlinear dynamical system can be characterized by the autonomous evolution of its state in time and its dependence on system parameters. As a parameter varies, the dynamics can change quantitatively and, at bifurcation points, qualitatively. When the governing equations are unknown, a data-driven model should therefore capture both elements from observational data, rather than reproduce the dynamics at a single operating condition only. Parameter-aware reservoir computing (PARC) is a model-free framework for this purpose, where the parameter is supplied to a reservoir computer through an additional input channel. PARC is trained on time series recorded at several parameter values, and the trained reservoir, run in closed loop as an autonomous dynamical system, generates trajectories at parameter values that were never observed. rc_prediction is an open-source Python package that implements this workflow. It provides multi-parameter training of a reservoir, autonomous closed-loop prediction at user-specified parameter values, parameter scans, and a standard echo state network for forecasting at a fixed parameter. Hyperparameter optimization and optional GPU acceleration through PyTorch are also provided. We use three benchmark dynamical systems as examples to demonstrate its usage. As one of the featured applications, here we illustrate the prediction of critical transitions and system collapse: trained only on pre-critical data, the model is queried beyond the training range to predict whether the system collapses, to estimate the critical parameter $p_c^{*}$, and to characterize transient lifetimes.

Systems and Control.title: Learning the Omega-Limit Partition from Approximate Koopman Invariants
Systems and Control.summary: Nonlinear dynamical systems with multiple omega-limit sets pose a fundamental challenge for global finite-dimensional Koopman modeling with continuous observables. A natural way to address this challenge is to decompose the state space into forward-invariant regions associated with distinct asymptotic behaviors and to learn a separate Koopman model for each region. This paper studies how to compute such partitions from data. We establish conditions under which Koopman-invariant observables, namely eigenfunctions associated with the unit eigenvalue, characterize the stationary partition induced by omega-limit sets. Building on this characterization, we develop OPAL (Omega-limit Partitions from Approximate invariants Learned from data), an algorithm that extracts partitions from approximate invariant observables. Numerical examples show that the recovered partitions capture the relevant asymptotic regions and support multiple regional linear Koopman models with significantly improved long-horizon prediction capabilities.

Systems and Control.title: A Mixed $H_{\infty}$--Passivity Approach for Leveraging Heat-Pump-Connected District Heating Systems as Frequency Support in Electric Power Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Heat-pump (HP)-connected district heating systems (DHSs) can support grid frequency by rapidly modulating HP electrical consumption while accommodating the resulting heat imbalance. Thermal-state-informed HP control improves EPS--DHS coordination, but introduces slower DHS dynamics and heat-side disturbance propagation at the electrical interface on the time scale of secondary frequency control. This paper formulates the regulated DHS as a grid-facing dynamic port and develops a mixed $H_\infty$--passivity framework for disturbance-independent temperature regulation while preserving a clean electrical response during secondary frequency control. Sufficient conditions guarantee local asymptotic stability of the EPS--HP--DHS interconnection across primary frequency control, secondary frequency control, and DHS regulation. These stability conditions are integrated with multi-channel $H_\infty$ attenuation of DHS-state-dependent electrical dynamics, heat-disturbance propagation, and DHS-regulation errors, yielding a tractable convex LMI program for controller synthesis. Cross-model validation deploys controllers synthesized on control-oriented EPS--DHS models, without retuning, on an open-source electromechanical IEEE 39-bus model coupled with four high-fidelity finite-volume DHS models retaining thermal transport, storage, and heat-loss dynamics. The resulting controller improves EPS--DHS coordination without compromising the grid-facing electrical response.

Systems and Control.title: Temporal and spatial couplings in the dynamics of human walking and running
Systems and Control.summary: Rhythmic behaviours such as walking and running are commonly modelled as dynamical systems around a stable limit cycle. To keep such models tractable, it is usually assumed that each step depends only on the previous one, that the limit cycle is fixed, and that the sagittal and frontal planes can be studied separately. Here, we test these assumptions in seven public datasets of human gait (71 participants), including 16 people who both walked and ran. We fit linear step-to-step maps and validate them by cross-validation, holding out more data where more data exist. At first sight, gait has memory: the state two steps back lowers the prediction error by up to 29\%. Yet most of this temporal coupling vanishes once the operating point may drift slowly and measurement noise is modelled; gait remains limit-cycle-like, around an operating point that moves. Running keeps more memory than walking in the same people. Spatial coupling between the planes is present in most participants, mainly from sagittal to frontal, but weak. This supports planar models of healthy gait, while a repeatable, task-dependent coupling index may serve as a measure of gait quality. The simple models are wrong, but useful enough.

Systems and Control.title: Learning Stabilizing Latent Feedback Controllers via Multi-Step Backward Losses
Systems and Control.summary: Can learned latent dynamics models support the design of feedback controllers that provably stabilize the original system? For linear time-invariant systems, we show that learning linear autoencoders and latent dynamics with multi-step prediction-reconstruction losses $\unicode{x2014}$ which we term "backward losses" as they encourage latent trajectories to reconstruct full state trajectories $\unicode{x2014}$ provably recovers the structure needed for stabilization. Specifically, a sufficiently long reconstruction horizon ensures that a minimum ${H}_\infty$-norm controller designed using the learned latent model stabilizes the original system through output-feedback via the corresponding encoder, provided the latent dimension is large enough to capture all non-stable modes of the underlying system. We also show why both reconstruction and a multi-step horizon are essential: forward prediction losses that require only low prediction error along latent trajectories admit global loss minimizers that discard unstable modes regardless of horizon length, while single-step reconstruction losses can yield latent models whose stabilizing controllers fail to stabilize the original system. Finally, experiments on a non-linear flexible-arm system illustrate the practical implications of our results for learning non-linear autoencoders and latent dynamics.

Systems and Control.title: Confidence-Modulated Safety Filtering for End-to-End Policies
Systems and Control.summary: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.

Systems and Control.title: Approximate Dynamic Programming for Link Reconfiguration to Reduce Malicious Input Controllability in Consensus Networks
Systems and Control.summary: Communication links influence how strongly a malicious input at one sensor affects a consensus network. We study how a defender can reduce this influence by selecting one additional link after observing the currently attacked sensor. The attacked sensor changes over time, and vulnerability is measured by the trace of a finite-horizon controllability Gramian. A prescribed local epsilon-greedy attacker response rule defines a discounted Markov decision process for the defender. Exact dynamic programming (DP) provides an optimal policy using the full Gramian payoff matrix and attacker transition model. We then introduce approximate dynamic programming (ADP) that learns from sampled attacker transitions and empirical Gramian costs estimated from measured impulse responses. Under conditionally unbiased costs and standard sampling and learning-rate conditions, the learned action-value table converges to the exact DP solution. The analysis uses Bellman contraction and bounds the effect of persistent Gramian estimation bias, establishing when measured responses recover optimal defender decisions without constructing the full payoff matrix. In simulations on 20- and 100-node graphs, empirical ADP rollout costs are within 0.23% and 1.76%, respectively, of exact DP. In a two-dimensional intruder tracking example, both policies reduce network-wide root-mean-square tracking error spread by approximately 25% relative to an unmitigated attack.

Systems and Control.title: Fast and Accurate Hydro Unit Commitment
Systems and Control.summary: We introduce a fast novel algorithm to commit hydro-generators. We show that our algorithm can commit 56 generators for 200 days 10,000 times faster than Hexaly, the leading commercial solver for scheduling problems, without sacrificing solution quality. Our method can commit 1792 generators for an entire year in approximately 20 seconds on commodity hardware. Hexaly is unable to solve problems of this size in reasonable time. We attain this runtime improvement by introducing a greedy-heuristic tailored for hydro units. We provide a direction for a possible proof that the error our solver makes decreases with the problem size. This is supported by our experimental results. We prove that our solver's runtime scales log-linearly in the number of generators and time periods.

Systems and Control.title: Incremental Stability of Gradient Flows under Generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz Inequalities and Its Implications for General Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Gradient flows of twice continuously differentiable strongly convex and convex objectives are, respectively, incrementally exponentially stable and non-expansive in the Euclidean metric. In this work, we investigate to what extent these properties extend to nonconvex objectives satisfying generalized Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequalities. For objectives with a unique minimizer, we establish conditions under which the gradient flow is contracting in a state-dependent Riemannian metric and incrementally exponentially stable. For objectives with nonunique minimizers, we generalize the non-expansivity of convex objectives to incremental stability for more general nonconvex objectives. We focus on incremental stability due to its implication to convergence to equilibrium points; when paired with a Lyapunov function it implies pointwise convergence to a minimizer and continuity of the endpoint map. Along the way, we derive new structural results for incrementally stable nonlinear systems and extend the analysis to Heavy-Ball and Dynamical Inertial Newton flows.

Systems and Control.title: Addendum to "Optimal Steering of a Linear Stochastic System to a Final Probability Distribution, Part II"
Systems and Control.summary: We hereby fill in a gap in an induction argument used in the proof of a theorem on state-covariance controllability of linear stochastic systems in an earlier paper by the authors. The mathematical statement is true. The missing point in the proof concerns the assertion that, in the canonical single-input case, the control can be assigned arbitrary endpoint values. We amend the argument by proving a slightly stronger induction statement that permits arbitrary finite endpoint jets of the control. An independent approach to homogeneous state-covariance controllability was provided in a paper by Abdelgalil and Georgiou (2025) as a corollary of strong controllability results on $\GLp(n,\mathbb R)$, and shown herein that it extends to the case of additive noise as well.

Systems and Control.title: Dynamic Persuasion: Managing Reputation under Censored Feedback
Systems and Control.summary: We study a long-run sender who repeatedly communicates about a state to a sequence of myopic receivers and whose credibility is a public score updated from past interactions. Receivers face a lemon loss and an opportunity loss, and their behavior depends on these only through a single index, the tolerance. Because the score records only detected misrepresentations, it rests above the sender's true honesty rate; we characterize this credibility premium in closed form. In a fluid limit in which the score adjusts slowly, no policy earns more than operating at a single credibility level, and the sender's gain from managing credibility equals the value of the premium: against receivers who correct for imperfect detection, that gain vanishes. At a fixed adjustment speed, every policy is bounded by the fluid value plus a term linear in the speed. We then study three policy classes, linear, (s,S), and threshold, obtain the optimal parameters of the linear and threshold classes in closed form, show how receiver losses shape them, and show that, under an approximation, the optimal (s,S) band collapses to a threshold. Simulations of the dynamics agree with the closed forms and indicate where the single-level conclusion stops: bands pay when switching modes is costly, and cycles pay when demand is seasonal.
Systems and Control.comment: 44 pages, 8 figures. A preliminary version of part of this work appears in Proc. IEEE CDC 2026

Systems and Control.title: How a group that cannot communicate knows itself by its enemy
Systems and Control.summary: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
Systems and Control.comment: 6 pages main text; 35-page SI Appendix included as an ancillary file. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23743441

Systems and Control.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
Systems and Control.summary: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.

Systems and Control.title: Quantifying Linepack Storage Potential of Hydrogen Networks
Systems and Control.summary: Future hydrogen systems depend on large-scale storage to balance supply and demand. Hydrogen networks can store energy in the pipelines themselves, but the potential of this linepack storage has not been quantified comparably to dedicated storage facilities. We transfer metrics established for conventional storage, such as volume capacity and full-cycle equivalents, to hydrogen networks. To evaluate them, we formulate an optimization problem maximizing linepack storage utilization, subject to non-convex PDE-based constraints describing transient gas flow. We solve the optimization problem over a full-year horizon to capture seasonal variations and to assess the interaction with cavern storage. For computational tractability, we propose a simulation-informed sequential convex programming approach with adaptive time stepping that reduces problem size by up to 98% at accuracy comparable to fixed-resolution methods. For the GasLib-40 topology with German scenario data, the network provides a volume capacity of 24 million normal cubic meters at 28 full-cycle equivalents per year.
Systems and Control.comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, submitted to the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy

Systems and Control.title: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model
Systems and Control.summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.

Systems and Control.title: Analog Realization and Measurement of a Forced Aliev-Panfilov Excitable Oscillator
Systems and Control.summary: A single resistor moves a discrete analog realization of the forced Aliev-Panfilov excitable oscillator from a chaotic operating point of the model to a regular one. In this model a rate parameter multiplies the complete right-hand side of the excitation equation, forcing term included. The input resistor of the excitation integrator sets that parameter, so no state, delay element, or controller is added. Sampled waveforms were recorded at two resistor values, with two independent runs each. The measured excitation excursion agrees with numerical integration to within three percent at the baseline setting and five percent at the rate-controlled setting. Between the two settings the excitation excursion contracts by a factor of thirteen. At the rate-controlled setting the recovery excursion exceeds prediction by a factor of eight. This excess traces to a displaced operating point on the state-dependent recovery rate. Thermal drift in the multiplier chain and leakage at the high-impedance recovery-rate divider could each produce it, and the present data do not separate them. A tested bipolar input stage strongly loads that divider, a constraint absent from the ideal equations. The divider, not the sub-hertz signal bandwidth, sets the amplifier input-stage requirement.

Systems and Control.title: A Tutorial on Shape Servoing of Deformable Objects-Part I: Fundamentals
Systems and Control.summary: In robotics, shape control (or shape servoing) refers to the automatic manipulation of a deformable object to achieve a desired shape. It involves a feedback loop that exploits the relation between robot motion and changes in the measured shape. This relation, known as the interaction Jacobian or, in this context, the deformation Jacobian, depends on the object's mechanical properties, geometry, and boundary conditions (e.g., where the object is grasped). Because these factors are often difficult to model accurately, the deformation Jacobian can be estimated locally from observed shape changes produced by commanded robot motions, without requiring a fine-tuned mechanical model. This article is the first of a two-part tutorial on data-driven Jacobian-based shape control of deformable objects. It introduces the central elements of the approach: the formulation of the shape-control problem, shape representation, estimation and online update of the deformation Jacobian, and a standard control law from the literature. It then assembles these elements into a complete shape-servoing loop, derives a local stability condition for this loop, and illustrates why some target shapes cannot be reached. Part II covers more advanced topics. Throughout both parts, a simulated planar example in which two robot arms manipulate an elastic rod observed by a camera illustrates the concepts.
Systems and Control.comment: Part I of a two-part tutorial. 9 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/nachocz/tutorial_on_shape_servoing_of_deformable_objects. Interactive demos: https://nachocz.github.io/tutorial_on_shape_servoing_of_deformable_objects/

Systems and Control.title: A Behavioral approach to Constrained Linear Quadratic Control: Feasibility and Optimality
Systems and Control.summary: This paper develops a constrained linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control framework within the behavioral approach. Unlike classical formulations that rely on state-input representations, our method treats both the system dynamics and the constraints as trajectory-level objects. The system is modeled through a kernel representation, while inequality constraints are captured using behavioral inequalities defined over infinite-dimensional convex cones. Using quadratic differential forms (QDFs) to encode performance indices, we formulate the constrained LQ problem as a convex variational optimization over trajectories. By employing Gateaux differentials, we derive the stationarity and complementarity conditions and show that they admit a representation as an augmented behavioral system whose unique decomposition into autonomous and controllable sub-behaviors yields a complete parameterization of all optimal constrained trajectories. The resulting conditions constitute a behavioral analogue of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) framework. A numerical example illustrates the effect of inequality constraints on the optimal behavior. The framework provides a general, trajectory-level representation for constrained optimal control and opens avenues for closed-loop and data-driven extensions.
Systems and Control.comment: Accepted for publication at IEEE Indian Control Conference 2027

Systems and Control.title: A Two-Wheeled Quadrotor with All-Clockwise Tilted Rotors for Level-Attitude Surface Locomotnion
Systems and Control.summary: Conventional wheel-equipped quadrotor UAVs must tilt their bodies to generate lateral forces, limiting their ability to maintain a desired attitude during lateral motion. This paper proposes a wheeled quadrotor with all-clockwise tilted rotors that uses surface contact as a constraint to generate propulsion along the contact surface without tilting the vehicle. We analyze feasible forces and system controllability under surface contact and optimize the vehicle design considering different rotor-spin configurations. The optimization results show that a configuration in which all four rotors spin clockwise can generate a larger tangential force than the conventional alternating-spin configuration. This approach enables both aerial and contact-based locomotion without additional rotor-tilting actuators or mechanisms. Simulation results demonstrate both hovering in free space and horizontal locomotion on a floor while maintaining a level attitude.

Systems and Control.title: Fundamental Limits of Sampling-Based Reachability: Geometry and Flow Distortion
Systems and Control.summary: Sampling-based reachability estimates reachable sets from finitely many simulated trajectory endpoints. Existing guarantees often control missed probability mass or approximation error relative to the convex hull of the reachable set, leaving the geometric error relative to the reachable set incompletely characterized. We study this error as a problem of support estimation under flow distortion. Our assumptions combine a uniform lower bound on the local volume density of the initial set, a lower bound on the sampling density, and a one-sided Lipschitz constant $μ$ for the vector field. These conditions admit initial sets with corners and dynamics that may expand or contract. In the fine-accuracy regime, $\tilde{\mathcal O}\bigl(2^ne^{nμT}(R/r)^n/(ρκ)\bigr)$ independent endpoint samples suffice for Hausdorff accuracy $r$ using the endpoint cloud. Here, $n$ is the state dimension, $T$ is the horizon, $R$ is the volume-equivalent radius, and $ρ$ and $κ$ quantify sampling density and local volume density. For $n\ge2$ and sufficiently small $κ$, a minimax lower bound over all estimators based only on independent endpoints matches these dependencies up to a dimension-dependent factor $2\cdot4^n$ and logarithmic factors, within the stated parameter range and when the state domain accommodates the construction. The exponential burden in dimension, and in the horizon for expanding systems, is therefore intrinsic to this observation model. Planar experiments illustrate the predicted effects of corners and contraction; robot-arm experiments show how empirical accuracy deteriorates with dimension.
Systems and Control.comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Extended version of the CoRL 2026 paper; submitted to IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control. Code: https://github.com/JeanLew01/reachapprox

Systems and Control.title: Biased Stochastic Gradient Descent under Local Geometry, with Application to Data-Driven LQR
Systems and Control.summary: We study stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with biased stochastic gradient oracles for objectives that are only locally smooth and locally gradient dominated, with constants that may grow with the objective value and are required only on a sublevel set. Such oracles arise in data-driven optimization and control, where the gradient must be estimated from noisy data through nonlinear procedures such as model identification or smoothing and truncation. We show that if the oracle bias decays sufficiently fast, even only in expectation, and the second moment of the oracle remains bounded, then, on an event of prescribed probability, the optimality gap converges to zero almost surely with an asymptotic rate, and in expectation with an explicit bound at every iteration that separates the contributions of the initial condition, the oracle bias, and the gradient noise. We illustrate the framework on the linear quadratic regulator (LQR), whose cost satisfies these properties only on sublevel sets and whose policy gradient depends on the unknown system matrices. We consider an indirect estimator, which identifies the system matrices online, and a direct zeroth-order estimator. We characterize the bias and the second moment of both estimators and show how to choose their parameters so that the convergence conditions hold. On an event of prescribed probability, both data-driven policy gradient methods converge to the optimal policy almost surely and in expectation, with guarantees for all iterations rather than at a single prescribed iteration. We compare the two estimators, and numerical experiments on the LQR illustrate the results.

Systems and Control.title: socx: GPU-Accelerated Chance-Constrained Stochastic Optimal Control using JAX
Systems and Control.summary: In this article, we present socx, a GPU-accelerated solver for lifted convex reformulations of linear stochastic optimal control under chance constraints, implemented in JAX. We demonstrate that by exploiting the sparse and independent structure of the problem, distributed optimization can reduce it to simpler problems: independent linear-quadratic tracking (LQT) problems and Euclidean projections onto sets. These simpler problems can be solved in parallel and then coupled using the constraints. To validate our solver, we run it on a hover-linearized 3D quadrotor and show a speed-up of up to $98\times$ over MOSEK and up to $2224\times$ over SCS. socx also solves horizons up to $N=1120$, whereas MOSEK runs out of memory at $N=320$. We present ablations to isolate the key components that enable the speed-up.

Systems and Control.title: Finite-Sample LTI System Identification from a Misspecified Finite Model Set
Systems and Control.summary: We consider the problem of finite-sample identification of an unknown LTI system from a finite hypothesis class. In contrast to existing results that assume the hypothesis class contains the true system, we consider the misspecified setting, where the true system does not belong to the hypothesis class. We first characterize the resulting estimation target and its dependence on the data-generation scheme. We then establish a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability that any identification algorithm must incur. Finally, we analyze the robustness of an existing exponential weighting-based identification algorithm to the misspecification and derive a finite-sample upper bound on its failure probability. Our results illustrate when using a misspecified finite hypothesis class can provide an advantage over identification without prior knowledge of the candidate systems.

Systems and Control.title: Robust Taylor-Lagrange Control for Safety-Critical Systems with Guaranteed Feasibility
Systems and Control.summary: The Control Barrier Function (CBF) method has been widely adopted in solving safety-critical control problems. However, the existence of a CBF is only a sufficient condition for system safety. The recently proposed Taylor-Lagrange Control (TLC) method addresses this limitation by providing a necessary and sufficient condition, but it is still vulnerable to the feasibility preservation problem (e.g., due to the inter-sampling effect when time is discretized). In this paper, we propose a robust TLC (rTLC) method to address the feasibility preservation problem and show how to use it to solve optimal control problems. Specifically, the rTLC method expands the safety function to an order higher than its relative degree using Taylor's expansion with Lagrange remainder, which allows the control to explicitly show up at the current time instead of a future time in the original TLC method. This implies that the safety constraint remains satisfied over the entire discretization time interval that follows. Moreover, the rTLC method naturally addresses the feasibility preservation problem with only a single hyper-parameter (the discretization time interval size during implementation), compared to significantly more parameters for its counterparts. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed rTLC method through an adaptive cruise control problem, and compare it with existing safety-critical control methods.
Systems and Control.comment: This version addressed one technical problem of the inter-sampling effect in rTLC

Systems and Control.title: Learned Terminal Costs for Short-Horizon Model Predictive Control of Autonomous Trucks in Interactive Highway Traffic
Systems and Control.summary: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.

Systems and Control.title: Reduced-Order Data Assimilation for Thermospheric Density Using Physics-informed SINDyc Models
Systems and Control.summary: Orbit prediction and space situational awareness require accurate thermospheric mass density, which responds nonlinearly to solar and geomagnetic forcing across several orders of magnitude. Physics-based general circulation models resolve that response but are computationally expensive, while empirical models run cheaply and carry no time-evolving atmospheric state. An autoregressive Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics with control (SINDyc-AR) model, derived from the Thermosphere-Ionosphere-Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIE-GCM), captures the dominant modes of variability and their dependence on the drivers at a fraction of the parent model's cost. An extended Kalman filter assimilates in situ observations from CHAMP, GRACE, GRACE-FO, GOCE, and Swarm into that model across several orbital configurations and geomagnetic conditions, with a linear DMDc model as reference. Assimilation reduces density error relative to open-loop prediction, most visibly during geomagnetic storms and under single-satellite coverage. The two reduced-order models perform comparably throughout. NRLMSIS 2.1 and HASDM can outperform the assimilated model far from the assimilated track, so results are framed as improvements over the open-loop forecast. An observation-calibrated global density record spanning August 2000 to December 2025 is released alongside this work.

Systems and Control.title: Learning Maximal Regions of Attraction on Compact Sets using Taylor Lyapunov Networks
Systems and Control.summary: We consider the problem of learning maximal Lyapunov functions to compute the maximal region of attraction of nonlinear dynamical systems using neural networks. Two obstacles limit existing neural-network approaches: 1) finite-width approximations can fail to preserve the strict Lyapunov inequalities near the equilibrium, where they become arbitrarily weak, and 2) training is necessarily performed on a bounded computational domain for which the classical Lyapunov and Zubov theorems do not directly apply. To address these issues, first we derive Lyapunov and Zubov theorems directly on a prescribed compact computational domain, characterizing the maximal region of attraction within that domain as the solution of a boundary-value PDE. Second, we introduce the Taylor Lyapunov network, an architecture that prescribes the quadratic leading-order term via the system's linearization and represents the higher-order remainder through a structured cubic factorization, guaranteeing that any network in this class is a valid local Lyapunov function by construction. Finally, we prove that Taylor Lyapunov networks are universal approximators of maximal Lyapunov functions on compact domains, and combine these results into an unsupervised, physics-informed training procedure. Numerical experiments on systems of varying dimensions and stability types show that the proposed architecture is efficient at estimating the maximum region of attraction.

Systems and Control.title: Control of Seizure Dynamics in a Bistable System with Pulsatile Inputs
Systems and Control.summary: Bistable neural population models describe transitions associated with epilepsy through the coexistence of a stable equilibrium representing normal neural activity and a stable limit cycle representing seizure-like oscillations. Perturbations that drive the system outside the equilibrium's basin of attraction can trigger transitions to seizure-like activity. Enlarging this basin enables the system to recover normal activity from a larger set of perturbed states, providing a model-based mechanism for reducing frequency of seizure initiation. Motivated by electrical brain stimulation, this paper investigates basin enlargement using pulsatile feedback control. Combining higher-order averaging with periodic near-identity transformations, we establish conditions under which nonzero-mean and zero-mean pulsatile feedback gains enlarge the basin of attraction and derive guidelines for pulse design. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical enlargement.

Systems and Control.title: A heuristic for optimal coordination of autonomous vehicles: real-time algorithms
Systems and Control.summary: When coordinating connected and automated vehicles at an unsignalized intersection, the crossing order and the vehicle trajectories must be decided jointly. For a fixed crossing order, the problem can be formulated conveniently in a bi-level form where each vehicle solves its own optimal control problem, whose optimal value is a function of its entry and exit times, and a coordinator optimizes these times subject to precedence constraints. We compute the first and second order sensitivities of lower-level problems, which are required to solve the upper-level problem, by means of algorithmic differentiation using the real-time software package \texttt{acados}. This implementation exploits tailored algorithms to obtain a computationally efficient implementation of the optimal coordination algorithm. We validate our implementation in numerical simulations that demonstrate both real-time feasibility and effectiveness of our algorithm.

Systems and Control.title: A heuristic for optimal coordination of autonomous vehicles: static problems
Systems and Control.summary: We consider the coordination of autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections, where trajectory planning and crossing-order decisions are intrinsically coupled, thereby making their simultaneous optimization intractable in practice. To this end, we propose a heuristic based on a hierarchical structure consisting of a series of nonlinear programs (NLP) in the lower level, which optimizes trajectories of each vehicle for a given crossing order, and a high-level heuristic to design new crossing schedules that exploits sensitivity information from the lower-level NLPs. Extensive numerical simulations across a broad range of traffic scenarios demonstrate that our strategy achieves substantially improved scheduling with respect to first-in-first-out ordering while preserving computational tractability.

Systems and Control.title: A heuristic for optimal coordination of autonomous vehicles: dynamic problems
Systems and Control.summary: The coordination of autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections requires deciding both the trajectories of the vehicles and their crossing order, with the additional difficulty that the set of vehicles to be coordinated changes as traffic flows through the intersection. Since the resulting mixed-integer optimal control problem is hard to solve online, we propose an arrival-triggered receding-horizon scheme built around a schedule-refinement heuristic: for a fixed crossing order, a single nonlinear program (NLP) optimizes all trajectories and crossing times, and the first-order sensitivities of the cost with respect to the vehicle schedule are used to select adjacent swaps that are likely to reduce the overall cost. Replanning is triggered only when a new vehicle arrives, the new vehicle is appended at the tail of the current crossing order, and a memory of evaluated swaps that persists across replanning steps avoids redundant computations. Simulations of traffic scenarios involving streams of a few hundred heterogeneous vehicles show that the proposed scheme recovers most of the optimality gap incurred by first-in-first-out scheduling.

Systems and Control.title: Dual-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Vehicle Scheduling and Multi-Energy Dispatch in Electric-Hydrogen-Transport Systems
Systems and Control.summary: Electric-hydrogen-transport systems (EHTSs) require coordinated scheduling of electric and hydrogen vehicles together with multi-energy dispatch. These operations form a sequential decision process: upstream vehicle scheduling (VS) determines service allocation and order, thereby endogenously shaping the electricity and hydrogen demands faced by downstream energy dispatch (ED). This paper develops a dual-agent reinforcement learning framework tailored to the heterogeneous decision structures. The vehicle-scheduling agent combines proximal policy optimisation (PPO) with a Plackett-Luce policy to learn vehicle-priority permutations, which are then mapped to feasible charger and refueller assignments through a greedy allocation. The energy-dispatch agent employs twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) for continuous storage and energy-flow control. The directional coupling between the two decision layers is analysed, revealing that updates to the upstream scheduling policy can shift the demand distribution experienced by the downstream dispatcher. A three-stage training mechanism is therefore introduced, combining layer-wise pretraining with concurrent fine-tuning to mitigate the effects of scheduling-induced distribution shifts on downstream ED learning. Year-long case studies show that the proposed framework achieves the lowest vehicle-service delay and energy cost among the 11 evaluated methods, demonstrating effective coordination between vehicle scheduling and multi-energy dispatch.

Systems and Control.title: Agentic process evidence
Systems and Control.summary: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations

Systems and Control.title: Safe Platooning under Input Constraints with Link-Wise Velocity String Stability
Systems and Control.summary: We propose a decentralized controller for vehicle platoons with different braking and propulsion limits. The method uses only local distance and velocity measurements and requires neither online optimization nor exact vehicle parameters. The design combines a braking-distance safety margin with an adaptive funnel that relaxes the spacing requirement during propulsion saturation. A standstill mechanism prevents backward motion and supports stop-and-go operation. Under explicit uniform conditions on the vehicle parameters, controller settings, and initial states, we prove that closed-loop solutions exist for all time, collisions are avoided, and input limits are satisfied. Moreover, each follower tracks its predecessor's velocity range with gain one, up to an explicit additive offset determined by the funnel width and the braking-distance term. This bound establishes link-wise velocity string stability. Both the offset and the bounds on speeds and spacing errors are independent of vehicle index and platoon length. Simulations with 2 to 100 followers illustrate safety and bounded velocity deviations under disturbances and actuator limits.

Systems and Control.title: LC-Resonance Placement Limits and Damping Recovery in Virtual-Admittance-Based Grid-Forming Inverter Control
Systems and Control.summary: Compact LC-filter design and inner-loop control must be coordinated for stable grid-forming operation. This paper quantifies how current-loop proportional gain constrains LC-resonance placement in virtual-admittance-based dual-loop control with unity voltage-feedback decoupling (VFD) and capacitor-voltage active damping. Equivalent-impedance analysis identifies gain-dependent contraction of the positive-resistance region. Delayed inverter-current feedback opposes VFD-assisted damping above one-sixth of the sampling frequency. Simple proportional-path frequency shaping recovers an admissible effective-gain window while retaining unity VFD and leaving the resonant path unchanged. Reduced-model criteria, checked against the complete model, link window closure to a nominal resonance-placement limit near one-third of the sampling frequency under single-sampled single-update operation over the studied gain range. A 3-kVA prototype demonstrates an 83.3% LC-product reduction at comparable voltage and nominal current crossovers. A separate comparison with the same high-resonance filter demonstrates stable operation at 2.68 times the unshaped nominal current crossover. Output-impedance analysis and grid-connected tests identify additional grid-dependent gain constraints.

Systems and Control.title: Executor-Side Progressive Risk-Gated Actuation for Agentic AI in Wireless Supervisory Control
Systems and Control.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence built on large language models shows promise for automating Open Radio Access Network supervisory control. However, action-level safeguards alone may be insufficient: evidence acquisition consumes time and shared resources, and network changes can invalidate approvals before release. We propose Progressive Risk-Gated Actuation (PRGA), an executor-side model and contract governing intents from assessment to release or termination. PRGA combines local checks with selective retrieval of coordination evidence to reduce acquisition costs while preserving mandatory evidence requirements. Version and lease rechecks prevent release under invalidated approvals, while reevaluation requires recorded progress within each transaction's retry budget. Building on this contract, we formulate evidence allocation to maximize the expected whole-period rate of timely valid releases under risk, quality-of-service, deadline, and shared byte-budget constraints. For energy-saving and slice-protection workloads with stable daily load cycles, thresholds are selected offline and interpolated using an online load-phase estimate. On average over modeled start phases and quota levels, the allocation policy improves timely valid release rates over arrival-order fetching and an offline-selected global threshold under identical quotas and release checks. In OpenAirInterface radio emulation, an immediate scripted resend after a version-mismatch refusal raises on-time receiver delivery from 77.3% to 89.9% at modest additional command cost.

Systems and Control.title: Compressed Orientation Reachability Maps for Sub-Second Robotic Needle Entry Point Planning
Systems and Control.summary: In the context of multi-stage trajectory planning for robotic percutaneous liver interventions, identifying a kinematically feasible entry point remains a critical computational bottleneck. Existing methods rely on exhaustive inverse kinematics or randomized searches, incurring delays of 13 to 27 seconds per target and limiting real-time intraoperative adaptation. This paper introduces an Orientation-Based Reachability Map (ORM) that precomputes the kinematic feasibility of a 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) serial manipulator across 188,873 workspace positions and encodes orientation feasibility into a compact, indexed 83 MB map. A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled runtime pipeline replaces live optimization with near-instantaneous array lookups. Experimental evaluation demonstrates a reduction in planning latency from 13.5-26.9 s to 0.289-0.349 s per target while maintaining high geometric fidelity, achieving a mean convex hull volume overlap ratio of 0.933 and a mean alpha-shape volume ratio of 0.976 relative to the baseline reachable point cloud. The proposed ORM framework enables sub-second entry point planning and provides an efficient computational framework for robotic needle insertion in percutaneous liver ablation.

Systems and Control.title: Which wind and solar modelling choices matter? Effects on capacity factors, energy droughts and European power system configuration
Systems and Control.summary: Europe's future power system will rely heavily on wind and solar power and must remain resilient during prolonged periods of low wind and solar generation, known as variable renewable energy (VRE) droughts. To capture such rare events, adequacy assessments increasingly draw on decades of weather data, but the conversion of weather into power is largely treated as fixed. It remains unclear which modelling choices in this conversion matter for representing these droughts, and whether they matter as much as the weather itself. Here we systematically compare these choices side by side (bias correction, wind speed extrapolation, capacity layouts, turbine and photovoltaic configurations, and wake losses) and trace their effects through VRE droughts to the design of a net-zero European power system, using 85 years of reanalysis data. We find that modelling choices barely change how often VRE droughts occur or when the system is stressed. They do, however, determine how much capacity is needed to withstand that stress. By altering the electricity delivered during droughts, they shift required capacity by up to 480 GW, which is comparable to the spread across the most critical weather years. Modelling exercises should therefore use multiple weather years; bias-correct and regionally validate weather inputs; explicitly represent resource heterogeneity, forward-looking technologies, and wake losses; and judge these choices by their effect on the low-generation tail, not only on the mean.

Systems and Control.title: Modeling and Parametrization of Large-scale Hydrogen Electrolyzers for Transient and Frequency Stability Analysis
Systems and Control.summary: Hydrogen Electrolyzers (HEs), particularly Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM)-based systems, are flexible loads capable of providing grid ancillary services and enhancing the stability of renewable-dominated power systems due to their fast electrical response. However, the literature often lacks clear guidance on the structure, modeling, and parametrization of large-scale HEs for transient and frequency stability analyses. This paper presents a detailed configuration for utility-scale HE plants, using the stack as the fundamental unit, supported by a realistic parametrization based on commercial components. Furthermore, this work extends the Generalized ESS Model (GEM), a linearized state-space model previously utilized with other converter-interfaced energy storage systems, to PEM HEs for the first time. To facilitate plant scalability, a robust method for scaling GEM matrices across different capacities is proposed. Finally, a measurement-based methodology is developed to estimate the GEM parameters and subsequently extract the equivalent electrical circuit parameters. Comprehensive simulations on the WSCC system under various disturbances validate the accuracy of the derived GEM, the effectiveness of the scaling approach, and the robustness of the parameter identification methodology.

Systems and Control.title: Multi-output LSTM soft sensors for industrial anaerobic co-digestion using LSTM-beta-VAE generative data augmentation
Systems and Control.summary: Anaerobic digestion (AD) requires close monitoring of key process variables, including pH, the ratio of volatile organic acids to alkaline buffer capacity and biogas production, to maintain biological stability and prevent process failure. While mechanistic frameworks such as the Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 are highly parameterised, computationally expensive, and difficult to calibrate for real-time applications, data-driven Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks offer a potentially more adaptable alternative. However, current data-driven approaches in AD are predominantly limited to single-output architectures that focus solely on production yields, as opposed to simultaneous prediction of vital stability indicators. Furthermore, industrial AD datasets are typically sparse and skewed toward steady-state operations. Baseline evaluations demonstrated this scarcity prevents standard algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost) and unaugmented LSTMs from recognising the transition to unstable operations, resulting in poor estimation of stability indicators. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a novel generative data augmentation framework using an LSTM-beta-Variational Autoencoder coupled with a multi-output LSTM (MO-LSTM) soft sensor. By synthesising physically valid sequences of these transitions to unstable operations from one year of full-scale plant data, the method safely populates sparse regions of the feature space. Trained on this augmented dataset, the MO-LSTM achieved robust simultaneous estimation across all targets. This approach mitigates data sparsity, providing a basis for hybrid mechanistic-data-driven modelling and early-warning soft sensors in industrial bioprocesses.

Systems and Control.title: Neuromorphic design of a rhythmic network
Systems and Control.summary: Central Pattern Generators (CPGs) have long inspired the design of rhythms that combine endogenous generation and exogenous interaction. In neurodynamics and engineering studies, CPGs have been primarily analysed and designed as networks of coupled oscillators. In contrast, the present article regards CPGs as networks that propagate events through excitable rather than oscillatory nodes. The proposed event-based perspective reduces the design of network-level rhythmic properties to the tuning of local nodal input-output characteristics. This reduction enables a distributed and robust design methodology: nodes can be tuned independently, they can be heterogeneous, and the global rhythm results from local event propagation rather than from a specific global tuning of the network parameters. The present article builds on previously introduced concepts that parallel existing characterizations of oscillators: the event describing function (eDF), which characterises the propagation delay of a node, and the event phase response curve (ePRC), which characterises the phase sensitivity of a node. Event-based CPGs made of excitable rather than oscillatory nodes emerge as a principled design framework for robust rhythm generation.

Systems and Control.title: Safe Unicycle Navigation Among Multiple Obstacles Under Bounded Disturbances: A Learning-Augmented CLF-CBF Approach (Extended Version)
Systems and Control.summary: This paper presents a robust control framework for safe navigation of a unicycle robot to a goal among multiple static obstacles under an unknown, time-varying disturbance. The controller solves a single real-time quadratic program (QP) that combines a goal-reaching term with one safety term per obstacle. The goal-reaching term is a cross-track control Lyapunov function built from body-frame tracking errors rather than a bearing angle, which keeps its Lie derivatives bounded everywhere, including the goal. Safety is encoded using robust control barrier functions, one per obstacle, each tightened by a closed-form, state-dependent disturbance bound. When stabilization and safety conflict, a slack variable relaxes only the convergence requirement, so that the safety constraints remain strictly enforced. Whenever the QP is feasible, the robust barrier constraints guarantee forward invariance of every obstacle's safe set under all admissible disturbances. Complementing this safety guarantee, a Lyapunov analysis yields an explicit ultimate bound on the distance to the goal. A learning-augmented variant replaces the fixed objective with a reinforcement-learning reference, which accelerates convergence when multiple constraints are simultaneously active. We further derive the obstacle separation below which the gap between two obstacles becomes too narrow to pass through under the robust constraints. For such gaps, a learned virtual goal for the Lyapunov function steers the robot around the obstacles without compromising safety. Simulations, a Monte Carlo study, and a comparison against a sampled-data robust baseline support the theoretical results.

Systems and Control.title: Safe World Model for Joint Trajectory and Beamforming Design of Mobile Base Stations
Systems and Control.summary: Mobile base stations (MBSs), including aerial and ground-based platforms, provide flexible wireless coverage through adaptive positioning. However, jointly optimizing their trajectories and digital beamforming is challenging because movement changes channel conditions and interference, while beamforming determines the resulting signal and interference powers. These coupled decisions also account for how current movements affect future positions and communication performance under mobility and safety constraints. We formulate this problem as a constrained Markov decision process that maximizes the time-averaged sum signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), subject to mobility, obstacle region avoidance, and transmit-power constraints. To support long-term planning and reduce the extensive environment interactions required by model-free reinforcement learning, we develop a SafeDreamer-based world model framework that learns latent system dynamics from experience and optimizes a joint trajectory and beamforming policy through imagined trajectories. Feasibility-preserving action mappings and safety cost signals incorporate operational constraints into policy learning. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves higher time-averaged sum SINR than the proximal policy optimization and deep Q-network baselines, while exhibiting improved sample efficiency and more reliable constraint satisfaction.

Systems and Control.title: Computing with Coupled Oscillator Networks: Optimization, Memory, and Modern AI Primitives
Systems and Control.summary: We explore how synchronization in coupled oscillator networks may be employed to perform a variety of computing tasks. These systems are becoming more attractive as an alternative to conventional digital computers due to the increasing energy demands of the latter, particularly for large-scale problems in machine learning and artificial intelligence. The ubiquity of coupled oscillator networks means that oscillator-based computing can be thought of as a universal computing paradigm encompassing systems with a diversity of physical realizations, e.g. as analog circuits, neurological systems, spintronic systems. The bridge between the dynamics of coupled oscillator networks and computational primitives they implement is the Ising model, which originates in statistical physics, and when applied to oscillator networks, explains the emergence of globally complex and disordered synchronization patterns from local interactions in the network. We discuss the application of coupled oscillator networks to three fundamental computing operations. First, oscillator networks as specialized hardware solvers of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, with the solution encoded in the synchrony patterns. Second, oscillator networks as associative memory systems, enabling storage and retrieval of data represented through phases of oscillations. Finally, oscillator networks as a dynamical implementation of attention, with synchronization providing the mechanism for the alignment of keys to queries. The ability of oscillator networks to implement these computational primitives paves the way for novel realizations of intelligent systems through a variety of physical substrates.

Systems and Control.title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference
Systems and Control.summary: Anaerobic digestion (AD) models can be challenging to calibrate against real data due to limited practical identifiability, data scarcity, and model complexity. Weighted least squares objective functions and gradient-based solvers using finite differences are often used in literature, but result in suboptimal parameter estimates and large uncertainty bands. This paper identifies the parameters of a reduced-order ADM1 by comparing the frameworks of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and Bayesian inference (BI), and quantifies uncertainties of parameters and outputs. Multirate experimental data are taken from a lab-scale AD reactor fed with agricultural substrates and operated at organic loading rates of 3$\,$g VS $\mathrm{m^{-3}d^{-1}}$. Global optima are found via global and gradient-based local search algorithms using forward sensitivities. Enhanced scatter search provides the best global search results. These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. Despite a high-resolution lab-scale dataset, the ADM1-specific inhibition parameter $K_\mathrm{I,nh3}$ is practically not identifiable with MLE, and shows a low output sensitivity, whereas a parameter for the effective ion concentration shows superb practical identifiabilty at high confidence with both MLE and BI. The present work lays a scalable base for calibration of nonlinear AD models by providing reliable simulations. It thus advances model-based monitoring and control applications of multirate processes such as agricultural AD plants.

Systems and Control.title: From Airspace Degradation to Deconfliction: Predicting Safety-Critical Traffic States through the Evolution of Multiscale Complexity Metrics
Systems and Control.summary: Growing air traffic demand is pushing airspace management towards the limits of its operational capacity, with steadily increasing workload for air traffic control officers, with direct consequences for safety. Understanding which traffic conditions give rise to safety-critical situations is therefore an essential open problem. Here we compare a large number of deconfliction events with equivalent conflict-free scenarios, extracted from thirteen weeks of air traffic control data over the Swedish Flight Information Region. We describe the traffic structure before each event through thirty sector-complexity metrics computed at multiple spatial and temporal scales, and use them as inputs of Machine Learning models. We find that the need of deconflictions can be predicted with an accuracy reaching $70\%$, but only when the traffic is described at the sector spatial scale. Predictability increases monotonically in the minutes preceding the clearance, showing that situations requiring deconflicting actions are not sudden occurrences, but rather the endpoint of a progressive degradation process.
