Social and Information Networks.summary: Predicting social network churn before it becomes visible in aggregate metrics remains an open challenge, particularly in enterprise settings where heterogeneous usage patterns, sparse data, and deployment constraints preclude standard supervised approaches. We formalize this problem as finite-step engagement projection over contributor-role Markov chains, with a stationary-distribution interpretation for ergodic chains in the long-run limit. For each engagement feature type within a network (e.g., Q&A, communities, articles, etc.), users are classified monthly into four behavioral states and a transition matrix is estimated from six months of history. Six-step propagation yields a label-free projection of the contributor mix; for ergodic chains, the Perron-Frobenius theorem establishes convergence under repeated propagation. Comparing projected future engagement to current engagement produces the Health Ratio, a single score requiring no trained model, no labels, and no infrastructure beyond SQL. Validated across seven rolling prediction windows on 11,500+ tenant-level networks, the Health Ratio achieves mean AUC 0.917 with a 156 times churn-rate gradient across risk tiers, outperforming all single-signal baselines and the growth-adjusted variant previously deployed in production. An ablation study shows that six-step propagation achieves similar churn discrimination to the eigenvector-based score. Deployed on Microsoft Engage since October 2025, the framework powers customer health monitoring and has enabled proactive intervention on at-risk networks before decline becomes visible in traditional metrics.
Social and Information Networks.comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Author manuscript accepted for publication in Microsoft Journal of Applied Research (MSJAR), Volume 23, Article 217

Social and Information Networks.title: Community detection in complex networks via node similarity, graph representation learning, and hierarchical clustering
Social and Information Networks.summary: Community detection is a significant challenge in analysing real graphs, including social, citation, biological, and many other networks. This article proposes three new, general, hierarchical frameworks to deal with this task. The introduced approach supports various linkage-based clustering algorithms, vertex proximity matrices, and graph representation learning models. We compare 364 module combinations on Stochastic Block Model graphs and real-life datasets. We observe that our best pipelines (Wasserman-Faust and the mutual information-based PPMI proximity, as well as the deep learning-based DNGR representations) perform competitively with the state-of-the-art Leiden and Louvain algorithms. At the same time, unlike the latter, they remain hierarchical. Thus, they output a series of nested partitions of all possible cardinalities which are compatible with each other. This feature is crucial when the number of correct partitions is unknown in advance, and we show that it is obtained at near-zero practical cost in terms of partition quality. On graphs composed of many small communities, our pipelines are more accurate than the reference solutions. Nevertheless, the downside of our approach is its time complexity, which confines the framework to networks of some 10000 vertices on personal machines.

Social and Information Networks.title: BaCon: Band-Concentrated Exponential Random Graph Models
Social and Information Networks.summary: Exponential-family random graph models ERGMs provide a parametric interpretable framework for modeling real graphs including the Web and social networks Fitted ERGMs may suffer from degeneracy matching observed graph statistics in expectation does not guarantee that the observed graph and similar ones are highly probable under the fitted distribution We introduce Band-Concentrated ERGMs BaCon a framework that avoids degeneracy by imposing a probabilistic constraint requiring at least $1-δ$ of the distribution probability mass to lie on the set of graphs with statistics within an $\varepsilon$-tolerance band around the observed statistics BaCons maximumentropy distribution still belongs to the exponential family while including a factor checking for inclusion in the tolerance band We derive the exact Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rule for this target and use a practical stochastic approximation procedure with a smoothed band membership during fitting Experiments on social networks across increasingly challenging model specifications show that BaCon substantially increases the probability mass assigned to graphs whose statistics are close to the observed ones while remaining estimable for specifications where standard ERGM estimation fails These results demonstrate that probability mass constraints are a principled way to mitigate degeneracy while retaining the benefits of exponential-family graph models

Social and Information Networks.title: Context-Aware Multimodal Claim Verification in Spoken Dialogues
Social and Information Networks.summary: Spoken factual claims often occur within multi-turn conversations, where surrounding dialogue can provide context unavailable from the claim alone. Yet most fact-checking research evaluates isolated text, leaving conversational audio under-studied. We introduce MAD2, a synthetic Multi-turn Audio Dialogues benchmark for spoken claim verification with 1,000 two-speaker dialogues, 1,230 sentence-level check-worthy candidate annotations, and approximately 10 hours of audio. We also propose calibrated multimodal fusion of a context-aware audio encoder and a dialogue-aware text model. Adding dialogue context improves verification across settings, although the gains vary by scenario. Past-only context often approaches local offline performance, suggesting its usefulness when future context is unavailable. Fusion achieves its highest mean advantage over text with full-dialogue context, but does not consistently or significantly outperform text across settings. Under full-dialogue context, exploratory subgroup results show greater performance variation across dialogue scenarios for text and fusion, but across spread styles for audio.
Social and Information Networks.comment: Published at SALMA 2026 (EMNLP workshop). ACL Anthology: https://aclanthology.org/2026.salma-1.12/

Social and Information Networks.title: When Platforms Pay Users to Correct Misinformation: Revenue Incentives and Governance Capacity in Weibo Annotations
Social and Information Networks.summary: Crowdsourced misinformation governance systems such as Community Notes and Weibo Annotations depend on sustained corrective labor. How monetary incentives shape participation and subsequent governance outcomes remains poorly understood. We conduct a mixed-methods study of Weibo Annotations, analyzing 102,994 posts and 431,407 comments from 2023--2026, alongside interviews with 15 contributors. We find concentrated corrective labor, limited observed display, and weak quality--engagement alignment. Policy introduction was associated with sharp increases in contributor participation and annotation production. Model-assisted quality followed its expected trajectory, evidence for additional display growth was inconclusive, and engagement per annotation fell below expectation. Public discussions and interviews reveal substantial verification demands, difficult-to-interpret review processes, uneven platform knowledge, and gaps in contributor protection. We identify four recurring bottlenecks in governance orchestration: participation, review, reach, and protection. Effective incentive design therefore depends on whether platforms can support these downstream processes as corrective labor expands.

Social and Information Networks.title: Follow or Surpass? Collaboration, Sound, and the Recognition of Influence in Lineages of Jazz Trumpet Players
Social and Information Networks.summary: Cultural fields cohere not only horizontally, through collaboration, but also vertically, through lineages of artistic influence. Considerable attention has been devoted to collaboration networks in various fields of creative production; however, we know less about the structure of artistic influence that is nevertheless key to individual artistic development and the evolution of genres. We examine the structure of such an influence network in a genealogy of 52 prominent jazz trumpet players, combining musicians' discographies, demographic characteristics, geographical locations, and audio analysis of more than 16,000 recordings with exponential random graph models. Direct collaboration, overlap in collaborators, and sonic context similarity, that is, the similarity of the recordings on which players appear, are each associated with an ascribed influence tie, net of the others. Not surprisingly, ascribed ties connect musicians whose recordings share a similar sonic context, but musicians also tend to collaborate with their influences and share collaborators with them. However, players whose recordings share a sonic context and who move in the same circle of collaborators can be thought of as peers or rivals, rather than as influences of each other, because lineage implies a succession predicated on difference as much as on continuity. Taken together, our findings suggest that a field's account of its own evolution is neither a record of who played together nor a map of shared sonic contexts, but a selective ordering that requires both. While our data do not permit a causal account, our aim is to provide a rich and varied methodological strategy and descriptive as well as inferential tools to understand the yet understudied vertical integration of cultural fields through influence ties.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Serving Chain-structured Jobs with Large Memory Footprints with Application to Large Foundation Model Serving
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: As a current trend in Artificial Intelligence (AI), large foundation models are increasingly employed as the core of AI services. However, even after training, serving such models at scale remains a challenging task due to their heavy resource footprints, particularly in terms of GPU memory. While recent works revealed unique characteristics of systems serving foundation models that distinguish them from traditional distributed computing systems, there is still a lack of fundamental understanding of the underlying system management problems. This work aims at addressing this gap by extracting a novel problem of "server chain composition" via block placement and cache allocation for serving chainstructured jobs with large memory footprints, which models a fundamental problem in serving large foundation models through pipeline parallelism. After showing the NP-hardness of the optimal solution, the focus is turned to developing scalable algorithms with guaranteed performance under state-of-the-art load balancing. Application of the proposed solution to a distributed large language model (LLM) serving system shows significant reduction of response times compared to state-of-the-art solutions.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Parallel Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics in Python: Task- and Data-Parallel SINDy with Numba, OpenMP, Threads and Multiprocessing for the Lorenz and Rössler Systems
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: The sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) recovers interpretable governing equations from time-series data by sparse regression over a library of candidate functions. As data sets, candidate libraries and the number of repeated fits grow, the cost of SINDy becomes dominated by the evaluation of the library matrix and its least-squares problems. We present an open-source Python implementation of SINDy in which a single set of loop-based kernels is just-in-time compiled with Numba and executed on a shared-memory multicore node by four interchangeable back ends: Numba prange, OpenMP directives through PyOMP, Python threads that release the global interpreter lock, and multiprocessing with shared memory. The normal equations are accumulated in one cache-blocked pass over the data, with an automatic fallback to a tall-skinny QR reduction for ill-conditioned problems. Two decompositions are studied on the Lorenz and Rössler systems: an ensemble (task-parallel) workload of 960 independent identifications and a library (data-parallel) workload of one trajectory with $2\times10^7$ samples and a fifth-order library of 56 candidate terms. All back ends recover the exact sparsity pattern in every identification, with coefficient errors identical to PySINDy. On a dual-socket Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4 node of the University of Houston-Downtown HPC cluster (24 cores, 48 hardware threads), the compiled serial code is 4.3-5.6x faster than PySINDy, the parallel back ends reach speed-ups of 14.8-20.3 on 24 cores (parallel efficiency 0.61-0.84), and the overall time to solution is reduced by up to 117x with respect to PySINDy. We analyse the differences between the back ends, the effect of the two sockets and of hyper-threading, and give practical recommendations.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/guillenrondonp/parallel-sindy

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: What Sets the Serving Speed of Looped Language Models? Measurements and Optimizations Graded by Exactness
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Looped language models apply one block of layers many times per token, so a serving engine pays every per-layer overhead once per loop; we measure serving for Ouro and Huginn-0125 in an open-source looped-model engine and grade our optimizations from bitwise-identical changes to those that require an accuracy check. At batch 1, fusing all loop submissions leaves Ouro throughput at 0.99x; the 5689 small kernels per token are the real cost, and fusing them behind rounding fences raises throughput 1.11-1.59x while 1014/1014 requests remain identical. An approximate fusion is no faster and misses a one-point GSM8K rule on 87 questions (61 and 62 correct versus 64), so we do not ship it. Huginn's released defaults avoid dead KV slots, reuse prefix-cache pages, and serve 1.77-3.16x faster than the base engine; Ouro reaches 1.65-2.15x and agent sessions 1.91-3.21x, while Huginn's noise and prefix-reuse changes stay within one point on all 1319 Huginn test questions; Huginn's packed prefill, -0.61 points on the same questions, meets that rule only on its point estimate. Position-keyed noise makes CPU cache reuse exact but still leaves 20 of 128 GPU full hits different, while loop fusion delays prefill admission and a 64-graph cache prevents eager fallbacks. Under prefill-decode disaggregation ExactLoop reaches up to 3.3x the base throughput with peer error handling disabled, and 3.1x in two of three runs with it enabled. Its transfer budget, sized to hold one request's KV in flight, cuts the commit tail from about one second under the earlier budget to 16 ms (base: 2.8 s), removing the polling rounds that the engine's interval would otherwise impose.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: An Investigation on Numerical Bugs in GPU Programs Towards Automated Bug Detection
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: General-purpose graphics processing unit (GPU) computing has emerged as a leading parallel computing paradigm, offering significant performance gains in various domains such as scientific computing and deep learning. However, GPU programs are susceptible to numerical bugs, which can lead to incorrect results or crashes. These bugs are difficult to detect, debug, and fix due to their dependence on specific input values or types and the absence of reliable error-checking mechanisms and oracles. Additionally, the unique programming conventions of GPUs complicate identifying the root causes of bugs, while fixing them requires domain-specific knowledge of GPU computing and numerical libraries. Therefore, understanding the characteristics of GPU numerical bugs (GPU-NBs) is crucial for developing effective solutions. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive study of GPU-NBs by analyzing 397 real-world bug samples from GitHub. We identify common root causes, symptoms, input patterns, test oracles that trigger these bugs and the strategies used to fix them. We also present GPU-NBDetect, a preliminary tool designed to detect numerical bugs across six distinct bug categories. GPU-NBDetect detected a total of 226 bugs across 186 mathematical functions in four libraries, with 60 of the bugs confirmed by developers. Our findings lay the groundwork for developing detection and prevention techniques for GPU-NBs and offer insights for building more effective debugging and auto-repair tool.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Published in Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), ISSTA 2025, associated with the 34th ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2025)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Distributed Linear Bandits for Freshness-Aware Preprocessing in MEC-Enabled Digital Twin Networks
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Digital twins (DTs) require timely updates from Internet of Things (IoT) devices to accurately represent the state of the corresponding physical systems, but transmitting large data volumes can compromise freshness. Moreover, different task classes have distinct computational demands and freshness requirements, while stochastic task generation and sizes complicate resource allocation. In this paper, we propose a freshness-aware framework in which multi-access edge computing (MEC) servers preprocess IoT data, reducing transmission volume and DT-server processing load. The framework establishes mutual support between DT and MEC servers. The DTs determine feasible CPU-allocation strategies guaranteeing class-specific age-of-information (AoI) requirements under specified workload, delay, and update-generation bounds. MEC servers collaboratively identify the feasible strategy minimizing expected freshness-normalized preprocessing delay. We formulate CPU-strategy selection as a fixed-confidence distributed best-arm identification problem in linear bandits, with MEC servers as agents and CPU allocations across task classes as arms. We employ DistLinGapE, a distributed collaborative learning method, to coordinate exploration and share observations. Numerical results show that the method identifies the optimal feasible strategy and reduces preprocessing delay when deployed under stationary task-class assignments and workload statistics. Collaboration yields an identification speedup nearly proportional to the number of participating MEC servers in the evaluated settings.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Workload-Static Optical Circuit Switching For Scalable LLM Inference Decode
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: LLM inference decode executes fine-grained collectives whose latency directly limits per-user interactivity, yet scale-up fabrics are still built from electronic packet switches designed for training. We observe that, for a given model deployment and parallelization, the communication structure of decode is fixed, and propose workload-static optical circuit switching (OCS): circuits are configured once per deployment, co-designed with model parallelism and with topology-aware collective schedules that turn spare accelerator ports into fewer communication phases or higher bandwidth. We evaluate this design with GXNET, a graph-based workload emulator coupled to analytical and flit-level network models grounded in hardware measurements. In a 576-accelerator scale-up domain serving 5T-parameter MoE models with up to 5M tokens of context, all-OCS fabrics improve interactivity by up to 65% and energy efficiency by up to 119% over 4:1 oversubscribed packet-switched fabrics.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Characterizing Serverless Workloads: A Large-Scale Analysis of Function-as-a-Service Platforms
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Serverless computing is a popular approach to application deployment without having to manage the underlying infrastructure. Its most common implementation is Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), in which applications are structured as fine-grained functions. FaaS providers face non-trivial tasks in the management of their platforms, including cold starts, auto-scaling, and scheduling. The design of optimized platforms requires an accurate understanding of realistic serverless workloads. However, existing research and platforms rely on insights from single, often outdated datasets. In this work, we conduct a large-scale, cross-platform comparative analysis of eight publicly available FaaS workload traces from major cloud providers (Alibaba, Azure, Huawei, IBM) and a scientific computing platform (Globus). We provide a comprehensive and up-to-date view of the serverless ecosystem by characterizing key dimensions such as invocation patterns, latency, cold start behavior, and resource utilization. Our analysis shows that although invocation patterns remain universal, execution times have shortened, shifting the performance bottleneck toward platform scheduling and dependency management. We also observe an architectural shift toward "Serverless 2.0" models, where concurrent, long-lived containers are increasingly utilized to bypass cold start penalties. Furthermore, we found resource over-provisioning and extreme skew in user request volumes. These findings provide actionable insights for designing more efficient FaaS platforms, informing improved approaches to targeted cold start mitigation, predictive resource management, and dependency-aware scheduling.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: ForgeKernel: Self-Evolving Kernels Catching and Surpassing Experts and Agents
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Purpose-built kernel agents can write high-performance GPU kernels, but existing systems generally lack cross-run knowledge accumulation and architectural evolution. Each run starts from the same initial knowledge, and later iterations largely optimize within an architecture fixed early in the search. We present ForgeKernel, a kernel-generation system that accumulates and reuses knowledge across runs while enabling continued evolution of kernel architectures. It analyzes the hardware behavior of a high-performance reference and distills validated architectural decisions into reusable knowledge of hardware mechanisms rather than imitating source code. It then seals a kernel that passes correctness and performance validation and uses it as the reference for the next optimization run, enabling architectural decisions to be revisited. Across 27 operators and 29 input configurations on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, ForgeKernel matches or beats its expert reference on 25 configurations, with a geometric-mean performance gain of 10%. On Ascend 910C, it outperforms the per-operator public best on the public case set of all 8 level-4 operators in the CANN-Bench Season 1 final leaderboard, with a geometric-mean gain of 25.1%, while its full-suite submission ranks first on the A3 leaderboard. As of 2026-10-30, public submissions generated by ForgeKernel rank first on all three CANN-Bench 2.0 solution leaderboards (Ascend 910C, 950DT, and 950PR) and on the SOL-ExecBench FlashInfer-Bench track.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Rethinking AI Cloud Infrastructure for Agentic Serving Systems with the Aries Experimentation Framework
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Autonomous agents challenge conventional LLM serving with long-lived, cross-component execution and evolving system state. These characteristics complicate controlled systems experimentation and attribution of end-to-end behavior across the serving stack. We present Aries, a full-stack experimentation framework that separates task specifications from execution configurations, reconstructs cross-component agent trajectories with correlated system telemetry, and exposes stateful tool execution through a consistent interface across heterogeneous sandbox substrates. We use Aries to conduct reproducible experiments on open agent harnesses and benchmarks. We complement these experiments with production traces from a commercial platform, grounding low-level systems research in observed production behavior. Our results show that (1) token-centric metrics miss non-inference bottlenecks, (2) retaining additional context yields diminishing accuracy benefits while reducing serving capacity, and (3) tool sandboxes alternate between long idle periods and short resource bursts, while current snapshot-based state management makes aggressive suspension costly. We then discuss the vision for agent-native serving systems designed around trajectory-level metrics, adaptive context management, and elastic sandbox resource management.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Quantum Advantage for Distributed Symmetry Breaking
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We present a distributed quantum algorithm that $3$-colors cycles in $O(1)$ rounds, with high probability. It follows that all locally checkable labeling problems (LCLs) that have round complexity $O(\log^* n)$ in the classical LOCAL model can be solved in $O(1)$ rounds in the quantum-LOCAL model, with high probability; this includes problems such as maximal independent set and maximal matching in bounded-degree graphs. This presents the first natural examples of graph problems with an asymptotic distributed quantum advantage for the LOCAL model; all prior examples that separate LOCAL and quantum-LOCAL are artificial problems constructed merely for the sake of demonstrating quantum advantage.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Impossibility of One-Way One-Round Quantum 4-Coloring via Matrix-Space Stability
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
We show that one-way one-round quantum-LOCAL algorithms cannot $4$-color directed cycles with high probability. This is the first lower bound in the high-probability quantum LOCAL setting that goes beyond the non-signaling and bounded-dependence models, exploiting the structure of distributed quantum algorithms.
  Our proof establishes a bidirectional connection between distributed quantum computing and extremal combinatorics. We obtain our lower bound by proving a Mantel-type stability theorem for weighted matrix spaces.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Local Distributed Computation under Crash Failures
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We study deterministic algorithms for locally checkable graph problems in the synchronous LOCAL model with crash failures, where a crashing node may send messages to only some neighbors. We introduce consistent neighborhoods: partial radius-$R$ views that agree locally across surviving edges and are complete without crashes. For $R=T+\ell+1$, these views allow local simulation of $T$-round fault-free algorithms that remain correct on subgraphs, satisfying constraints wherever the radius-$\ell$ checking neighborhood contains no crash. On graphs with at most $n$ nodes and maximum degree at most $Δ\geq3$, we construct these views in $O(\min\{n,(Δ-1)^R,RΔf\})$ rounds when a crash bound $f\geq1$ is globally known; the first two bounds require no knowledge of $f$. For $Δ=2$ or girth greater than $2R$, including forests, $O(R)$ rounds suffice. Our upper bounds are essentially tight in suitable parameter regimes. One crash can force $Ω(n)$ rounds even for $R=3$ on diameter-two graphs. For each fixed $Δ\geq3$ and sufficiently large $R$, we prove a $(Δ-1)^{R-O(\sqrt R)}$ lower bound even with crashes restricted to round beginnings. We also prove an $Ω(ΔRf)$ lower bound when $R\geq4\lceil\log_{Δ-1}f\rceil+4$ and $n\geqΔRf$. For locally checkable labeling (LCL) problems, we preserve $O(\log^* n)$ complexity under any number of crashes whenever this bound holds without faults on all graphs with a fixed degree bound. In contrast, we construct an LCL on graphs of maximum degree at most five with fault-free complexity $Θ(\log n)$ and crash-tolerant complexity $Θ(n)$. Finally, any fault-free sinkless-orientation algorithm can be transformed to tolerate any number of crashes with only one additional round, guaranteeing correctness even at surviving nodes adjacent to crashes.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: TapeSAC: Automated, Pareto-Optimal Fine-Grained Memory Management for Large Model Training
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Selective activation checkpointing (SAC) decides which activations to save for the backward pass and which to recompute: each choice is a point in the plane of peak memory and recomputation time, and the goal is that plane's Pareto frontier. Current practice falls short of this goal. Hand-tuned policies fix a single point that does not adapt when the model, batch or kernels change; PyTorch's SAC reruns each block's forward pass in program order, recomputing values the backward pass never reads; and the memory budget of torch.compile treats recomputation as free or forbidden and selects saved tensors by bytes alone, an assumption that fails for the custom kernels that produce many of a large model's activations.
  We present TapeSAC, which automates SAC in eager PyTorch without editing the model's forward code. TapeSAC records each block's forward pass at the dispatcher and, during backward, replays only the producers of the values autograd consumes, so saving a tensor eliminates every producer needed only for it. A planner selects the saved tensors from measured recomputation costs under a single limit on step-peak memory. On Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, replay alone reduces step time by 3.0% and 1.7% versus full checkpointing at no greater memory cost; memory-aware planning raises these gains to 6.3% and 13.9% under a 90%-of-device-memory limit. The evaluated hand-tuned policies fall short of this memory-recomputation frontier and, on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, run out of memory at larger batches. Over 500 steps on real data, TapeSAC reduces training time by 8-11%; on Qwen3.5-397B, it is 2.7% faster than a model-specific hand-tuned policy while using 14% less memory.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: How does the number of sampled opinions affect the time required to reach consensus in distributed consensus dynamics? We study the synchronous $h$-Majority, in which every node independently samples $h$ nodes uniformly at random with replacement in each round and adopts a most frequent sampled opinion, breaking ties uniformly at random. We show that $h$-Majority achieves the nearly-optimal trade-off between the sample size and the consensus time, among a broad class of consensus dynamics. In particular, we prove the following results. For every sample size $h \ge 3$ and for every initial configuration, we prove that the process reaches consensus with high probability within $$\widetilde{O}\left(1+\min\left\{\frac{1}{\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\}},\frac{\sqrt{n}}{h}\right\}\right)$$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $p_{\max}$ is the largest initial fraction of nodes supporting any single opinion. This is the first bound on the consensus time for $h$-Majority that holds for every $h\ge3$ and every initial configuration. When the initially most popular opinion has a sufficiently large lead over every other opinion, we show that all nodes adopt this opinion with high probability within $O(\log n/\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\})$ rounds. We establish a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for any fixed update rule that treats all opinions symmetrically and that selects either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Accelerating Offloading-Based MoE Inference by Interleaving Concurrent Requests
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Expert offloading enables large mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models to run locally, but conventional batching stalls the GPU while missing experts are fetched. A popular remedy, known as prefetching, is to predict what experts will be needed soon and fetch them using idle link bandwidth. Imprecise prediction, however, wastes bandwidth and GPU memory on fetching unnecessary experts. Our key finding is that prefetching can be harmful when there is an expert cache in GPU memory. This is because as the cache includes more necessary experts, expert prediction becomes less precise. Our key insight is that proper request scheduling beats prefetching. Building on this insight, we present Bevy, an MoE inference system based on runahead inference for concurrent requests. A request whose experts are available can run ahead to later layers while other requests wait for fetches, revealing the experts it needs next. Bevy can then fetch the missing experts so identified while computing ready requests, overlapping computation and fetching without predicting expert selections. Running requests separately, however, repeats reads of shared weights in GPU memory and increases compute time. To limit this cost, Bevy's self-balancing scheduler batches ready requests at each layer and prioritizes lagging requests, adapting their grouping as expert availability changes. Across two local platforms, Bevy delivers up to 3.46$\times$ the decode throughput of llama.cpp and up to 1.55$\times$ that of the fastest prefetching baseline.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Replica-Aware Split Inference for Edge IoT Systems
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Split Inference (SI) addresses the hardware resource limitations of Internet of Things (IoT) devices by distributing tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) model segments across multiple IoT devices. However, a device failure can interrupt the inference pipeline. This paper proposes a replica-aware recovery approach that deploys replicas of TinyML model segments originally hosted on failed devices onto surviving devices. We formulate the joint selection of replica hosts and communication protocols as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem that minimizes post-reconfiguration inference latency, accounting for computation and transmission latencies, under flash memory and runtime memory constraints. Simulations using MobileNetV2 on heterogeneous IoT networks compare the proposed approach with four baselines. We implement the model in a network of 15 IoT devices with a maximum link-rate reduction of 75%, and show that MILP approach achieves an average modeled end-to-end inference latency that is 6.8% lower than that of Computation Greedy and 18.3% lower than that of Random. Index Terms TinyML, split inference, Internet of Things, fault tolerance, replica placement.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: A RISC-V Simulator for the Tenstorrent Tensix Architecture
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
RISC-V based AI accelerators have become popular and not only for AI and ML, but also as vehicles for exploring HPC workloads more generally. Tenstorrent are one example, and whilst they document their Tensix architecture in detail and develop their software stack openly, running code has historically required a physical card, and their recently released simulator targets hardware equivalence rather than introspection. In this paper we present Wolfpine, a community developed RISC-V simulator for the Tensix architecture, supporting both the Wormhole and Blackhole generations and integrating seamlessly with the TT-Metal software stack.
  Constructed entirely from publicly available documentation, open source software and measurements on physical hardware, Wolfpine is written in pure Python for readability and ease of modification. An opt-in, provenance-tracked cost model adds timing fidelity incrementally, and typed event streams, per-component tracing and timeline export enable programmers to identify and diagnose performance bottlenecks that the hardware itself hides.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Author accepted version of paper in the RISC-V for HPC SC26 workshop

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation requires linear time
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Synchronising the clocks of processes is a fundamental problem in distributed computing. We consider message-passing systems in which processes start in an arbitrary initial state (self-stabilisation) and up to $f$ processes may be non-transiently faulty. It is well known that synchronising clocks \emph{exactly} is at least as hard as consensus and requires $Θ(f)$ time. In contrast, without self-stabilisation, clocks can be synchronised \emph{approximately} much faster, in time independent of the number of non-transient faults [Srikanth and Toueg, JACM 1987; Welch and Lynch, Inf. Comput. 1988].
  In this work, we show that deterministic self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks require $Ω(f)$ time to stabilise. This gives the first non-trivial time lower bound for these tasks, whose time complexity has remained open for over two decades [Dolev and Welch, JACM 2004; Dolev, Függer, Schmid and Lenzen, JACM 2014]. In particular, this answers the open question whether self-stabilising approximate clock synchronisation tasks are as hard as consensus or as easy as approximate agreement [Lenzen and Rybicki, JACM 2019].
  The results show that guaranteeing \emph{both} transient and non-transient fault-tolerance simultaneously is expensive even for approximate synchronisation tasks. The lower bounds hold in a very strong model: the faulty processes can only crash, the local clocks of processes have no clock drift, and the message delay is bounded and known to all processes. The proof is based on a combinatorial topological argument showing that no fast finite-state protocol can ensure that the clocks behave consistently across all executions. To our knowledge, this is the first use of topological arguments to prove time lower bounds in the self-stabilising setting.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: FenixWalk: Adaptive Sampling for Large-Scale Dynamic Graphs on Heterogeneous Architectures
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Random walks are fundamental to graph analytics, yet executing them efficiently on large, evolving graphs remains challenging. Existing approaches must balance sampling efficiency, update overhead, and memory consumption. Sampling structures optimized for throughput often incur substantial memory overhead and costly maintenance, whereas lightweight alternatives can suffer from high sampling latency on high-degree vertices or skewed weight distributions. These challenges become more pronounced on heterogeneous CPU--GPU platforms, where host memory provides capacity but GPU memory limits the amount of graph data that can benefit from parallel acceleration.
  We present FenixWalk, a memory-efficient random-walk system that combines unified in-place sampling with selective GPU acceleration for large-scale dynamic graphs. At its core, FenixWalk employs an in-place Fenwick representation that supports both rejection sampling and inverse-transform sampling without duplicating edge-level weight storage. This representation enables expected O(1) weight lookup for rejection sampling, together with O(log d) prefix sampling and updates. To exploit heterogeneous hardware efficiently, FenixWalk maintains the complete graph and its sampling structures in host memory while selectively placing frequently reused vertex-local samplers on the GPU. By transferring compact walker states instead of repeatedly migrating graph partitions, the system reduces cross-device communication and makes effective use of limited GPU memory. Experiments on large real-world graphs and representative random-walk workloads demonstrate that FenixWalk achieves average speedups ranging from 2.06x to 400.57x over existing random-walk systems.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: VeriNC: Finding Design Risks of In-Network Computing Systems
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
The emergence of programmable switches has brought in-network computing (INC) into the spotlight in recent years. By offloading computation directly onto the data transmission process, INC improves network utilization, reduces latency to sub-RTT levels, saves link bandwidth, and maintains throughput. However, INC disrupts the transparency of traditional networks, forcing developers to consider network exceptions like packet loss and out-of-order. If not properly handled, these exceptions can lead to violations of application properties, such as cache consistency and lock exclusion. Usual testing cannot exhaustively cover these exceptions, raising doubts about the correctness of INC systems and hindering their deployment in the industry.
  This paper presents VeriNC, the first general-purpose tool for verifying INC systems. VeriNC provides a high-level specification language and saves developers 67.2% lines of code on average. To help better understand the behavior of the system, VeriNC offers configurable network environments. VeriNC enables developers to express INC-specific correctness properties. VeriNC translates developer-specified systems into state transition representations, performs model checking to detect potential design risks, and reports violation traces to developers. We propose optimizations for INC-specific scenarios to address the challenge of state space explosion. We modeled INC systems across four application domains and identified design risks with VeriNC in seconds. VeriNC has also been adopted to guide the design of a new INC protocol. Based on our verification experience, we summarize lessons that help develop a correct INC protocol. We further reproduce them in real systems to confirm the validity of our verification result.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted at IEEE ICNP 2026 (Best Paper Award). Extended version with appendix, 16 pages, 12 figures

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: LeanSparse: Memory-Efficient Serving for Native Sparse-Attention LLMs
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Sparse attention limits the history read by each query, but serving long contexts still requires substantial GPU memory. Existing KV offloading systems retain the full history of indexer keys on GPU, limiting decode concurrency. Prefill's temporary memory demand can further delay admission even when enough memory remains for the same request's subsequent decode. We present LeanSparse, a serving system that reduces both decode's persistent memory use and prefill's temporary memory demand. Our design exploits two observations: prefill consumes historical data one layer at a time, and decode can identify promising candidates before comparing their original indexer scores. During prefill, LeanSparse streams layer histories through two reusable GPU buffers, overlapping next-layer loading with ongoing model computation. During decode, coarse-to-fine indexing searches compact representations and retrieves original indexer keys only for candidate refinement. Separate indexer key and KV caches reuse data across generation steps. We implement LeanSparse in SGLang and evaluate it on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. At 950K context length, LeanSparse supports 2.95$\times$ as many concurrent requests and achieves 2.14$\times$ decode throughput over HiSparse. On multi-turn Open-SWE traces, it reduces median time to first token from 21.6 to 0.6s and median session completion time by 17.7% relative to ECHO.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: FedCSGA: Client Selection Based on Genetic Algorithm for Federated Learning
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of machine learning models across distributed clients while preserving data privacy. In practical deployments, FL relies on selecting a subset of clients in each communication round to reduce communication cost, mitigate stragglers, and improve training efficiency under heterogeneous data and system conditions. In heterogeneous edge computing environments, both statistical heterogeneity and system heterogeneity significantly affect convergence efficiency and model performance. However, existing client selection methods often address these factors independently, overlooking their coupled and dynamic impact across communication rounds. To address this limitation, we propose FedCSGA, a Client Selection method for Federated learning based on a Genetic Algorithm. FedCSGA encodes client subsets as chromosomes and evaluates these subsets through a non-linear fitness function that jointly integrates resource-aware metrics and history-aware participation weighting. This design captures subset-level interactions, mitigates persistent selection bias, and balances statistical utility with system efficiency. Extensive experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR- 100, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that FedCSGA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse heterogeneity settings, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 7.0% and faster convergence with fewer communication rounds. These results validate the effectiveness of jointly modeling statistical and system factors to achieve robust and efficient learning in heterogeneous federated environments.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Running a 20B Video Diffusion Transformer on Consumer Hardware: A Deployment and Measurement Report for MiniMax H3 on Apple Silicon
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: We report the end-to-end deployment and measurement of MiniMax H3, a 20.38-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer (DiT) - the count measured from the safetensors headers of the Q8 checkpoint as deployed locally (Section 3.2) - running entirely on consumer Apple Silicon hardware: an Apple Mac mini with M5 Pro chip and 64 GiB of unified memory. Using the official bf16-to-Q8 (8-bit, group size 64) quantization path executed locally on the machine, we produced a working text-to-video pipeline with no cloud dependency. We document the full deployment procedure, including two non-trivial blockers and their fixes, and report measured figures for build time, peak memory, and per-clip render latency across four resolution tiers (Draft 384x640 through Native 768x1344). A 15.08-second 576x1024 clip rendered in 4838.49 seconds with a measured MLX peak of 27.467 GiB. We further operated the system as an unattended production pipeline, completing 17 clips in 26.49 hours with zero render failures. A blind human review of the 17 production clips (generation prompts withheld) averaged 3.12, 3.18, and 2.94 out of 5 for structural integrity, temporal consistency, and visible artifacts. All figures in this report are our own measurements except where explicitly labeled as third-party data. This is a systems/empirical report; we make no claim of model innovation.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Also published as a Zenodo record, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23803987

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: EvoCache: Accelerating Browser Large Language Model Delivery with Public Cache Anchors
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can run directly in a browser, but first use typically requires downloading model files that are hundreds of MiB or even several GiB in size. The same LLM is often repackaged by different publishers; these files share substantial content, yet byte differences prevent whole-file caches from reusing them. We propose EvoCache, a browser-managed LLM delivery system. EvoCache uses public cache anchors that are stored in advance by the browser and independent of browsing history to reconstruct losslessly the publisher version requested by a site. A site specifies only the target, while the browser selects the anchor and performs reconstruction, keeping both hidden from the site. An audit of 1,000 public repositories finds that 61 of the 100 most popular LLMs are offered by multiple publishers and that 98.1% of overlapping versions cannot be reused by whole-file caching. Across 23 cross-publisher model-package pairs, EvoCache achieves a median traffic reduction of 77.3% and outperforms every comparator. Across 240 real end-to-end browser experiments, EvoCache reduces network traffic by 78.9% and page-ready time by 64.2% relative to ordinary full downloads. For cached data left by other sites, EvoCache also protects users' cross-site cache privacy by using the same return time for cache hits and misses.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Distributed LTL Synthesis under Arbitrary Message Adversaries
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Reactive synthesis is the problem of generating a program that produces outputs satisfying a logical specification for every input stream. We study distributed synthesis for two processes communicating in rounds over unreliable links, with at least one message delivered in every round. Despite this delivery guarantee, we show that synthesis from linear temporal logic specifications is undecidable, even when messages carry the processes' complete causal histories.
  More generally, we give a complete characterization of the communication restrictions that make synthesis decidable. Restrictions are described by a message adversary $A$, a set of allowed infinite graph histories: sequences of communication graphs, each specifying which messages are delivered in a round. Iterated chromatic subdivision associates these histories with points in the unit interval, yielding an image $π(A) \subseteq [0,1]$. For every $ω$-regular message adversary $A$, synthesis is decidable if and only if $π(A)$ is nowhere dense.
  In the decidable cases, our procedure takes a deterministic parity automaton for $A$ and a specification, decides realizability, and constructs a realizing distributed algorithm whenever one exists. Further, our topological arguments shed new light on the fundamental requirements of synthesis. They show that, for $ω$-regular message adversaries, synthesis is decidable if and only if consensus is repeatedly solvable in bounded time. This links two previously unrelated problems from formal verification and distributed computing through the processes' uncertainty about communication.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Online Draft Co-Training for Speculative Decoding in Large-Scale, Long-Context RL Post-Training
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates rollout generation, which dominates the cost of reinforcement learning (RL) post-training. Online co-training keeps the draft aligned with the evolving policy, further increasing acceptance length and speedup. However, training large models on long contexts requires context parallelism (CP) and pipeline parallelism (PP), and co-training drafts under this layout poses two obstacles: (1) the draft's branch attention is unsupported by causal CP, and (2) the target features that the draft consumes are spread across PP stages. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of online draft co-training in NeMo-RL. For CP, we extend packed, load-balanced zigzag ring attention by merging rank-local branch attention with causal main-sequence attention. For PP, TapChannel transports intermediate target features across stages via a separate path, leaving the pipeline schedule unaffected. Experiments show that co-training keeps the policy's reward and accuracy close to the no-draft baseline while delivering $1.48$--$2.25\times$ rollout speedups and $1.19$--$1.88\times$ end-to-end training speedups across model scales up to 122B. Our CP design achieves strong scaling at 256K sequence length with significant memory savings over prior work, and our PP transport incurs modest overhead. Code can be found at https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/RL/issues/3698.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: ReWY: Faster Backpropagation for Delta-Rule Attention - From 7 to 3 Matrix Multiplications
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective.
  We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/flashserve/ReWY.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: EvoCG: Self-Evolving Precision Control for Faster Conjugate Gradient
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Modern GPUs offer far higher throughput in low precision than in FP64, but exploiting this in conjugate gradient (CG) solvers is difficult because tolerance to reduced precision evolves with the Krylov state. We present EvoCG, a mixed-precision CG solver that treats tile-wise precision as an online control action rather than a fixed setting: a reinforcement-learning policy in the iteration loop selects per-tile precision from the evolving solver state, made profitable by co-design with a Tile-CSC unified mixed-precision SpMV kernel and a low-overhead in-loop runtime. Across 47 SPD matrices from eight scientific domains, EvoCG is the fastest solver overall, with geometric-mean speedups of 2.52x, 3.06x, 2.48x, 1.93x, and 6.99x over cuSPARSE, PETSc, Ginkgo, Mille-FP64, and Mille-Mixed. On the same substrate, it improves time-to-solution over EvoCG-FP64 by 1.28x at only 11.4% more iterations and 1.09% overhead, with FP64-recomputed final true-residual norms nearly identical to those of FP64, and extends to Jacobi-preconditioned CG without retraining, yielding a further 1.15x geometric-mean speedup over EvoCG-FP64.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted in the ACM SIGPLAN Symposium on Principles and Practice of Parallel Programming (PPoPP'27)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: ELMoE-3D: Leveraging Intrinsic Elasticity of MoE for Hybrid-Bonding-Enabled Self-Speculative Decoding in On-Premises Serving
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become the dominant architecture for large-scale language models, yet on-premises serving remains fundamentally memory-bound as batching turns sparse per-token compute into dense memory activation. Memory-centric architectures (PIM, NMP) improve bandwidth but leave compute underutilized under MoE's low arithmetic intensity on high batch sizes. Speculative decoding (SD) trades idle compute for fewer target invocations, yet verification must load experts even for rejected tokens, severely limiting its benefit in MoE especially on low batch sizes. We propose ELMoE-3D, a hybrid-bonding (HB)-based HW-SW co-designed framework that unifies cache-based acceleration and speculative decoding to offer overall speedup across batch sizes. We identify two intrinsic elasticity axes of MoE---expert and bit---and jointly scale them to construct Elastic Self-Speculative Decoding (Elastic-SD), which serves as both an expert cache and a strongly aligned self-draft model accelerated by high HB bandwidth. Our LSB-augmented bit-sliced architecture exploits inherent redundancy in bit-slice representations to natively support bit-nested execution. On our 3D-stacked hardware, ELMoE-3D achieves an average $6.6\times$ speedup and $4.4\times$ energy efficiency gain over naive MoE serving on xPU across batch sizes 1--16, and delivers $2.2\times$ speedup and $1.4\times$ energy efficiency gain over prior accelerator baselines.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA) 2027

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Minimizing Bottleneck Overload Risk in Online Edge Task Placement under Workload Uncertainty
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: In edge computing, tasks must be placed on servers of finite capacity before workloads are realized, often with only workload means and variances known. An assignment balanced on expected load can still leave a server with more fluctuations than its residual capacity can absorb. Per-server risk constraints can enforce a prescribed overload tolerance but do not distinguish the assignments that meet it by how close the riskiest server comes to the limit. We show that, for independent tasks, placement preserves a period's total variance and total residual capacity, and decides only how fluctuation, measured by standard deviation, is paired with residual capacity across servers. The risk ratio, the ratio of fluctuation to residual capacity, parameterizes a server's worst-case overload probability over all aggregate workload distributions with given mean and variance. We minimize the largest risk ratio, attained at the risk bottleneck. Risk-Bottleneck Placement (RBP) places tasks in descending order of standard deviation, each on the server with the smallest post-assignment risk ratio, and refines the assignment with relocations and swaps within a finite per-period online budget. On small instances solved exactly by enumerating every assignment, minimizing the maximum expected utilization leaves the largest risk ratio 25.66-29.19% above its exact minimum on average, even with risk-minimizing tie-breaking, and the corresponding gap for RBP is 1.77-2.64%. In trace-derived multi-period simulations at two workload pressures, RBP reduces the worst-server overload probability by 26.0% and 18.0% relative to the best baseline and remains the lowest at every tested pressure and scale.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: LiquidCP: Decoupling Attention Tasks from Communication and Kernel Boundaries in Context Parallelism
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Context parallelism (CP) partitions long sequences across GPUs for LLM training and inference. For variable-length training and full prefill, attention-balanced placement can leave token loads uneven, while ring execution repeats overhead at each computation and communication step. In stage-serialized decode CP (DCP), long-running tasks delay dependent work and leave substantial GPU hardware idle. We propose LiquidCP, which unifies training and inference through a common model of Transfer, Compute, and Reduction tasks with tile-level dependencies, decoupling attention tasks from communication and kernel boundaries. For training and full prefill, MegaRing incorporates BuddyRing placement to balance attention and token loads, and coalesces ready KV regions during forward attention to amortize overhead. For decoding and mixed batches, MegaDCP selects history-KV splits by jointly modeling the completion of attention and its dependent reductions. A shared persistent GPU-resident engine executes both designs. Compared with the fastest baseline per configuration on eight H100 GPUs, MegaRing achieves geometric-mean core-attention speedups of $1.23\times$ forward and $1.18\times$ backward, and accelerates a Transformer layer by $1.08$--$1.16\times$. MegaDCP achieves geometric-mean core-attention speedups of $1.20\times$ for decode-only and $1.35\times$ for mixed batches. In vLLM serving with KV prefix cache, it achieves an average time-to-first-token speedup of $1.22\times$.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Beyond Compression Ratio: High-Throughput KV Compression for Disaggregated LLM Serving
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary:
KV cache compression reduces the communication volume of disaggregated large language model serving, but its practical benefit depends not only on compression ratio and model quality, but also on how efficiently the compression pipeline executes. This requirement becomes increasingly important as modern serving systems adopt high-bandwidth interconnects, where inefficient compression can offset a substantial portion of the saved communication time.
  This paper presents \system, a high-throughput KV cache compression data path built on top of \kvserve. \system improves compression execution in two complementary ways. First, it fuses the distribution transformation and low-bit quantization stages into a KV-aware \tilelang kernel, eliminating intermediate tensor materialization and redundant memory accesses. Second, it replaces the original lossless compression backend with an open, extensible, and searchable backend based on \lc, enabling high-performance compression operator pipelines. The fused kernel achieves up to $5.9\times$ speedup, while the new lossless backend increases compression throughput from below 90~GB/s to over 500~GB/s. Across the evaluated workloads, \system reduces job completion time by up to $2.04\times$. End-to-end evaluation shows that these optimizations allow KV compression to retain meaningful communication benefits under modern high-bandwidth network.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Accepted by The 22nd Annual IFIP International Conference on Network and Parallel Computing (NPC 2026)

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Reasoning about Shared-Qubit Concurrency in Quantum Computing
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: In this paper, we develop a semantic model for the parallel execution of quantum circuits, providing a formal foundation for studying shared-qubit concurrency in quantum computing. As in classical shared-memory concurrency, parallel quantum circuits may interfere with one another through operations on shared qubits. However, quantum entanglement and the noncommutativity of quantum operations introduce additional challenges for reasoning about their correctness. To address these challenges, we generalise the classical Owicki-Gries method to quantum computing at the level of quantum circuits. Our approach enables compositional reasoning about parallel quantum circuits by separating the verification of individual components from the analysis of interference between them. We formulate proof rules for establishing the correctness of parallel quantum circuits and prove their soundness with respect to the proposed semantic model.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: InfiniLoRA: Disaggregated Multi-LoRA Serving for Large Language Models
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: LoRA enables efficient customization of LLMs and is widely used in multi-tenant and multi-task serving. However, emerging model architectures such as MoE significantly increase LoRA memory cost, making existing coupled LoRA serving designs poorly scalable and prone to tail-latency inflation. We present InfiniLoRA, a disaggregated LoRA serving system that decouples LoRA execution from base-model inference. InfiniLoRA introduces a shared LoRA Server with parallelism-aware execution, SLO-driven provisioning, and critical-path optimizations, including GPU-initiated communication and hardware-specialized LoRA kernels. Experiments show that InfiniLoRA can achieve an average $3.05\times$ increase in serviceable request rate under strict latency SLOs, and improve the percentage of LoRA adapters satisfying the SLO requirement by 54.0\%.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 16 pages. SIGOPS ATC 2026 camera-ready version with a revised manuscript and updated author list. Shixuan Sun is the corresponding author

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: GC-MoE: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with FP8/FP4 Grouped GEMM via CUDA Green Contexts
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Under expert parallelism, mixture-of-experts (MoE) layers pay all-to-all token dispatch, grouped GEMMs, and a combine step in every layer. In decode each rank holds only 1-256 tokens: dispatch latency and weight traffic dominate while tensor-core utilization is inherently low. In fused operators such as DeepGEMM's Mega MoE, dispatch and computation overlap only by sharing every SM: dispatch warps compete with TMA/MMA and epilogue warps for registers, shared memory, and issue slots; every phase shares one CTA resource budget, synchronization spans the whole SM array, and every replay ends with a workspace-clean pass and a cross-rank barrier. We present GC-MoE, an open-source FP8/FP4 MoE inference operator for NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that uses CUDA Green Contexts to split the device into a small communication partition and a large compute partition. Each role gets its own kernel, resource budget, and synchronization domain, so dispatch and GEMM tune independently. A three-node CUDA Graph (four on Hopper with fused shared experts) launches the dispatch and grouped-GEMM kernels as concurrent roots; a token-ring handshake starts computation on the first filled ring blocks, and double-buffered receive counters remove the trailing cross-rank barrier between replays. The compute partition runs operand-swapped tcgen05 block-scaled MMA on Blackwell and register-A WGMMA with in-register FP4 decoding on Hopper, with fused SwiGLU, requantization, and optional shared experts. On 8 H20 GPUs GC-MoE accelerates DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode by 1.188x on average on both the routed and shared-expert suites (peaks 1.296x and 1.353x); on 8 B300 GPUs it accelerates GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.106x (1.123x with fused shared experts, peak 1.209x), beating Mega MoE at all 54 measured points at matched accuracy. GC-MoE reserves only 20 of 148 SMs on B300 for dispatch.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: When the Consumer Is an Agent: Execution-Grounded Service-Level Agreements
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act as service consumers. They select operations and report whether a task is complete. In an asynchronous distributed service, an accepted call or immediate state read does not establish that the required state became observable by its deadline. We introduce execution-grounded completion contracts, which treat completion as a service-level outcome. An independent control plane observes a deadline-bound service-state predicate, admits completion, and directs recovery while the agent performs the task. We evaluate placement and deletion in a live multi-provider data service with heterogeneous models and an injected transfer delay. Across policies, some tasks that missed the deadline were accepted and some that met it were rejected. Under enforcement, accepted completions remained consistent with later observations; all included healthy tasks completed, and unresolved faulted tasks terminated as unverified. The results show that completion of these tasks can be governed by independent observation of service state rather than by the agent's self-assessment.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 22 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for the 24th International Conference on Service-Oriented Computing (ICSOC 2026), Springer LNCS. Followed by the companion artifact paper, accepted in the ICSOC 2026 Artifact Evaluation track. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23000442

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: PhotonZip: Lifecycle-Aware Compression for HDF5-Based Synchrotron Workflows
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Synchrotron detectors generate data at rates that challenge storage and I/O systems. Compression can reduce data movement, but codec-only measurements do not capture the end-to-end behavior of HDF5 workflows. We present PhotonZip, a lifecycle-aware compression framework that tests candidate modes through a common HDF5 path and selects among eligible measured configurations according to either compression ratio or round-trip throughput. Its modular filters preserve standard HDF5 access when the required plugin is available. Across four beamline-derived datasets, PhotonZip reaches lossless compression ratios up to 1.629$\times$ and HDF5 write throughput up to 3.40GB/s write and 7.75GB/s read. The throughput-oriented configuration achieves 1.529$\times$ lossless data reduction while improving HDF5 write and read throughput by 21.2\% and 15.0\%, respectively. Lossy preview modes provide up to 16$\times$ data reduction and reduce preview latency by up to 8.35~s in the evaluated file-per-rank HDF5 configuration.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables, accepted by IFIP NPC 2026

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: LoopKV: Loop-Aware KV Cache Compression for Serving Looped Transformers
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Looped transformers apply a shared block several times per token to improve accuracy without adding parameters. For models such as Ouro that keep a separate key-value (KV) cache per loop, cache memory limits the batch size that amortizes repeated weight reads. Uniform-bit quantization and fixed rules per loop do not allocate precision according to each layer's sensitivity in each loop. Measurements on Ouro show that quantization sensitivity varies across (loop, layer) cells, and the sum of individual cell damages approximates the overall output damage. Sharing damage also varies by cell, with later loops generally tolerating sharing better. Skipping low-attention values to save reads produces errors that compound across loops. LoopKV uses a one-time offline profile to choose 4-bit storage, 2-bit storage or reuse of the final loop's KV for each cell. The planner minimizes reads under budgets for predicted damage and storage. During decoding, each loop reads the high 2 bits of each 4-bit value and fetches the low bits only where its own attention weights require 4-bit precision. A single fused kernel in vLLM executes the plan. Serving Ouro-1.4B on one RTX PRO 6000, the memory-optimized LoopKV-M plan stores 35% less KV than uniform 4-bit quantization (KIVI-4) on the same fused kernel and CUDA graph. It sustains 1.7-2.2x KIVI-4's goodput under a latency service-level objective with a 16K-token maximum length. None of its averages on six public benchmarks falls significantly below BF16's.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: The Agent Board: Kanban for Machines; Durable Coordination for Agents That Outlive the Conversation
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Harnesses for large language models have converged on a single-threaded shape: one agent, one history, one machine, one sitting. That shape fails work that spans many agents, outlives any one model call, or waits on systems that are not agents. We describe the Agent Board, the coordination substrate in the Corvic harness. The board is a durable, shared table of semi-semantic tasks: a few exact fields the system routes on, and a free-form body that only language models read. Agents post tasks, watch tasks, and block on them, ending their turn and holding no process until a matching post wakes them. A system agent, the Board Keeper, acts as the interrupt handler for the board: it carries events from non-agent parts of the harness onto the board, matches them to waiting tasks by reading their prose, and allocates new agents for tasks that name a kind of agent rather than an instance. Loadable coordination policy kernels give statuses and roles meaning for a given pattern of work, without the board enforcing them. The design mirrors the kanban board a human team puts on a wall. We argue it is what persistent agent products such as Meta Muse, OpenAI dots and SpaceXAI Grok Bot need once an agent must wait, hand off work, or work with agents from another vendor. We view the board as an operating-system scheduler for agents and state where the analogy breaks. We separate what the mechanism guarantees from what it leaves to convention, and report a trace from a live board and three small simulated pilots. In the pilots, the wait cost of the board was flat in wait length while naive polling grew about 165-fold, but a plain external watcher was cheaper than the board. The Board Keeper matched prose waiters with no false wakes but missed 3.6 percent of real wakes.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Ekka: Automated Diagnosis of Silent Errors in LLM Inference
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: LLM serving frameworks are quickly evolving with a complex software stack and a vast number of optimizations. The rapid development process can introduce silent errors where output quality silently degrades without any explicit error signals. Diagnosing silent errors is notoriously difficult due to the substantial semantic gap between the high-level symptoms and the low-level root causes. We observe that diagnosis of silent errors can be effectively framed as a differential debugging problem by leveraging the existence of semantically correct reference implementations. We propose Ekka, an automated diagnosis system that identifies root causes by systematically aligning and comparing intermediate execution states between a target and a reference framework. We constructed a benchmark of real-world silent errors from popular serving frameworks, where Ekka shows 80% pass@1 diagnosis accuracy and 88% pass@5 diagnosis accuracy, outperforming state-of-the-art systems. Ekka also diagnoses 4 new silent errors from serving frameworks, all of which have been confirmed by the developers.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Energy-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Reinforcement learning for language models alternates between generating responses and training the policy. These stages place different demands on GPUs, creating opportunities to reduce clock frequency with little loss in throughput. Selecting frequencies online is difficult because response lengths change and frequency trials themselves consume time and energy. We present EE-RL (energy-efficient RL), an online controller that selects separate frequencies for generation and training during RL execution. It compares candidate settings with a prediction of the default GPU governor on the same token workload, and keeps the most energy-efficient setting that meets a throughput threshold. The controller then monitors throughput and energy and adjusts frequencies as the workload changes. Fixed-frequency sweeps on H100 and GB200 show GPU energy savings of up to 28.2% per valid training token across synchronous and asynchronous execution, while largely preserving throughput. EE-RL turns this headroom into online savings, reducing GPU energy per valid training token by up to 16.9% at a modest throughput cost.
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.comment: Rahul and Nitin are co-first authors

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: RESHPart: Feedback-Reshaped Spectral Embedding for Hypergraph Partitioning
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: With scalable Laplacian solvers now available, the next frontier is to exploit them more effectively for high-quality hypergraph partitioning. In this work, we revisit spectral hypergraph partitioning from the perspective of spectral embedding geometry. Through a systematic analysis of circuit hypergraphs and controlled synthetic (hyper)graphs, we identify a ray-like embedding structure that helps explain the effectiveness of projection-based partitioning. We further show that the geometry of spectral embeddings can be systematically influenced through Laplacian design and hyperedge reweighting. Guided by these insights, we propose FRESHPart, a feedback-reshaped spectral partitioning framework that refines the spectral embedding through Geometry Feedback and Search Feedback, producing embeddings that are better aligned with projection-based partitioning. On the Titan23 benchmark, FRESHPart achieves average cut reductions over hMETIS of 13.09% at $ε=2\%$ and 25.21% at $ε=20\%$, surpassing the strongest previously reported results (12.16% and 22.53%, respectively), while completing every benchmark in under 120 s on a single GPU.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Runway Characters: Serving a 57B Video Diffusion Transformer for Real-Time Conversation
Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.summary: Conversational video characters must generate video as fast as it plays, for one user at a time: at 24 fps, a sustained 166.7 ms per four-frame chunk at batch size one, with only a few chunks of buffering. We describe the system behind Runway Characters, which serves a $\approx$57B-parameter autoregressive video diffusion transformer (four denoising passes per chunk) at 704$\times$1088 and 24 fps on four H100 GPUs with a voice agent in the loop. Each chunk takes 240 attention calls, each reading a 5,788-slot KV cache in which only 757 tokens are new, and 29% of the original step was whole-cache work repeated in every call. We move that work to write time (a ring cache, RoPE and FP8 quantization applied once per write, and a delta rotation when positions reset), fuse the tensor-parallel all-reduce into the FP8 GEMM with in-switch reduction, and give the decoder that turns latents into video frames its own GPU. Without the fused kernel, our optimizations cut the diffusion step from 240.9 to 159.3 ms (1.51$\times$, 24.5 fps sustained) with no detected degradation in lip-sync scores; the fused kernel, rolled back once in production and since re-enabled, reaches 147.4 ms (1.63$\times$, 43% of FP8 peak). In seven weeks of production the worker averaged above 23.5 fps in 99.5% of sessions that streamed for at least a second, and our pipeline takes 0.49 s of a 2.1 s median conversational turn. On the same GPUs, the two open-source real-time video systems we benchmarked, at four denoising passes, miss real time or add over a second of latency (one by estimate), at a third to half of our resolution.

Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Compu.title: Easy Multi-Precision Acceleration via Vectorization
