The semantic stream is controlled by Motion-Grounded Semantic Conditioning, which replaces purely linguistic word embeddings with motion-language representations to provide motion-aligned semantic priors for long-tailed lexical triggers of gestures. The beat stream is further regularised by an Inertial Beat Prior, an anthropometry-weighted arm-chain module that reduces jitter and improves rhythmic consistency without constraining semantic frames. Objective evaluations and subjective experiments show that DuoGesture outperforms strong baselines, while component ablations confirm the complementary roles of semantic grounding, stochastic stream selection, and biomechanical regularisation. We encourage readers to view our demos and qualitative illustrations, which are available on the project page: https://ferdinandpaar.github.io/DuoGesture/.

Sound.title: Rel2Traj: Inter-Source Relation-Aware Trajectory Generation for Text-To-Spatial-Audio
Sound.summary: "A car drives from front left to front right while a dog follows it." Such a description specifies no particular trajectory, yet imposes a constraint on the joint motion of both sources that must hold at every frame. Existing text-to-spatial-audio methods can position and move each sound source according to its description, but none of them ensures or verifies that such inter-source relations hold. We therefore propose Rel2Traj, which parses the description into sources, relations, and anchors, jointly generates the trajectories of all sources using a relation-conditioned diffusion model, and finally renders sounds from a pretrained text-to-audio model along these trajectories to produce binaural audio. For training and evaluation, we construct a synthetic dataset from a controlled language of source motions and inter-source relations. A single frame-wise relational geometry defines both our evaluation metric, the Relation Satisfaction Rate (RSR), and an auxiliary training loss. On motion-relation combinations held out from training, Rel2Traj maintains all relation types, whereas every baseline fails on at least one. A listening test further confirms that listeners recognize the described relations. To our knowledge, this is the first text-to-spatial-audio work to model relations among moving sources as explicit geometric constraints.
Sound.comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027

Sound.title: GSLM2: Multi-Stream Speech Representation Learning and Generative Spoken Language Modeling
Sound.summary: Generative spoken language models (SLMs) offer a route to learning linguistic structure purely from speech, yet they lag far behind text-based models in both capability and data scaling efficiency. We identify two bottlenecks underlying this gap: the limited linguistic quality of existing speech units and the reliance on a single stream of discrete units to represent speech. Multiple codebooks are widely used to encode acoustic features but rarely to represent speech semantics. We present GSLM2, which learns and models complementary properties of speech at multiple levels of abstraction. Its encoder, SpidR 2.0, uses self-supervised learning with differentiable prediction heads to induce high-quality discrete units at multiple levels. A multi-stream SLM then jointly models these units using a shared temporal backbone, stream-specific predictors, and an autoregressive head that captures cross-stream dependencies. Across training data sizes and model scales, up to 6M hours and 6.5B parameters, GSLM2 consistently improves linguistic competence while scaling more efficiently with data. As a result, it substantially narrows the gap between spoken and text-based LMs; across read and conversational speech domains, we shrink the gap by about two orders of magnitude on sWuggy, sBLIMP, and tSC, while also outperforming competitive speech-text systems on all three tasks. We open-source the training code and model checkpoints at https://github.com/facebookresearch/gslm2.
Sound.comment: Equal contribution by Yosuke Higuchi and Tom Fizycki. Core contribution by Mahi Luthra, Charles-Éric Saint-James and Azeez Syed

Sound.title: Sub-Band Spectral Matching with Localized Score Aggregation for Robust Anomalous Sound Detection
Sound.summary: Detecting subtle deviations in noisy acoustic environments is central to anomalous sound detection (ASD). A common training-free ASD pipeline temporally pools frame-level representations into a band-preserving feature vector and scores anomalies using a single nearest-neighbor match. However, this global matching can inflate normal-score variance through two effects. First, when normal sounds exhibit band-wise variability, a single global neighbor forces all bands to share the same reference, increasing band-level mismatch. Second, cosine-based matching is energy-coupled, allowing a few high-energy bands to dominate score computation under normal energy fluctuations and further increase variance. We propose BEAM, which stores temporally pooled sub-band vectors in a memory bank, retrieves neighbors per sub-band, and uniformly aggregates scores to reduce normal-score variability and improve discriminability. We further introduce a parameter-free adaptive fusion to better handle diverse temporal dynamics in sub-band responses. Experiments on multiple DCASE Task 2 benchmarks show strong performance without task-specific training, robustness to noise and domain shifts, and complementary gains when combined with encoder fine-tuning.
Sound.comment: Accepted at IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing (TASLPRO)

Sound.title: Microphone Geometry Aware Regional Target Speaker Extraction
Sound.summary: Regional target speaker extraction (RSE) aims to extract speech originating from a specified angular region, relaxing the requirement for precise target speaker location when performing location based speech extraction. However, existing RSE methods typically assume a fixed microphone array configuration and microphone number, limiting their applicability to unseen microphone geometries and varying numbers of microphones. In this work, we propose a geometry-aware RSE framework capable of extract with varying microphone array geometry and microphone numbers. Specifically, we introduce an attention-based multichannel front-end to encode inter-microphone phase information, together with a spatial audio reconstruction-based auxiliary objective to improve the front-end spatial representations quality. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves SI-SDRi by 5.1 dB over geometry-aware baselines across microphone arrays with four-microphones, while maintaining a performance gap of less than 0.6 dB compared with a tetrahedral geometry-specific baseline when evaluated on the tetrahedral microphone array.

Sound.title: ResMamba: A Dual-Path Convolution-Mamba Model for Music Genre Classification
Sound.summary: Music genre classification remains a fundamental yet challenging task in music information retrieval, requiring models that capture local time--frequency patterns and long-range temporal dependencies. To address this, we propose ResMamba, a hybrid architecture that augments a ResNet-style four-stage backbone with Mamba blocks. Building upon the selective structured state space sequence model, ResMamba first adapts the selective SSM into a 4D-compatible residual Mamba block that captures global dependencies at linear complexity. We then design the ConvMamba dual-path block, which combines this adapted Mamba branch with a parallel convolutional branch through a learned $1\times1$ fusion, jointly modeling global sequential context and local spectro-temporal patterns. Furthermore, we adopt a multi-scale fusion head that aggregates hierarchical representations across all four stages. Experiments on the GTZAN dataset demonstrate that our full ResMamba model achieves a 5-fold cross-validation accuracy of $88.99\% \pm 1.58\%$, surpassing the strongest published method in our comparison (88.64\%). All models are trained from scratch without any pretraining, external data, or data augmentation. Beyond GTZAN, ResMamba also generalizes to the larger FMA benchmarks under the same training protocol, attaining $64.52\% \pm 1.88\%$ on FMA-Small under 10-fold cross-validation --- the best published from-scratch result --- and $65.75\%$ on FMA-Medium under the official artist-level split, surpassing the widely cited SVM baseline of Defferrard \textit{et al.} (63\%).

Sound.title: 8 Bits to End the Loudness War: Lossless Floating-Point Compression for Audio Streams
Sound.summary: We present a native extension to the Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC) providing lossless compression for IEEE 754 single-precision (binary32) floating-point audio, alongside a survey and empirical benchmark of existing floating-point compression methods. While professional recording hardware increasingly adopts 32-bit float converters and digital audio workstations process sound exclusively in floating-point math, consumer distribution remains constrained to fixed-point integer PCM. Through Dynamic Positional Alignment (DPA), our implementation achieves approximately 44.1% compression ratios on natural multi-stage ADC recordings--matching the storage footprint of standard 24-bit integer FLAC--and approximately 60.2% on complex digital workstation masters. By preserving dynamic peaks beyond 0 dBFS, the format also allows listeners to undo clipping, providing a practical technical path away from the loudness war with virtually no storage overhead. We do not claim to introduce a fundamentally new compression paradigm; our approach is conceptually similar to the floating-point mechanism in WavPack (which remains undocumented in published literature). Instead, this paper compares existing methods, provides theoretical grounding for why they succeed or fail, benchmarks current codec implementations, and contributes a reference implementation of a proven method within the FLAC ecosystem.
Sound.comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables. Source code, Internet-Draft specification, and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/aliheidary1381/flac-with-float-coding

Sound.title: Learning Timeline-Preserving Speech-to-Speech Translation
Sound.summary: Speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) increasingly preserves what is said and how it sounds, but not necessarily when speech and silence occur. For dubbing and other temporally grounded applications, matching total duration is not enough: speech and pauses must also occur at corresponding moments. We formulate timeline-preserving S2ST, which aims to preserve the source endpoint and salient internal pauses on a shared absolute timeline. We present TransDubber, an end-to-end autoregressive system that learns this temporal structure directly from aligned target waveforms, without inference-time frame-level timing control or post-hoc temporal correction. To provide this supervision, we construct 642K exactly duration-matched English-Chinese speech pairs by translating and synthesizing target speech on source-defined temporal scaffolds. Training combines a progressive supervised curriculum with verifier-guided reinforcement learning to balance translation quality and temporal alignment. On a 4,353-utterance test set spanning read and spontaneous speech, TransDubber increases the proportion of translations within 2% of the source duration from 25.6% to 61.5% and pause-alignment F1 from 0.118 to 0.550 compared with UniSS, while maintaining competitive translation quality. Our analysis shows that aligned supervision establishes timeline following, while reinforcement learning refines temporal precision and partially offsets the translation-quality cost of strict synchronization. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of our data and training framework for timeline-preserving S2ST. Audio samples, code, datasets, and pretrained models are available at https://zhishengzheng.com/transdubber/.

Sound.title: Text-to-music Generation via Structured Captions AND Interpretable Evaluation
Sound.summary: Text descriptions of music are central to the performance of text-to-music generation (TTM) methods, but creation of paired text information for music generation is relatively under explored. Here, we propose training latent diffusion/flow-based music generation models conditioned on structured captions (SCAPs) and compare with typical free-form captions via a set of controlled ablations. We compare free-form vs. structured captions, partial vs. full information coverage, and global vs. temporal text information during training, by fine-tuning different configurations of a pretrained flow-based diffusion transformer (DiT) and using a multi-stage inference-time prompt rewriter. Further, we introduce a new text-alignment evaluation protocol inspired by Davidsonian Scene Graphs (DSGs) for a fine-grained, interpretable measure of faithfulness of TTM methods. With multiple metrics, we show 1) that fine-tuning our DiT on SCAPs significantly improves text-alignment on music generation outputs while also improving quality, and 2) our proposed Music DSG metric better correlates with human preference than CLAP.

Sound.title: Spatial DJ: Spatial Audio Control for Arbitrary Loudspeaker Layouts
Sound.summary: Object-based spatial audio promises render-anywhere playback, yet deploying it in a new venue still requires two tasks that are rarely addressed together: acquiring the physical loudspeaker geometry and enabling creators manipulate spatial audio while listening through the target loudspeaker system rather than a headphone proxy. We present Spatial DJ, a system for on-site loudspeaker layout acquisition and real-time spatial audio rendering and control, using head-worn AR in a coordinate frame aligned to the physical loudspeakers. In an 18-loudspeaker room, we evaluate calibration accuracy, repeatability, and control latency, and conduct an 18-participant listener study comparing diffuse and orbiting point-source rendering configurations applied to vocal and instrumental layers. Orbiting point-source conditions received higher ratings of perceived immersion, energy, and novelty than the diffuse baseline. Beyond this controlled setting, four representative deployments illustrate reuse of the same system across heterogeneous loudspeaker venues.

Sound.title: VoxServe: Streaming-Centric Serving System for Speech Language Models
Sound.summary: Speech Language Models (SpeechLMs) are increasingly deployed for streaming speech generation, where audio playback must start quickly and never stall. Serving them requires running two very different model components on the same system. An autoregressive LLM backbone emits audio tokens, and a codec converts chunks of those tokens into waveforms. Existing systems run the two as separately scheduled stages, and therefore either serialize them, let them interfere, or strand capacity by placing them on separate devices. We observe that overlapping the backbone and the codec on separate parts of the GPU raises throughput. Although this increases codec latency, most chunks can tolerate it, as long as it neither lies on the critical path of time-to-first-audio (TTFA) nor causes a playback stall. Based on this insight, we present VoxServe, a SpeechLM serving system that allocates GPU resources according to the urgency of chunks. VoxServe executes work on three asynchronous lanes. The LM lane runs the backbone on a large partition of the GPU's streaming multiprocessors, the background codec lane runs on a small partition beside it, and the urgent lane uses the whole GPU. The scheduler queues each request to the LM lane and routes every chunk the backbone completes by its urgency. A request's first chunk and chunks close to their playback deadline go to the urgent lane, and the rest are batched on the background lane. On Qwen3-TTS, VoxServe sustains 1.5x the request rate of the best existing system at a 200ms TTFA target without playback stalls. The code of VoxServe is available at https://github.com/vox-serve/vox-serve.
Sound.comment: The code is available at https://github.com/vox-serve/vox-serve

Sound.title: Paediatric-HGNN: A Hybrid Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Detecting Disfluency in Children's Speech via Multiscale Acoustic Fusion
Sound.summary: Automated stuttering detection (ASD) systems struggle with paediatric speech due to high acoustic variability in developing voices and the subtle distinction between pathological stuttering and typical developmental disfluencies. We introduce Paediatric-HGNN, a framework using a Context-aware Part-whole Interaction Network (CaPIN) tailored for paediatric data. Instead of conventional 1D signal modelling, our approach builds a heterogeneous graph capturing hierarchical relationships between lexical units (word nodes) and fine-grained acoustic segments (frame nodes). Trained on curated paediatric corpora (UCLASS and FluencyBank), Paediatric-HGNN achieves 82.4% weighted accuracy and a Typical Disfluency F1-score of 0.386. Modelling hierarchical lexical-acoustic interactions captures developmental "searching" behaviour, offering a more robust and interpretable tool for early clinical intervention.

Systems and Control.title: Lifted Schrödinger Bridges for Gaussian Mixture Endpoints: Projection Gaps and Path-Space Obstructions
Systems and Control.summary: We study stochastic density control between Gaussian-mixture endpoint distributions under Brownian prior dynamics. Since the direct Schrödinger bridge between Gaussian mixtures is generally not available in closed form, we introduce a lifted path-space construction in which each trajectory is augmented with a source--target component label. Consequently, the problem decomposes into Gaussian component-to-component Schrödinger bridges with explicit marginal, drift, and cost formulas, while the mixture-level assignment reduces to a finite-dimensional entropic coupling problem with a Sinkhorn scaling form. We then analyze the projection obtained by discarding or forgetting the label. By construction, the projected law satisfies the original Gaussian-mixture endpoint constraints, but its relative entropy generally differs from the lifted relative entropy by a nonnegative conditional label-information gap. This gap reveals a path-space obstruction: the lifted optimizer cannot, in general, be identified with the direct unlabeled Schrödinger bridge after projection. We also derive the posterior-averaged Markov drift associated with the projected marginal flow, prove a kinetic-energy upper bound, and identify a common path-potential condition under which the projection gap vanishes. Several numerical illustrations showing density and shape control are recorded for a self-contained exposition.
Systems and Control.comment: 37 pages; revised version of a journal submission with a new section on duality certificates

Systems and Control.title: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
Systems and Control.summary: There has been increasing interest in methodologies that incorporate physics priors into neural network architectures to enhance their modeling capabilities. Among these methodologies, Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs) and their variants have gained considerable attention. These architectures explicitly encode Hamiltonian mechanics both in their structure and loss function, resulting in desirable properties and additional modeled information. A crucial limitation of HNNs is their reliance on data on the target system's generalized momenta. This severely hampers their applicability when the analytical form of the generalized momenta is unknown, which frequently is the case in real-world applications. The goal of the present work is to develop a general extension of Hamiltonian-based architectures that addresses this issue by simultaneously learning the system's generalized momenta, Hamiltonian structure, and dynamics from data. The proposed architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytical form is unknown, and only (potentially non-sequential) data on the state and its derivatives is available. A dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum, and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints are considered as canonical examples to assess the performance of the proposed architecture.

Systems and Control.title: Singular Perturbations for Control Systems Safety
Systems and Control.summary: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) offer a powerful theory for enforcing safety in dynamical systems. Yet, applying this framework to complex systems is challenging when subsystems are feedback-interconnected and operate at different timescales. Such structures arise naturally in multiphysics systems and in control architectures where physical plants interact with optimization, estimation, and control algorithms. In many of these settings, safety involves only part of the system, motivating the design of reduced-order certificates. Inspired by singular perturbation theory, we establish sufficient conditions, involving separation between slow and fast dynamics, under which a reduced-order safety certificate can be lifted to the full interconnected system. Specifically, we construct a composite CBF ensuring forward invariance of a lifted subset of the original safe set. We also show that the certified safe set expands monotonically as the tuning parameter accelerating the fast dynamics is reduced. Numerical results validate the approach on two robotic systems: a planar 2-DoF manipulator with motor dynamics and a 6-DoF UR10e manipulator controlled by a suboptimal optimization algorithm.

Systems and Control.title: Sub Terahertz LEO Satellite Communication: Is Doppler Shift a Major Challenge?
Systems and Control.summary: In this work, we investigate the impact of Doppler frequency shift on sub-terahertz low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications using OFDM transmission. To comprehensively evaluate the severity of the Doppler shift impact on sub-terahertz satellite-to-ground links, we first put together an evaluation framework that jointly accounts for major Doppler-induced and non-Doppler-induced signal impairments in such systems. We then compare and contrast three possible engineering approaches to deal with Doppler shift in such a communication system. Our study concludes that (i)~while just ignoring the Doppler effect in such high-frequency and high-mobility systems substantially compromises the performance and reliability, (ii)~most of the negative effects can be eliminated by implementing only a small set of low-complexity measures. We particularly show that even a single Doppler shift estimation over a 5-min-long satellite pass over the ground user location may be sufficient to ensure high performance throughout the entire connectivity period. Hence, while Doppler shift is an important effect to account for in sub-terahertz LEO satellite communications, it should not constitute a critical design challenge for these emerging systems.

Systems and Control.title: Differentiable Iterative Learning Control for Black-Box Position-Commanded Manipulators
Systems and Control.summary: High-accuracy repetitive tracking is challenging for position-commanded manipulators whose low-level controllers are inaccessible, while constrained model-based iterative learning control (ILC) can require substantial manual parameter tuning. We present Differentiable Iterative Learning Control (Diff-ILC), an online bilevel framework that adapts the parameters of a constrained ILC update between physical robot executions. A closed-loop differential model is identified once from paired smooth perturbations and subsequently kept fixed. At each trial, a constrained quadratic program computes a feasible command correction, while a real-anchored next-trial prediction defines a task-level objective. Hypergradients are obtained by implicitly differentiating the locally active KKT system, enabling multiple computational parameter updates without additional robot executions. Experiments on a 6-DoF DOBOT CR3 across unseen planar and three-dimensional trajectories show substantially faster physical-trial convergence than fixed-parameter model-based ILC. Across the four primary trajectories, after only two trial-to-trial updates, Diff-ILC achieves 78.8% and 76.4% lower mean joint-vector and Cartesian RMSE, respectively, than fixed-parameter model-based ILC.

Systems and Control.title: Ranking the Parameters Shaping Grid Dynamics
Systems and Control.summary: Generator and transmission line parameters do not shape the time-domain behavior of a power system equally; a parameter that dominates one dynamic property can be almost invisible to another. This paper studies how the physical parameters of a detailed and general nonlinear differential algebraic equation (DAE) grid model shape the properties that decide whether system states such as frequencies, voltages, and angles can be inferred, observed, controlled, and kept stable. The rankings are conditional as they depend on where grid sensors and actuators sit, on the operating region and the disturbance, on the network topology, and on other settings that the operator chooses. The framework combines DAE trajectory sensitivities, variational Gramians, and stability margin sensitivities to measure how much each parameter reshapes the network dynamics. On three benchmark systems, the rankings show where dynamic leverage concentrates and where the control-theoretic metrics disagree, and they point to how parameter studies can guide calibration, sensor and actuator placement, and security assessment. The proposed methods herein are also scalable and can be tested on grids with tens of thousands of buses.

Systems and Control.title: Co-design of Output-Feedback Neural Network Control Barrier Functions and Observers for Stochastic Jump-Diffusion Systems
Systems and Control.summary: In this paper, we present a framework for designing controllers for partially observed continuous-time stochastic systems. We use the notion of control barrier functions (CBF) and provide an upper bound to the probability of state trajectories violating the system's safety when starting in an initial region. Our framework co-designs a neural network-based controller, an output-feedback observer, and a control barrier function for the given system. Although CBF requires full state information, we formulate CBF conditions over an augmented state space of actual and observer states. We train the neural networks simultaneously by defining appropriate loss functions, and finally demonstrate the effectiveness through two case studies: a linear DC motor and a nonlinear system.

Systems and Control.title: Reduced Order Observers for Monocular Visual Inertial Odometry
Systems and Control.summary: This work develops a reduced order observer framework of monocular visual-inertial odometry (VIO). The key idea consists in considering the gravity vector in the body-frame as an additional state and constructing an appropriate output that relates the monocular bearing measurements and their time derivatives to the body-frame velocity. This eliminates the need for the estimation of the landmark positions, leading to a six-dimensional linear time-varying (LTV) observer for the body-frame velocity and gravity, endowed with uniform global exponential stability guarantees. These estimates are subsequently used to recover the orientation almost globally, up to an unknown constant yaw offset, and the position up to an unknown constant translation. The mixed-bearing framework is further extended to account for the inertial measurement unit (IMU) biases, yielding a twelve-dimensional LTV observer endowed with local exponential stability guarantees. Numerical simulations are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed observers.

Multiagent Systems.title: DRO: A Python Library for Distributionally Robust Optimization in Machine Learning
Multiagent Systems.summary: We introduce dro, an open-source Python library for distributionally robust optimization (DRO) for regression and classification problems. The library implements 15 DRO formulations and 9 backbone models, enabling 85 distinct DRO methods. Furthermore, dro is compatible with both scikit-learn and PyTorch through a unified interface, and uses approximation techniques to reduce runtime for some computationally demanding formulations. Comprehensive documentation is available at https://python-dro.org.

Multiagent Systems.title: Streaming Right Multiplication over Grammar-Compressed Matrices: A Memory-Bounded GPU Engine for Genotype and Graph Data
Multiagent Systems.summary: Grammar-compressed matrices store a matrix's non-zero structure as a RePair straight-line program (SLP), supporting matrix-vector products in time and space proportional to the compressed size. We target the regime where this is decisive on a GPU: when the uncompressed matrix exceeds device memory, so footprint (not floating-point throughput) is the binding constraint. Our SLP is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of out-degree 2, and the right product $y=Mx$ is a single bottom-up sweep (leaves to roots): a conflict-free gather. We make the grammar properly layered (every nonterminal child one level below its parent) via pass-through completion, which inserts identity nodes to carry values upward until consumed. This yields a streaming evaluation in which each level reads only the level below and writes the next, so the live set fits in two alternating read-only/write-only buffers instead of scaling with the whole grammar. On genotype matrices, where a polygenic score is exactly the right product $y=Gβ$, a CUDA implementation shows a clear space advantage: a device footprint 3.5 to 8 times smaller than a materialized cuSPARSE CSR baseline, single-vector times within a small factor of cuSPARSE, and consistently lower GPU energy. Because the sweep needs only an associative and commutative combine, the same engine evaluates any homomorphism into a commutative monoid over the grammar by swapping a small leaf/combine/emit policy; the same reachability sweep scales to a billion-edge Software Heritage graph (261 TB dense, 21 times smaller serialized than cuSPARSE's CSR). We frame this as an algorithm-engineering case study: structural metrics (depth, live-set width, completion cost) are measured, architecture-independent grammar properties, whereas time and energy are profiled on a single board.
Multiagent Systems.comment: Accepted at ALENEX 2027 (SIAM Symposium on Algorithm Engineering and Experiments). 16 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Artifact evaluated (Availability and Reproducibility badges). Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23139248; data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22677747

Databases.title: Speculative Ad-hoc Querying
Databases.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) invite substantial effort and investment, yet agentic systems can spend much of their time waiting for tools. This paper explores how a small auxiliary LLM can reduce these waits by speculatively preparing a database while the primary LLM reasons.
  The challenge is that the auxiliary model must anticipate the primary model's actions before the primary model takes them. Our key insight is that database systems give the speculator a structural advantage: it need not predict the exact next query. Instead, it can prepare work shared by many plausible queries. Predicting query shapes enables advance compilation, predicting data access warms caches, and predicting broader data requirements enables precomputation of superset results that subsequent queries can refine.
  We present Wonder, a system that exploits this advantage for analytical SQL workloads. Wonder constructs reusable superset queries, materializes their components, and rewrites subsequent queries against the resulting temporary tables. Its scheduler prioritizes foreground queries while using reasoning intervals for speculative preparation. The same engine supports humans writing SQL, using incomplete queries to guide speculation and displaying intermediate results as they type.
  In a replay-based evaluation of agent workflows, Wonder reduces SQL execution time by up to 31.8% and combined primary-agent reasoning and active SQL time by up to 22.6%, with approximately 6% higher recorded main-agent and prediction API cost and 10% more read I/O on the full dataset. A separate 24-participant study finds significantly lower query latency on both analytical tasks and improved time-to-answer on one, with 87.5% of participants reporting increased productivity.

Databases.title: N2E: A General Framework to Reduce Node-Differential Privacy to Edge-Differential Privacy for Graph Analytics
Databases.summary: Differential privacy (DP) has been widely adopted to protect sensitive information in graph analytics. While edge-DP, which protects privacy at the edge level, has been extensively studied, node-DP, offering stronger protection for entire nodes and their incident edges, remains largely underexplored due to its technical challenges. A natural way to bridge this gap is to develop a general framework for reducing node-DP graph analytical tasks to edge-DP ones, enabling the reuse of existing edge-DP mechanisms. A straightforward solution based on group privacy divides the privacy budget by a given degree upper bound, but this leads to poor utility when the bound is set conservatively large to accommodate worst-case inputs. To address this, we propose node-to-edge (N2E), a general framework that reduces any node-DP graph analytical task to an edge-DP one, with the error dependency on the graph's true maximum degree. N2E incorporates two main techniques: a distance-preserving clipping mechanism that bounds edge distance between neighboring graphs after clipping, and the first node-DP mechanism for maximum degree approximation, enabling tight, privacy-preserving clipping thresholds. By instantiating N2E with existing edge-DP mechanisms, we obtain the first node-DP solutions for tasks such as maximum degree estimation. For edge counting, our method theoretically matches the error of the state-of-the-art, which is provably optimal, and significantly outperforms existing approaches for degree distribution estimation. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework achieves up to a 2.5x reduction in error for edge counting and up to an 80x reduction for degree distribution estimation.

Databases.title: Self-Refining Prompt Induction for Streaming Text-to-SQL
Databases.summary: Text-to-SQL assistants for streaming engines must handle dialect-specific types, windowing rules, and temporal semantics, including constructs poorly handled by generic prompts. We present Self-Refining Prompt Induction (SRPI), an offline method that converts generation failures into reusable dialect instructions while keeping model weights fixed. A Refiner revises the Generator's prompt using reference-conditioned feedback from three LLM judges; a sampled regression guard checks earlier successes, and a separate Compressor reduces prompt length. Inference uses the frozen prompt without retrieval or query repair. We evaluate cross-domain and cross-model transfer on Confluent Cloud Flink SQL using a controlled synthetic workload seeded by 30 expert-written examples, with 335 induction examples and 257 questions from held-out domains. The same induced prompt improves mean judge scores across seven Generators by 7.1-19.2 percentage points, including an increase from 85.3% to 97.5% for the induction model. A separate compression study reduces prompt length by 52.7% with a 0.19-percentage-point score decrease. An assistant using the induced prompt is in early access, with initial user feedback to inform subsequent refinement.

Databases.title: NovaFilter - A Rule-Based ETL Staging Framework for Fault-Tolerant Relational Databases
Databases.summary: NovaFilter is a completely new approach to deriving structured relational data from heterogeneous input data in different data formats. It combines consistency checks, rule-based data transformation, and a human-in-the-loop example discussion. Using these three components, NovaFilter stores all transformation knowledge in an explicit rule base, which is continuously expanded through the example discussion with the user. The resulting data transformation process is deterministic, transparent, and reusable. As a result, the method can replace conventional ETL scripts and offers a completely new strategy for transforming data between different data models and schemas. Its main advantage is that users without programming skills (e.g. domain experts) can answer the example discussion and thus it is a building block for democratization of ETL script developement.

Databases.title: DistOptimize: Automatic Optimization of Distributed Protocols
Databases.summary: Distributed consensus and consistency protocols are difficult to reason about yet foundational to the cloud; as such, they often undergo a rigorous proof and formal verification process before deployment. The same level of rigor is rarely applied to protocol modifications, which occur frequently in production and threaten to compromise safety. In this paper, we introduce DistOptimize, an automatic optimizer for distributed protocols that uses well-known optimization techniques to modify existing protocols without the risk of safety violations. DistOptimize adapts throughput optimizations from academic languages to frameworks used in production, verifying the correctness of the rewrites in Rocq and automating their application through a combination of calibration and ILP-based search space navigation. Applied to both fundamental distributed protocols and protocols used at AWS, DistOptimize improves throughput by up to 4x while increasing latency by at most 0.3ms.

Databases.title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics
Databases.summary: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.

Databases.title: One Success Isn't Reliability: Thinkingbox, a Sandbox and Benchmark for Agents in Stateful Business Workflows
Databases.summary: Recent agent benchmarks increasingly ground evaluation in executable environments, from code repair to web navigation, app APIs, and function calling. Yet completing consequential work beyond code requires more than producing a plausible response or valid tool call: agents must gather missing information over multiple turns, follow domain policies, coordinate dependent tools, and realize the correct persistent state transition without collateral effects. In this paper, we introduce Thinkingbox, a sandbox for tool-agent-user interaction that provides isolated MCP-compatible tool sessions, complete execution traces, and outcome evaluation over terminal backend state. Built on this sandbox, Thinkingbox-bench contains 507 policy-conditioned workflows across business scenarios, including retail, hospitality, auto insurance, neobank internal IT, and consulting IT/HR support. Each attempt is evaluated by task-specific executable checks that accept valid trajectories while rejecting wrong, missing, or extra effects; designated tasks additionally check required properties of the final response. Our experiments reveal that even the strongest proprietary and open-weight models show steep reliability drops: Claude Opus 5 falls from 66.50% pass@1 to 47.53% pass^20, and Kimi-K3 from 57.37% pass@1 to 17.60% pass^20. Moreover, many failed trials terminate cleanly after valid state-changing actions, so response- or tool-call-level signals poorly proxy end-to-end completion. Thinkingbox-bench reveals a large gap between occasionally finding a successful trajectory and reliably completing stateful business tasks. We release Thinkingbox, Thinkingbox-Bench, and Thinkingbox-integrated reinforcement learning framework.

Emerging Technologies.title: Starfield: Demand-Aware Satellite Topology Design for Low-Earth Orbit Mega Constellations
Emerging Technologies.summary: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) mega-constellations are emerging as high-capacity backbones for next-generation Internet. Deployment of laser terminals enables high-bandwidth, low-latency inter-satellite links (ISLs); however, their limited number, slow acquisition, and instability make forming a stable satellite topology difficult. Existing patterns like +Grid and Motif ignore regional traffic, ground station placement, and constellation geometry. Given sparse population distribution on Earth and the isolation of rural areas, traffic patterns are inherently non-uniform, providing an opportunity to orient inter-satellite links (ISLs) according to these traffic patterns. In this paper, we propose Starfield, a novel demand-aware satellite topology design heuristic algorithm supported by mathematical analysis. We first formulate a vector field on the constellation's shell according to traffic flows and define a corresponding Riemannian metric on the spherical manifold of the shell. The metric, combined with the spatial geometry, is used to assign a distance to each potential ISL, which we then aggregate over all demand flows to generate a score for each satellite's link selection. Inspired by +Grid, each satellite selects the link with the minimum Riemannian distance along with its corresponding angular links. To evaluate Starfield, we developed a custom, link-aware, and link-configurable packet-level simulator, comparing it against LAMP, +Grid, Motif, and Random topologies. For the Phase 1 Starlink, simulation results show up to a 30% reduction in hop count and a 15% improvement in stretch factor across multiple traffic distributions. Moreover, static Starfield, an inter-orbital link matching modification of Starfield, achieves a 15% improvement in stretch factor under realistic traffic patterns compared to +Grid. Experiments demonstrate Starfield's robustness under traffic demand perturbations.

Emerging Technologies.title: Who Audits Whom, on What Substrate, with What Evidence? An Independence-Graded Audit Protocol for Agentic AI
Emerging Technologies.summary: Agentic AI systems plan, invoke tools, and act with limited supervision; they are now both the subject of audits and, increasingly, the auditor. Independence-the foundation of assurance-is still applied to them as a binary. We argue that it must be graded along three orthogonal axes: principal independence (who controls the auditor), substrate independence (an auditor that shares the auditee's foundation-model family, toolchain, or guardrails fails with the auditee), and evidence independence (whether evidence is attestable rather than self-reported). Each axis has precedent; the contribution is to grade all three on a single audit, aggregate them by the weakest link, and apply the same rubric when the auditor is itself an agent. We give the model a formal basis by transplanting the beta-factor model of common-cause failure from reliability engineering. We also provide a seven-step protocol whose outputs a third party can verify, a structural detectability analysis of a procurement-controls agent audited at three grades, and a closed-form study of the model in which, at a declared common-mode share of 0.90 for a same-family auditor and a declared reporting probability of 0.6 for an internal team, a conventional internal audit of an agent-a real audit team, a second agent, and provider logs-surfaces 5.9% of the faults it could in principle see and, independently of those two values, none at all in half of the fault classes. Because an evidence grade says who could have altered a record, not what the record covers, every load-bearing record also carries a declared-scope predicate, and reports carry a false-flag rate beside the detection floor wherever the auditor's own performance has been measured. We map the triple to the EU AI Act as amended, ISO-IEC 42006, UK public-sector risk-management guidance, and audit-regulator practice.

Emerging Technologies.title: Enhancing Edge AI System Security with a Stacked Hardware Security Controller for Robust and Energy-Efficient Anomaly Detectio
Emerging Technologies.summary: In recent years, the growing adoption of Edge AI systems has been accompanied by a surge in security threats. Edge AI deployments face an rapidly evolving spectrum of security threats, from side-channel information leakage to ad- versarial model manipulation and physical device tampering. Conventional security mechanisms such as malware scanners and resource-intensive firewall solutions are unsuitable due to edge AIs typically limited computational resources, strict energy budgets and thermal constraints especially in battery-powered and field-deployed environments. This paper proposes a stacked, hardware-based security mechanism that enables low-overhead, continuous detection of anomalous execution patterns. Anomaly detection utilizing hard- ware performance counters and physical sensors outperforms software-based alternatives by providing key capabilities such as tamper-resistant root-of-trust isolation, negligible runtime overhead, and resilience against compromised operating systems. Experimental analysis shows that adversarial or malicious ap- plications produce observable deviations in sensor and thermal readings on Edge AI systems and hardware-based anomaly detection provides effective and low-overhead anomaly detection.

Emerging Technologies.title: Side-Channel Attack Prevention for Post Quantum Cryptography Algorithms: A 3D-Shield Approach
Emerging Technologies.summary: Despite their theoretical quantum attack resistance, practical implementations of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms remain susceptible to side-channel attacks. This includes all standard algorithms selected the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) such as Kyber/ML-KEM, Dilithium/ML-DSA, Falcon/FN-DSA and SPHINCS+/SLH-DSA. This paper proposes an alternative defense for side-channel resilience based on 3D integration that uses 3D hardware to shield the underlying cryptographic activity by introducing decoy keys and physical shielding through stacking. The proposed approach can complement other security measures (such as masking and shuffling) on protecting Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) that move computation to dedicated NTT chips. We outline the construction of our approach and validate the effectiveness on a generic attack targeting intermediate computation inside an NTT butterfly.

Emerging Technologies.title: Can Agentic AI Undermine Its Own Assurance Loop? Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance for Cognitive Network Digital Twins
Emerging Technologies.summary: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Network Digital Twins (NDTs) are increasingly combined to form Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) that translate operational intents into network changes and support closed-loop management. However, a network change may achieve its intended objective while disrupting the monitoring or recovery mechanisms needed for subsequent decisions. For example, a service may be rerouted while its latency-monitoring traffic continues along the original path, producing measurements that no longer reflect the service's performance. We propose Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance (CLDA), an assurance mechanism that augments agentic AI-enabled NDTs with dependency-aware validation. In our framework, an agentic AI planner generates and refines network plans, while the NDT evaluates the projected network outcomes of these plans. CLDA extends this analysis using a Loop Dependency Graph (LDG) that connects service requirements to monitoring mechanisms, forwarding paths, failure domains, and recovery prerequisites. CLDA projects candidate actions onto these dependencies, checks intermediate states of multistep plans, and supports deterministic make-before-break repairs using temporary monitoring mechanisms. Unlike the Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner, CLDA uses explicit, deterministic rules for assurance decisions and repair. We evaluate CLDA through controlled reconfigurations, a 240-trial LLM-based planning campaign, and live network execution. A separate synthetic study examines deterministic assurance scalability across network models representing up to 1,024 routers.

Emerging Technologies.title: Machine-Learned Compact Subspace Generation for Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction within Density Matrix Embedding Framework
Emerging Technologies.summary: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), an extension of quantum selected configuration interaction (QSCI), is a promising hybrid quantum-classical paradigm for molecular ground-state energies. By replacing variational optimization with quantum sampling, QSCI avoids barren plateaus and directly reconstructs correlated wavefunctions. However, existing configuration recovery mainly enforces symmetry constraints without targeting the most physically relevant configurations, often yielding oversized subspaces and costly classical diagonalization. We introduce QSCI-RBM, a compact subspace generation protocol based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), and integrate it within Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET). The RBM learns the distribution of dominant determinants from hardware samples, generating high-probability configurations. Sampling was performed on IBM Heron R1 (\texttt{ibm\_torino}) for CH$_5$NO, R2 (\texttt{ibm\_fez}) for C$_2$H$_4$, and R3 (\texttt{ibm\_boston}) for the larger H$_2$O benchmark and the protein-ligand system. After validating on these benchmarks of increasing active-space size, we simulate the inhibitor Carmofur bound to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (M\textsuperscript{pro}), fragmented into ten DMET impurities. Both DMET-QSCI-RBM and a DMET-SQD baseline reach chemical-potential self-consistency within four $μ$-iterations. At the converged chemical potential, DMET-QSCI-RBM lies within $0.05\,\mathrm{mHa}$ of DMET-FCI while accessing on average only $0.22\%$ of the symmetry-preserving configuration space, versus $0.55\,\mathrm{mHa}$ at $33.0\%$ for DMET-SQD, leading to a $\sim$153-fold subspace reduction. RBM-assisted expansion thus yields far more compact hardware-derived determinant spaces at equal or better accuracy, reducing classical overhead for scalable quantum embedding of biological systems on real hardware.

Emerging Technologies.title: Online Bayesian Calibration under Gradual and Abrupt System Changes
Emerging Technologies.summary: Bayesian model calibration is central to digital twins and computer experiments, as it aligns model outputs with field observations by estimating calibration parameters and correcting systematic model bias. Classical Bayesian calibration introduces latent parameters and a discrepancy function to capture bias, but suffers from parameter-discrepancy confounding and is typically formulated as an offline procedure under a stationary data-generating assumption. These limitations are restrictive in modern digital twin applications, where systems evolve over time and may exhibit both gradual drift and abrupt regime shifts. While data assimilation methods enable sequential updates, they generally do not explicitly model systematic bias and are not robust to abrupt changes. We propose Bayesian Recursive Projected Calibration (BRPC), an online Bayesian calibration framework for streaming data under simulator mismatch and nonstationarity. BRPC extends projected calibration to the online setting through a two-stage filtering procedure: first, unconditional filtering of the calibration parameters, followed by conditional filtering of the model discrepancy function given the estimated calibration parameters, which mitigates parameter--discrepancy confounding, while the online filtering enables bias-aware adaptation under gradual system evolution. To handle abrupt changes, we integrate BRPC with restart mechanisms that detect regime shifts and reset the calibration process, yielding a unified approach to mixed nonstationarity. We provide theoretical analysis, including a tracking error bound of the model discrepancy estimate under gradual evolution, given accurate calibration parameter estimates and false-alarm and detection behavior of restart mechanisms. Empirical results on synthetic and plant-simulation benchmarks demonstrate BRPC outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Same Words, Different Judgments: How Preferences Vary Across Modalities
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) is the dominant framework for aligning AI systems to human preferences. However, evaluation protocols for such data were designed for text and have not been validated for speech. We present the first intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)-based, controlled cross-modal study of human and synthetic preference annotations, comparing text and audio evaluations of identical semantic content across 100 prompts. We show that achieving \textit{good} (audio) to \textit{near good} (text) agreement within either modality (ICC(2,$k$) $\approx$ .81 audio, .74 text) requires $\sim$9 raters and modalities show marked differences in how people report preferences: audio raters exhibit narrower decision thresholds, reduced length bias, and more user-oriented evaluation criteria, with near-chance cross-modality agreement. We demonstrate that synthetic ratings can be used to effectively predict inter-rater agreement, thus serving as an early signal for stimulus selection and proxy for human annotations. Together, these findings argue that evaluation protocols for audio preference data require modality-specific design rather than direct adaptation from text. Code, data, and the audio corpus are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sciminds/same-words-different-judgements
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. I examine how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations. Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under a large language model (LLM) measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjustment for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages reduces the composite association. The adjusted confidence intervals include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion also changes what the combined Dull score conveys. These comparisons show how item groupings and occupational characteristics shape the interpretation of exposure estimates. Occupational profiles offer a starting point for selecting contrasting research settings. Establishing desired automation or realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Frame-Level View and Image-Quality Annotation Tool for Fetal Echocardiography: Comparison with Spreadsheet Annotation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Objective: To develop the Cardiologist Annotation Tool (CAT) for frame-level cardiac view and image-quality annotation in fetal echocardiography and compare it with spreadsheet-based annotation.
  Methods: CAT provides cine playback, frame navigation, and keyboard-based labeling without manual frame-range entry. Experts annotated 25 studies using both methods, and spreadsheet annotations were audited for predefined data-entry errors. In a randomized crossover study, six medical students annotated two normal studies, one with each method, against an expert reference.
  Results: Among 1,746 spreadsheet-annotated files, 6.2% contained major or critical data-entry errors, more frequently in congenital heart disease than normal studies (10.9% vs 3.4%). CAT yielded more annotated view segments per clip (3.6 vs 1.5). Rates of labeled and correctly labeled frames per minute were 1.77 and 1.68 times those with spreadsheets, respectively (both P = 0.031), with gains in all six students. No detectable difference in view-label accuracy was observed.
  Conclusion: CAT eliminates manual frame-range entry and enables finer-grained, structured annotation of fetal echocardiography, providing a practical approach to preparing datasets for AI research.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Using profiles of cognitive capability to assess AI suitability for workplace tasks
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Organisations deploying AI face a scoping problem: which tasks can be automated, which should remain with humans, and which are best shared between the two. Aggregate benchmark scores provide little insight into where systems will succeed or fail in practice, while human judgements of model capabilities quickly become outdated. We introduce a pipeline that profiles agents and tasks using a shared set of core cognitive capabilities. Cognitive capability profiling infers an agent's capabilities from performance on a benchmark battery annotated for the cognitive demands of each item. Task requirements weighting elicits from domain experts the relative importance of these same capabilities for their work. As both use a common set of cognitive dimensions, they can be updated independently as models and roles change, and combined to estimate AI suitability at the level of a domain, organisation, role, or individual duty. We validate capability recovery on synthetic agents, profile six AI systems, and elicit task requirements from 410 employees across six occupational domains. AI systems differed more across cognitive dimensions than across model families, while workplace activities converged on a shared cognitive core. The resulting scores provide a comparative scoping tool for identifying promising candidates for piloting and areas where current systems are unlikely to be well suited. We discuss extending the framework to profile human workers alongside AI systems, moving from AI suitability towards human-machine task allocation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Rethinking the UI of GenUI: A Tale of Two Designs
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Generative user interface (GenUI) tools use large models to create UI mockups from high-level descriptions; a recurring interaction paradigm starts with an unstructured prompt, followed by depth-first generation of a polished, high-fidelity prototype. To examine how it supports early-stage, 0-to-1 design exploration, we contrast this paradigm with structured input, breadth-first workflow, and low-fidelity generation. In our study, 24 industry professionals in early-stage product and UX design used a commercial GenUI system and our research prototype as study-era instances of each paradigm for a comparative evaluation. Findings show that 1) structured input surfaces key facets but raises entry barriers; 2) breadth-first workflow reveals more possibilities, but previewing multi-screen UX ideas remains hard; and 3) despite low fidelity's value, participants rated high fidelity as better suited to their design stage and to communicating ideas. Our findings contribute a model-agnostic, design-level account of how GenUI users specify intent, traverse alternatives, and interpret fidelity.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Go-Go-Go: the game of Go without turns
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
The study of variants of classic games has a long history, with chess alone inspiring countless variants that have been proposed, analyzed, and studied. The game of Go, despite rivaling chess in age, cultural relevance, popularity, and strategic depth, has seen drastically fewer variants.
  We introduce Go-Go-Go, a variant of the classic game of Go where there are no turns, and players play stones simultaneously and asynchronously on the board. The variant (which is to be played through a computer) includes a basic mechanism to avoid excessive spamming of moves, by imposing a minimal delay between moves that depends on their relative spatial distance. Apart from the lack of time discretization, most of the ruleset of the original game is either directly maintained or adapted in a natural way that preserves the original spirit. The first playtesting indicates that this results in the preservation of much of the emerging strategies and "flavor" of Go, while replacing the long strategic reasoning with fast paced, instinctive action fueled by quick reflexes. Play testers also report the need to balance immediate but suboptimal reactions with more reasoned but slower plays.
  We offer a publicly available, playable, OpenSource, and online reference implementation of Go-Go-Go at http://gogogo.di.unimi.it

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Smartphone-Aided VR Exergames for HIIT: Gamifying Fitness with Real-Time Pose Estimation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
This paper introduces an innovative virtual reality (VR) exergame system designed to gamify High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) workouts through 11 predefined combo moves, including squat-punch combinations, bilateral arm strikes, and diagonal stretch combos. Unlike conventional tracking methods that often rely on wearable motion capture suits or limited headset-based sensors, our system uses a standard smartphone camera placed on a tripod to capture full-body movement. This approach offers a cost-effective and scalable alternative, particularly well-suited to the fast, dynamic motions typical of HIIT routines.
  The smartphone footage is processed in real time using a pose estimation algorithm, with extracted biomechanical data analyzed by a backend server built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI models to structured data sources and tools, and a GPT-4o large language model. The system generates personalized assessments of form accuracy, movement efficiency, exercise intensity, and potential injury risks, tailored specifically to high-impact, time-sensitive exercises.
  A within-subject study involving 20 participants (ages 18-25) compared experiences in VR and Non-VR HIIT sessions. Results indicated significantly higher enjoyment (Mean = 3.5 vs 2.8, p = 0.02), improved immersion/focus (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.8, p = 0.03), and increased likelihood to recommend (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.7, p = 0.04) under the VR condition. Confidence to continue did not differ significantly between conditions (p = 0.15), while perceived intensity remained comparable. The MCP system showed strong agreement with expert evaluation (87.5%, N = 10 sessions, one certified trainer), supporting its reliability as a feedback tool.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: You Know What You Will Like: People Predict Their Own Ratings Better Than Recommender Systems
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Recommender systems usually learn what people want from what they have done. Platforms could also ask people directly, but asking is costly: 98.8% of the prompts in our data went unanswered. Theories of statistical prediction imply that a person's own forecast adds little to a recommender algorithm built from many people's behavior. Theories of dispersed knowledge imply that people hold information about their own taste that the data lack. We test the two with the MovieLens Beliefs dataset. In 2023-2024, a homepage prompt asked members how they expected to rate movies they said they had not seen. Of 26,020 such expectations, 551 from 277 members were followed by a rating at least a day later. We compare each expectation with four benchmarks: the platform's own predicted rating, two collaborative-filtering models (matrix factorization and an item neighborhood), and a stack trained on other members' outcomes. The trained models use each member's latest ratings. People predict their own ratings more accurately than all four benchmarks (correlation 0.69, against 0.34 for MovieLens and 0.54 to 0.59 for the trained recommenders). Added to all the machine forecasts and features, the expectation lowers out-of-sample mean squared error by 26%. The gain holds when models are trained on earlier expectations and tested on later ones. A member's earlier expectations about other movies do not replace the current one. In ordering a member's own movies, the trained recommenders are statistically indistinguishable from the person. On old, heavily rated movies, the machines do as well or better. The results reconcile the two theories: the crowd's data suffice where they are rich, and the person adds information about the specific item. We derive four design principles for preference elicitation and recommender evaluation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Working paper. 23 pages, 3 figures, 10 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Cognitive and Behavioural Effects of Haptic Feedback for ROV Teleoperation in Hazardous Environments
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Teleoperating a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) in complex underwater environments presents unique challenges. Dynamic, three dimensional obstacles and unseen water currents pose real risks to expensive robotic hardware in environments in which recovery can be next to impossible. This paper explores the cognitive effects of haptic feedback to improve vehicle safety in such environments. An in-water study is analysed with a ROV exposed to controlled cross-currents, with environmental information presented via a soft and vibrating haptic touchpad.
  Results demonstrate that while encountering an unseen cross-current significantly increases an operator's physical and temporal demand, the introduction of haptic feedback mitigates these factors and improves self-assessed performance. Interestingly, the haptic condition also produced the highest levels of mental demand and operator frustration. Despite this increased mental workload, operators drove the ROV significantly faster when receiving haptic cues compared to the current-only condition, indicating a higher level of user confidence. Ultimately, these findings suggest that while haptic feedback may initially require more cognitive processing to interpret unseen hazards, it successfully enhances operator awareness and promotes more confident navigation in hazardous environments.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted for IEEE Telepresence 2026

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Perceived Trust and Transparency in AI-Altered vs. Human-Written LinkedIn Posts
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: People increasingly draft a social media post themselves and then let an AI model refine it (AI-altered), a common but understudied middle case between fully human-written and fully AI-generated content. We ask whether this changes how trustworthy and transparent readers perceive the post to be, and whether they can even tell. We first analyze real ChatGPT conversations (WildChat) to find how people actually alter social media posts, which we use to design realistic alteration prompts. We then run a pre-registered, within-subjects online experiment (n=214) in which participants rate unlabeled human-written and AI-altered LinkedIn-style posts for perceived trustworthiness and transparency, and separately judge whether each post was AI-altered. We find that AI-alteration itself has no detectable effect on either perceived trustworthiness or transparency (both estimates near zero, not significant). At the same time, readers did not reliably detect AI-alteration (49\% accuracy, near chance) and defaulted to assuming human authorship when unsure. However, our analysis shows significant differences in transparency and trustworthiness ratings across the specific post, the AI model, as well as the prompt used to alter it. For instance, more detailed prompts raise both perceived trustworthiness and transparency but also make the alteration more detectable. Surprisingly, the prompt that shifted ratings most also asked the model to add one new idea absent from the original post: readers nonetheless rated this AI-invented, unverifiable content as more trustworthy and transparent.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Measuring the collaboration, not the agent
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Benchmarks for visualization agents score the agent alone; the human only supplies reference answers. For high-dimensional data this misses what matters: the knowledge of which variables count is held by on-site experts, not by the model, so the useful question is how well an analyst and an agent do together. We study one specific form of collaboration, the agent proposes a view, the analyst accepts, rejects, or modifies it, and those judgments are kept for later sessions, and propose five measures for it: complementarity, intervention efficiency, appropriate reliance, knowledge retention, and agency. The first four are computed from interaction logs alone. We test the measures, not people: in a testbed for parallel-coordinates design on public manufacturing data (UCI SECOM), with a simulated analyst whose behavior we control, all four are computable and respond to the controlled differences. Whether they reveal anything about real analysts is the next step; we release the testbed for it.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Embedding User Comments into Long-Form Reading: Design and Evaluation of Contextual Comment Presentation
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Online comments offer perspectives on long-form articles but are often separated from the passages they discuss, requiring readers to navigate back and forth and mentally reconstruct comment-text relationships. To preserve these relationships while maintaining reading continuity, we explored contextual comment presentation that makes comments locally accessible at the passages they address. We compared Text-End, Sentence-End, Between-Line, and Click-to-Show in a within-subject study with 24 participants using constructed comments and fixed sentence-level anchors. All three local layouts reduced initial-reading scrolling, with no significant condition effects on accuracy or elapsed task time. Sentence-End and Between-Line received higher comment-accessibility ratings than Text-End, while Click-to-Show received higher physical-demand ratings than Text-End and Sentence-End. Preferences remained distributed across all four layouts.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 29 pages, 11 figures, 7 tables

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Cracked Mirror: How People Perceive Gender Performance by Large Language Models
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: How do large language models (LLMs) perform gender under zero-shot prompting, and how do people interpret those performances in conversation? Drawing on gender performativity, we examine how gendered meanings emerge through generated language, conversational context and human interpretation. In a preregistered randomised online experiment, 1,060 participants each had five short conversations with an LLM. We used minimal prompts to elicit performances from "very masculine" to "very feminine" and asked participants to rate their partner's perceived gender after each conversation. Mean ratings shifted in the direction of the prompts, but ratings at the extremes were closer to the midpoint than the prompt labels implied. When prompted to perform as "neither masculine nor feminine", the models were perceived as slightly masculine on average. Ratings varied across models and conversation topics. Women and men gave similar ratings at the extremes, but women rated the models as more masculine across the intermediate prompt levels. Participants' explanations illustrate how they drew on writing style, emotional expression and conversational interests, sometimes questioning the stereotypes behind their judgements. These findings suggest that conversational AI acts as a cracked mirror of gender norms. Models reproduce recognisable cues, and people interpret and sometimes challenge the meanings those cues carry.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Preprint, under review; main article and supplementary material

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: At work, people develop skills through experience: novices acquire skills by completing tasks, while experts retain theirs through continued practice. AI assistance changes this process by offering workers a choice between solving tasks independently and accepting the AI's answers. While relying on AI saves immediate effort, it can also displace the practice needed to acquire and retain skills, including those required to oversee the AI. We extend an existing accept-or-solve model to a sequence of tasks in which workers' skills evolve through independent practice and reliance on AI. We compare myopic workers, who maximize immediate utility, with strategic workers, who also value their future skills. We show that novices can become trapped at low skill levels, while experts may lose skill, even as AI-assisted outcome accuracy remains high. Strategic workers, by contrast, may choose to solve independently even when AI is more accurate, recognizing the future value of acquiring and retaining their skills. We then study incentives that reward correct independent work and characterize the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention. We show that independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire sufficient skill, eliminating the need for continued incentives. Counterintuitively, supporting a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs, either by enabling self-sustaining independent work or by lowering the payments needed to maintain proficiency. Our findings thereby shift the focus from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations can sustain human expertise over time, and which skills are worth investing in.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 30 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Moritz Diener and Daniel Hendriks contributed equally

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Patients With Personality: Realistic Patient Simulation through Controlled Diversity and Selective Disclosure
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Realistic patient simulation is a key requirement for developing and testing clinical LLMs at scale without costly user studies. Existing simulators lack realism and controllability: they overshare information and miss the variability of real patient behavior. Here, we introduce PatientsWithPersonality (PWP), a patient simulation framework that generates realistic yet diverse patient responses through explicit personality parametrization over a latent patient state. Grounded in the six-dimensional HEXACO personality model, it gives fine-grained control over conversational style, cooperativeness, and information disclosure. We evaluate PWP in the first direct comparison of different patient simulators under a shared protocol, anchored in transcripts of real physician-patient encounters. Clinicians judge PWP conversations as realistic at least as often as the recorded encounters themselves and far more often than prior simulators, and almost never flag them as "too informative". Our simulator also reproduces the disclosure pacing of real patients, and its HEXACO-conditioned personality traits can be recovered by clinicians and an autorater. PWP further shows a substantially wider behavioral range than the closest baseline. In a downstream benchmark, LLMs interviewing patients simulated by PWP perform closest to how they perform on the real encounters, whereas prior simulators make the task easier. PWP thus provides a realistic, steerable, and diverse patient population for improving and benchmarking clinical LLMs.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted at Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026, Proceedings Track. 27 pages, 10 figures, 10 tables. Code: https://github.com/mo374z/PatientsWithPersonality

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Evaluating Human-LLM Alignment on Visualization Preference
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: There are often multiple valid visualizations, spanning different chart types, visual encodings, and aesthetic choices, that can all support a user's goal of analyzing a dataset. Determining which of these candidate visualizations is most appropriate, however, remains challenging. Prior work has leveraged expert-curated taxonomies to guide visualization design and subsequent quality evaluation, a practical evaluation model must also account for human-centric factors. Latest visualization tools integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate and refine visualizations, using LLM-as-a-judge to provide design feedback. Without a deeper understanding of whether, and in what ways, human and LLM perceptions of visualizations align, there is a real risk of deploying low-quality agents that do not reflect human judgment. We study this question through a pilot experiment - we formulate the problem as a preference task over curated chart pairs and compare the judgments of state-of-the-art vision models with those of a panel of human annotators. We establish a cautionary tale: such judges risk filtering out informative, compelling displays. We find that frontier models collapse human subjectivity, a rich signal that reveals contrasting design choices, into near-deterministic verdicts.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: IEEE VIS 2026 (VISxGenAI Workshop)

Human-Computer Interaction.title: A Graph-Based Conceptual Modeling Framework to Design for Human-Robot Coordination
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Studies of human-robot interaction in dynamic and unstructured environments show that as more advanced robotic capabilities are deployed, the need for cooperative competencies to support collaboration with human problem-holders increases. Designing human-robot systems to meet these demands requires an explicit understanding of the work functions and constraints that shape the feasibility of alternative joint work strategies.
